papers.title: Machine Unlearning
affiliations: University of Toronto
Vector Institute
University of Wisconsin-Madison
papers.venue: 42nd IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (IEEE S&P 2021)
papers.one_liner: SISA trains an ensemble of isolated models on disjoint data shards, checkpointed per slice, so deleting a point only retrains one partial model.
papers.summary: When users ask for their data to be deleted (GDPR's right to be forgotten), a trained model may still remember it. The only obviously correct fix, retraining from scratch without that data, is very expensive for deep networks. This paper proposes SISA training (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, Aggregated). The data is split into S disjoint shards, and one model is trained on each shard in complete isolation. Each shard is further split into R slices that are added to training one at a time, with the weights saved before each new slice. At test time the S models vote. To delete a point, only the model whose shard holds it is retrained, starting from the checkpoint saved just before that point's slice. The result is exactly as if the point had never been used. The authors define unlearning as matching the distribution of models trained without the point, explain why differential privacy cannot provide this, and derive the expected number of points to retrain for sequential and batched requests. Simple tasks see 4.63x (Purchase) and 2.45x (SVHN) speed-ups with under 2 points of accuracy lost. ImageNet gains only 1.36x with large accuracy loss, which transfer learning helps reduce. Knowing who is likely to request deletion enables distribution-aware sharding, which cuts the cost further.
papers.problem: Regulations such as the GDPR, CCPA and PIPEDA give individuals a right to have their data erased, and because ML models can memorize training data, erasure must also reach the trained models. Retraining from scratch gives a provable guarantee but is too expensive to repeat for every request on large DNNs. Prior unlearning methods were either limited to non-adaptive statistical-query learners, gave only probabilistic (DP-style) guarantees, or applied only to simple model classes.
papers.core_idea: Limit where each training point can have influence. Every point affects only one constituent model (shards trained in isolation), and within that model only the training stages after its slice was added (checkpointed slices). Unlearning then means retraining a small part of the pipeline from a saved state that never saw the point, which gives an exact, easy-to-explain guarantee at a fraction of the retraining cost. Predictions are recovered by aggregating the constituent models, for example with a majority vote.
papers.setting: centralized supervised learning (deep neural network classifiers trained with SGD); unlearning requests arrive sequentially or in batches; uniform or known non-uniform request distributions
contributions: A definition of unlearning (Def. III.1): the distribution of models obtained by training on D plus d_u and then unlearning d_u must equal the distribution obtained by training on D alone. The authors also argue why DP with epsilon > 0 cannot give this.

Six goals for an unlearning strategy: intelligibility, comparable accuracy, reduced unlearning time, provable guarantees, model-agnostic, and limited overhead. These are used to rule out strawman approaches (DP, certified removal, SQ-based unlearning, decremental learning).
SISA training: Sharding, Isolation, Slicing and Aggregation, which needs only small changes to existing pipelines.
Analytical expected retraining cost (number of points to retrain) for sharding and slicing, under sequential and batched processing of requests.
An epoch recalibration rule so that sliced training takes the same total time as unsliced training, with no loss in accuracy.

An empirical study on MNIST, Purchase, SVHN, CIFAR-100, ImageNet and Mini-ImageNet. For simple tasks SISA loses little accuracy. For complex tasks it loses much more, and transfer learning narrows the gap.
Distribution-aware sharding (Algorithm 1), which groups likely-to-be-deleted points into a few small shards when the provider knows the request distribution.
method_steps: Partition the training set D (size N) uniformly at random into S disjoint shards D_1..D_S, each of size about N/S, and record which shard and slice each point belongs to.
Partition each shard D_k uniformly into R disjoint slices D_k,1..D_k,R.

For each shard k, independently (no gradient or parameter sharing between shards), train the constituent model M_k incrementally. Step 1: start from a random initialization and train on D_k,1 for e_1 epochs, then save the parameters (M_k,1). Step i: continue from M_k,i-1 and train on the union D_k,1..D_k,i for e_i epochs, then save M_k,i. M_k = M_k,R.
Set the epochs per step so that total training time matches unsliced training. With e_i = e/R and e' the epochs without slicing, use e = 2R e'/(R+1) (Eq. 1).

At inference, feed the test input to all S constituent models and aggregate. Use a label majority vote by default, or average the post-softmax prediction vectors and take the argmax (better for complex tasks). The aggregator must not be trained on the training data.

When an unlearning request for d_u arrives, look up its shard k and slice r. Delete d_u, load the checkpoint M_k,r-1 (the saved state before slice r was introduced), and retrain steps r..R on the updated slices. Replace M_k with the new model. The other shards are untouched.
Optionally buffer K requests and process them as a batch. Retrain every affected shard, starting from the smallest affected slice index in that shard.

Optionally, when the distribution of deletion probabilities p(u) is known, use distribution-aware sharding (Algorithm 1). Sort points by p(u) and fill shards in that order, starting a new shard whenever the expected number of deletion requests in the current shard, E(chi_i) = n * mean p(u), reaches a constant C <= 1. This concentrates high-risk points in fewer, smaller shards.

key_definitions.name: Unlearning (Definition III.1)
key_definitions.plain: A training mechanism supports unlearning if training on the data plus a point and then unlearning that point produces exactly the same distribution of models as training without the point at all. Because training is random, it compares distributions of models, not individual parameter values.
key_definitions.formal: D' = D union {d_u}; D_M = distribution of models from mechanism M trained on D' then unlearning d_u; D_real = distribution of models from M trained on D; M facilitates unlearning iff D_M = D_real

key_definitions.name: Plausible deniability / certificate
key_definitions.plain: The provider must convince the user that the updated model could plausibly have been trained without their data. Here the evidence is the training algorithm itself (e.g. auditable SISA code), not a matching set of weights.
key_definitions.formal: M_not_du must be a sample from the distribution of models trained on D \ d_u

key_definitions.name: Why DP is not unlearning
key_definitions.plain: Epsilon-DP bounds how much any single point can change the model, but the bound is never zero, so a point still has a small influence. Unlearning needs zero influence, which would require epsilon = 0, and then the model could learn nothing from the data.
key_definitions.formal: unlearning requires epsilon = 0, which contradicts learnability (violates goal G2)

key_definitions.name: Shard
key_definitions.plain: A disjoint subset of the training data. Each shard gets its own constituent model, and each point belongs to exactly one shard.
key_definitions.formal: intersection_k D_k = empty, union_k D_k = D, |D_k| ~ N/S

key_definitions.name: Slice
key_definitions.plain: A disjoint piece of a shard. Slices are added to training one at a time, and the model is checkpointed before each new slice.
key_definitions.formal: intersection_i D_k,i = empty, union_i D_k,i = D_k

key_definitions.name: Constituent model
key_definitions.plain: One of the S replicas of the model, trained in isolation on a single shard.

key_definitions.name: Task complexity
key_definitions.plain: An informal notion based on input dimensionality, model depth or capacity, and the number of samples per class. MNIST, Purchase and SVHN count as simple; CIFAR-100, ImageNet and Mini-ImageNet count as complex.

key_definitions.name: Batch K baseline
key_definitions.plain: Buffer K unlearning requests, then retrain the whole model from scratch. This is the same as SISA with S = R = 1 in the batch setting.

key_definitions.name: 1/S fraction (lone shard) baseline
key_definitions.plain: Train a single model on a 1/S fraction of the data, discard the rest, and retrain only when a deleted point falls into that fraction.

key_definitions.name: Unlearning goals G1-G6
key_definitions.plain: G1 intelligibility, G2 comparable accuracy, G3 provably reduced unlearning time, G4 provable guarantees, G5 model-agnostic, G6 limited overhead.

theory.name: Eq. 1 (epoch recalibration for slicing)
theory.statement_plain: If each of the R slice-steps is trained for an equal share e_i = e/R of e total epochs, the work matches unsliced training on D = N/S points for e' epochs exactly when e = 2R e'/(R+1).
theory.assumptions: Training time depends only on the number of samples processed; each slice-step is trained equally long.
theory.significance: Lets sliced and unsliced models be compared at equal training time. Under this rule slicing showed no accuracy loss (Fig. 5).

theory.name: Best-case single-request speed-up
theory.statement_plain: For a single request, sharding gives an expected S times speed-up over full retraining, slicing gives a best-case speed-up of up to (R+1)/2, and the two combined give a best-case (R+1)S/2.
theory.assumptions: Uniform shards and slices; retraining time linear in the number of points; parallelism ignored.
theory.significance: The headline intuition for the design. Note it is a best case: the expected slicing gain under uniform requests (Eq. 4) is at most 1.5x.

theory.name: Eq. 2 (sequential sharding cost)
theory.statement_plain: With S uniform shards and K requests processed one at a time, the expected total number of points to retrain is E[C] = (N/S + 1/(2S) - 1) K - K^2/(2S). It is upper-bounded by N K / S, which is tight when K -> 0 and N/S >> 1, so doubling S halves the cost. As K -> N the quadratic term dominates.
theory.assumptions: Data shuffled and evenly split; each request hits any shard with probability 1/S; shard sizes stay roughly constant. Derived via binomial sums (App. D).
theory.significance: Closed-form cost model showing a linear gain in S for small K.

theory.name: Eq. 3 (batched sharding cost)
theory.statement_plain: If K requests are processed as one batch, the expected number of points to retrain is E[C] = N(1 - (1 - 1/S)^K) - K. For small K this is about N(1 - exp(-K/tau)) with tau = (-ln(1 - 1/S))^-1, and it approaches N - K as K grows. So the benefit of sharding disappears once K is comparable to S.
theory.assumptions: Shard index of each request i.i.d. uniform; the number of hits per shard is Binomial(K, 1/S) (App. E). The main text prints exp(K/tau), apparently a sign typo; App. I uses exp(-K/tau).
theory.significance: Explains the empirical rule that the gains vanish when K > 3S.

theory.name: Eq. 4 (sequential slicing cost)
theory.statement_plain: For one request landing uniformly in one of R slices of a shard with D points, the expected retraining work is E[C] = e'D(2/3 + 1/(3R)). With R = 1 this is e'D (no gain). As R -> infinity it tends to (2/3)e'D, so the expected speed-up from slicing alone is at most 1.5x.
theory.assumptions: Uniform requests; epoch recalibration from Eq. 1; points per slice D/R constant (gives an upper bound); App. F.
theory.significance: Slicing gives a modest but free speed-up, with diminishing returns (it plateaus for R > 20).

theory.name: Eq. 5 (batched slicing cost)
theory.statement_plain: For K batched requests within a shard, retraining starts from the smallest affected slice index r_min: E[C] = (2e'D/(R(R+1))) * (R(R+1)/2 - (E[r_min^2] - E[r_min])/2). The moments come from the expected minimum of n uniform draws, E[min] = (na+b)/(n+1) (App. G). When K >> R the cost is about e'D (no speed-up). For K << R there is a significant speed-up.
theory.assumptions: Requests are sampled uniformly with replacement (verified numerically to be harmless when K << N); App. H.
theory.significance: Shows slicing helps only when the batch is small relative to R.

theory.name: Lone-shard (1/S fraction) baseline cost (App. I)
theory.statement_plain: In the sequential setting the lone-shard baseline costs a factor 1/S of SISA's cost (Eq. 19), i.e. it is S times faster. In the batched setting E[C] = (N - K)/S.
theory.assumptions: Same as Eq. 2-3.
theory.significance: Training on less data is always faster to unlearn. The case for SISA rests on its much better accuracy, especially on complex tasks.

theory.name: Empirical linearity of training time
theory.statement_plain: Training time grows linearly with the number of training samples. This was measured on SVHN, Purchase and MNIST on an RTX 2080 Ti, 5 repetitions (Fig. 3).
theory.assumptions: Fixed hardware and software stack.
theory.significance: Justifies using the number of points to retrain as a hardware-independent proxy for unlearning time throughout the analysis.

papers.complexity: Training: the total cost equals that of a single model when slice epochs are recalibrated (Eq. 1). Shards could be trained in parallel, but the paper deliberately does not count this. Storage: R checkpoints per shard, O(SR) saved parameter states, linear in the number of slices. This is argued to be cheap (about $0.023-0.058/GB/month versus GPU rental at $0.25-0.90/hour), and checkpointing is already common practice. Hyperparameter tuning: O(SR) models in general, O(R) when shards are uniform and share hyperparameters. Unlearning one request: retrain one constituent on at most N/S points. Expected cost is roughly N K/S points for K sequential requests (Eq. 2), with an extra slicing factor of (2/3 + 1/(3R)) per request (Eq. 4). Batched cost is N(1-(1-1/S)^K) - K (Eq. 3). Inference: S constituent forward passes plus aggregation. This is not analyzed in the paper (my observation).

datasets: MNIST (60k, 28x28, 10 classes)
Purchase (250k, 600 features, 2 classes per Table I; curated following Shokri et al. from the top 600 purchased items)
SVHN (604,833, 32x32x3, 10 classes)
CIFAR-100 (60k, 100 classes; used for transfer learning)
ImageNet (1,281,167, 224x224x3, 1000 classes)
Mini-ImageNet (128,545, 224x224x3, 100 classes; supervised version)
models: MNIST: 2 conv + 2 FC layers
Purchase: 2 FC layers (MLP)
SVHN: Wide ResNet-1-1
CIFAR-100 / ImageNet / Mini-ImageNet: ResNet-50
baselines: Retrain from scratch / batch K baseline (SISA with S = R = 1)
1/S fraction (lone shard) baseline: train on only one shard's worth of data
metrics: Number of points to retrain (proxy for unlearning time)
headline_results: Purchase: 4.63x speed-up over retraining from scratch for 8 unlearning requests (about 0.003% of the data) with S = 20 shards and R = 50 slices, losing under 2 percentage points (PP) of accuracy.
SVHN: 2.45x speed-up for 18 requests (about 0.003%) with S = 20, R = 50, losing under 2 PP of accuracy.
ImageNet (ResNet-50): 1.36x speed-up for 39 requests with the same S and R, but a top-5 accuracy drop of 19.45 PP.
Mini-ImageNet: 8.01x speed-up for 4 requests, with a 16.7 PP accuracy drop (footnote 1).

ImageNet with label majority vote: average top-5 accuracy drop of 16.14 PP (batch K top-5 = 92.87%) and average top-1 drop of 18.76 PP (batch K top-1 = 76.15%). Averaging prediction vectors instead improves top-1 by 1.68 PP and top-5 by 4.37 PP, cutting the top-5 gap to 11.77 PP. The same pattern holds on Mini-ImageNet.
Transfer learning (ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet, transferred to CIFAR-100): at S = 10 the top-1 gap shrinks to about 4 PP and the top-5 gap to under 1 PP.
Simple tasks: more than 20 shards costs over 5 PP of accuracy, and more than K = 3S requests makes retraining time fall back to the batch K baseline.

Regime: sharding gives most of its benefit when the number of requests is below 0.075% of the dataset; with S fixed to 20, slicing helps only below 0.003%. Google's right-to-be-forgotten data (Bertram et al.) suggests real request rates are around 1e-6 of the dataset, and the paper says this is 3 orders of magnitude more requests than prior work handled.

Slicing does not reduce accuracy once epochs are recalibrated (Fig. 5, SVHN and Purchase). Combined speed-up at 0.003% requests grows almost proportionally with S, while extra slices give diminishing returns (Fig. 7, roughly 2x on SVHN and 4x on Purchase at S, R up to about 20; read from the figure).

Distribution-aware sharding (SVHN, three simulated countries with p = 3e-6, 3e-5, 6e-6 and data fractions 0.7717, 0.1001, 0.1282): creates 19 shards and lowers the expected number of points to retrain. Accuracy is 94.4% versus 95.7% for uniform sharding.
Aggregation choice barely matters on easy datasets (Purchase, SVHN). On ImageNet and Mini-ImageNet, averaging prediction vectors recovers noticeably more accuracy (Figs. 13-14).
Accuracy falls as the average number of samples per class per shard falls (Fig. 15).

limitations: Constituents are weak learners: accuracy drops sharply on complex tasks (ImageNet top-5 down by 16-19 PP), and even simple tasks lose more than 5 PP once S > 20.
Speed-ups exist only in a narrow regime (K < 3S; requests below 0.003-0.075% of the dataset). For larger K, SISA degrades to the cost of full retraining.
The cost analysis assumes requests are uniform and independent, shard and slice sizes stay constant, and retraining time is linear in the number of samples.
Slicing only works for stateful iterative learners such as SGD-trained models. It does not help greedy learners such as decision trees.
Slicing needs extra storage for O(SR) checkpoints, and hyperparameters may need re-tuning for sharded or sliced training (slices interact with batch size).

Distribution-aware sharding needs a precisely known and stationary request distribution. It produces shards of unequal size, which costs about 1.3 PP of accuracy under majority vote, and grouping users by deletion likelihood may harm fairness.
The provider is assumed honest. There is no way to verify externally that unlearning happened, only an audit of the code.
Learned aggregators (e.g. a mixture-of-experts style controller) would themselves need unlearning, so SISA is restricted to aggregation that does not use the training data.
Ensemble inference costs S forward passes and S models' worth of serving memory, which the paper does not discuss (my observation).
The best-case slicing speed-up of (R+1)/2 can be confused with the expected speed-up, which is at most 1.5x under uniform requests (Eq. 4) (my observation).

Minor inconsistencies in the text: the contributions claim about a 2 PP drop with transfer learning, but Sec. VII-C reports about 4 PP top-1 (and under 1 PP top-5) at S = 10. The text calls 95.7% vs 94.4% 'one percent point'. The asymptotic form of Eq. 3 is printed with exp(K/tau).
future_work: Aggregation strategies beyond majority vote that cope with imbalanced shard sizes (for distribution-aware sharding).
Data replication across shards to strengthen constituents, while limiting replication of points likely to be deleted.
Coreset selection, to cut learning and therefore unlearning cost.
Verifiable unlearning when the service provider is not trusted.
The ethical and fairness implications of grouping users by likelihood of deletion.
Better partitioning and aggregation for complex learning tasks; unlearning without isolation.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: SISA is the canonical exact-unlearning baseline that most later efficient-unlearning papers compare against or extend, so the student should be able to reproduce it, cost model included. Its closed-form expected retraining costs (Eqs. 2-5) are ready-made theory tools for analyzing any partition-based scheme, and its definition gives a clean way to argue exactness. The main pitfalls are the accuracy cost on complex tasks, the narrow regime where speed-ups exist (K < 3S), and its dependence on uniform request distributions. Each is a natural starting point for an improved algorithm. The shard/slice/checkpoint idea carries directly over to federated (clients as shards), continual (tasks as slices) and LoRA-based settings, which other papers in this collection explore.
open_questions: Design sharding schemes (class-balanced, clustering-based, or with deletion-aware replication) that keep constituent accuracy high on complex tasks without breaking exactness.
Develop aggregation rules for heterogeneous or imbalanced shards that are either independent of the training data or cheaply unlearnable themselves.
Build hybrid schemes that use exact SISA retraining for some requests and certified or approximate per-shard updates for others, and analyze the combined cost and guarantee.
Adapt distribution-aware sharding when the request distribution is unknown or drifts over time (online re-sharding), with fairness constraints across user groups.
Cut slicing's storage cost, e.g. by storing parameter-efficient (LoRA) deltas per slice, and extend the cost model to count storage and inference.
Find mechanisms that let a user verify or audit that SISA unlearning actually happened without trusting the provider.

papers.title: FairSISA: Ensemble Post-Processing to Improve Fairness of Unlearning in LLMs
affiliations: IBM Research
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Socially Responsible Language Modelling Research (SoLaR)
papers.one_liner: Shows SISA-trained language-model ensembles can be less fair (equalized odds) and fixes this with three Hardt-style post-processing variants, one provably optimal.
papers.summary: SISA is an exact unlearning method: it splits training data into S disjoint shards, trains one model per shard, and combines predictions by majority vote, so deleting a point only retrains one shard's model. This paper asks whether that efficiency costs fairness for language models. The authors fine-tune BERT, DistilGPT2 and GPT2 as toxic-text classifiers on HateXplain with S = 1, 3, 5, 7 shards. Fairness is measured with equalized odds (EO): the gap in true- and false-positive rates between posts that mention a sensitive topic (religion or race) and posts that do not. Accuracy drops steadily as S grows. EO moves up and down with S and is often worse than for a single model, so SISA can make models less fair. To fix this without retraining, they adapt Hardt, Price and Srebro's (HPS) equalized-odds post-processing to ensembles in three ways: (1) aggregate votes, then post-process; (2) post-process each shard model, then aggregate; (3) 'ensemble post-processing', one linear program over the whole vector of S predictions plus the attribute. They prove (3) gives the most accurate predictor that exactly satisfies equalized odds using only shard outputs and the attribute. Empirically, (2) usually gives the best trade-off and (3) the highest accuracy at moderate EO.
papers.problem: Unlearning methods change how models behave, but their effect on fairness was barely studied, and not at all for language models. SISA is attractive for LLMs because it is exact and works with any architecture. However, it trains each model on a smaller shard and combines them by voting, and this could change group-level error rates. A cheap fix is needed that does not involve retraining the expensive models.
papers.core_idea: Leave the SISA models as they are and correct their outputs after the fact. Hardt et al.'s derived-predictor linear program (LP) chooses randomized flip probabilities that satisfy equalized odds at minimum loss. The paper extends it from one binary prediction to the full vector of S constituent predictions: one variable per (prediction pattern, group) pair, 2^(S+1) variables in total. The objective and the TPR/FPR constraints stay linear, so the problem is still an LP, and its solution is the optimal equalized-odds predictor derived from the ensemble.
papers.setting: Centralized supervised fine-tuning of pretrained language models (binary toxic-text sequence classification), trained with SISA shards; fairness post-processing at inference time.
papers.unlearning_type: exact (SISA; the paper studies the fairness of SISA ensembles and proposes fairness post-processing, but runs no actual deletion requests in its experiments)
contributions: Claimed to be the first study of how unlearning interacts with fairness for LLMs, focusing on the SISA exact-unlearning framework.

Empirical accuracy-fairness study of SISA (S = 1, 3, 5, 7 shards, no slicing) on HateXplain toxic-text classification with BERT, DistilGPT2 and GPT2: accuracy falls as S increases, and EO varies non-monotonically and can be worse than a single model.

Three ways to apply HPS equalized-odds post-processing to SISA ensembles: Aggregate-then-Post-process HPS(MAJ(Y1..YS)), Post-process-then-Aggregate MAJ(HPS(Y1),...,HPS(YS)), and Ensemble Post-processing (a new LP over the joint ensemble predictions).

Proposition 1: ensemble post-processing is an LP in 2^(S+1) variables, with coefficients computable from the joint distribution of (Y1..YS, A, Y), and its solution is an optimal equalized-odds derived predictor for the ensemble. The authors note the result is of independent interest beyond unlearning.

An extra experiment where one shard is deliberately balanced ('fair') and the others are not. Unmitigated SISA's EO roughly doubles compared with random splitting, and ensemble post-processing gives the highest accuracy at low EO.
method_steps: Randomly split the fine-tuning set D into S disjoint, roughly equal shards D1..DS. Slicing is not used, because storing per-slice LLM checkpoints is too expensive.
Fine-tune one pretrained LM (a Hugging Face sequence classifier) per shard, giving constituent models M1..MS. Epochs are chosen from {S, S+1, S+2} by validation accuracy.
At inference, collect the binary predictions Y1_hat..YS_hat (toxic or not) and the binary sensitive attribute A (whether the text mentions religion, or race).

Option 1, Aggregate-then-Post-process: compute the majority vote MAJ(Y1..YS), estimate its joint distribution with (A, Y), and solve the 4-variable HPS LP for p_ya = Pr(Y_tilde=1 | MAJ=y, A=a) under equal-TPR and equal-FPR constraints. Output a randomized Y_tilde.
Option 2, Post-process-then-Aggregate: for each constituent k, solve its own 4-variable HPS LP to get HPS(Yk_hat), then take the majority vote of the S post-processed (randomized) predictions.

Option 3, Ensemble Post-processing: estimate the joint distribution of (Y1..YS, A, Y). Solve one LP over p_(ybar,a) = Pr(Y_tilde=1 | prediction vector = ybar, A=a) for every ybar in {0,1}^S and a in {0,1} (2^(S+1) variables), minimizing the expected loss subject to equal TPR and equal FPR across groups and 0 <= p <= 1. Output a randomized Y_tilde from a lookup on (prediction vector, A).

When an unlearning request arrives, SISA retrains only the affected shard's model. The paper does not discuss it, but the post-processor would then have to be refit: one small LP for option 2, the global LP for options 1 and 3.

key_definitions.name: Exact unlearning
key_definitions.plain: The model after unlearning has exactly the same distribution as a model retrained from scratch without the deleted data.
key_definitions.formal: Dist(U(A(D), Du, Dr)) = Dist(A(Dr)), with Dr = D minus Du

key_definitions.name: Approximate unlearning
key_definitions.plain: The unlearned and retrained model distributions only need to be statistically close, usually in a differential-privacy-like sense.
key_definitions.formal: U(A(D),Du,Dr) is (eps,delta)-indistinguishable from A(Dr) (DP-style)

key_definitions.name: SISA
key_definitions.plain: Split the data into S disjoint shards (each optionally split further into R slices with checkpoints), train one constituent model per shard, and combine predictions by majority vote. To unlearn, retrain only the affected shard, starting from the slice that held the deleted point.
key_definitions.formal: D = D1 u ... u DS (disjoint); prediction = MAJ(M1(x),...,MS(x))

key_definitions.name: Majority voting (MAJ)
key_definitions.plain: Output the label that most constituent models predict.
key_definitions.formal: MAJ(Y1..YS) = argmax_{y in {0,1}} n_y, where n_y = |{i in [S]: Yi = y}|

key_definitions.name: Sensitive group (toxic-text setup of Baldini et al. 2022)
key_definitions.plain: A text belongs to the sensitive group if it contains at least one term related to a sensitive topic (religion or race), and to the complementary group otherwise. Coarse-grained groups are used, e.g. 'mentions any religion'.
key_definitions.formal: A = 1 if the text mentions the sensitive topic, else 0

key_definitions.name: Equalized odds
key_definitions.plain: Given the true label, the prediction should not depend on the sensitive attribute, i.e. both groups have equal true-positive and false-positive rates.
key_definitions.formal: Pr(Y_hat=1 | A=0, Y=y) = Pr(Y_hat=1 | A=1, Y=y) for y in {0,1}

key_definitions.name: EO metric (scalar)
key_definitions.plain: A single number for how far the predictor is from equalized odds; lower is better. The text does not say exactly how the TPR and FPR gaps are combined (e.g. max or average).
key_definitions.formal: unclear from text; some combination of |TPR_0 - TPR_1| and |FPR_0 - FPR_1|

key_definitions.name: Derived predictor / HPS post-processing
key_definitions.plain: A new, possibly randomized, predictor Y_tilde that sees only the original prediction Y_hat and the attribute A. It is chosen to satisfy equalized odds with minimum expected loss.
key_definitions.formal: min_{p_ya} E[l(Y_tilde, Y)] s.t. Pr(Y_tilde=1|A=0,Y=y) = Pr(Y_tilde=1|A=1,Y=y) for y=0,1; 0<=p_ya<=1; p_ya = Pr(Y_tilde=1 | Y_hat=y, A=a). An LP in 4 variables.

key_definitions.name: Ensemble post-processing LP
key_definitions.plain: HPS generalized so that the derived predictor sees the whole vector of S constituent predictions, with one flip probability per (prediction pattern, group) pair.
key_definitions.formal: min_{p_(ybar,a)} E[l(Y_tilde,Y)] s.t. equal TPR and FPR across A; 0<=p_(ybar,a)<=1; p_(ybar,a) = Pr(Y_tilde=1 | Y1=ybar1,...,YS=ybarS, A=a), ybar in {0,1}^S

theory.name: Proposition 1 (ensemble post-processing is an optimal-fair LP)
theory.statement_plain: The ensemble post-processing problem (Eq. 4) is a linear program in 2^(S+1) variables p_(ybar,a). Its coefficients can be computed from the joint distribution of (Y1_hat..YS_hat, A, Y), and its solution is an optimal equalized-odds predictor derived from Y1_hat..YS_hat and A, i.e. it has minimum expected loss among all derived predictors satisfying EO.
theory.assumptions: Binary labels Y, binary sensitive attribute A and binary constituent predictions. The derived predictor may depend only on (Y1_hat..YS_hat, A) and may be randomized. The joint distribution of (Y1_hat..YS_hat, A, Y) is known; in practice it is estimated from data, and the paper does not say which split. The loss is defined on label pairs, and the proof expands it as misclassification probabilities. Optimality is with respect to that distribution only, so there is no finite-sample or generalization guarantee.
theory.significance: It generalizes Hardt et al. (2016): S = 1 recovers the 4-variable HPS LP. Inference from the definitions (not stated in the paper): HPS(MAJ(...)) is itself an EO-satisfying derived predictor of (Y1..YS, A), so ensemble post-processing is never worse in expected loss than Aggregate-then-Post-process on the fitting distribution. Post-process-then-Aggregate need not satisfy EO exactly, because a majority of EO predictors is not necessarily EO, so it falls outside the guarantee. The proof (App. B) writes the objective and the TPR/FPR constraints as sums of p_(ybar,a) times probabilities of the joint distribution.

theory.name: HPS LP (Hardt, Price, Srebro 2016; prior result used)
theory.statement_plain: For a single binary predictor and a binary attribute, the loss-minimizing equalized-odds derived predictor is the solution of an LP in the 4 variables p_ya.
theory.assumptions: Binary Y_hat, A, Y; known joint distribution; the derived predictor depends only on (Y_hat, A).
theory.significance: This is the building block for all three FairSISA variants.

papers.complexity: Not measured in the paper; no timing results are reported. Structurally, SISA trains S constituent models on about N/S samples each, and unlearning retrains only the affected constituent (from the pretrained initialization, since slicing is dropped). Inference needs S forward passes. The authors drop slicing because per-slice LLM checkpoints are too costly to store. Post-processing costs: Aggregate-then-Post-process solves one 4-variable LP; Post-process-then-Aggregate solves S independent 4-variable LPs; Ensemble Post-processing solves one LP with 2^(S+1) variables (256 for S = 7), which grows exponentially in S, and its estimated joint distribution over 2^S prediction patterns per group becomes sparse as S grows. All three are negligible next to LLM retraining.

datasets: HateXplain: about 20K Twitter and Gab posts. Offensive and hate are merged into one 'toxic' class against normal (binary). Sensitive attributes are religion and race at the coarse-grained level (e.g. 'any religion'); gender annotations exist but are not used.
models: BERT
DistilGPT2
GPT2 (in the appendix). All are Hugging Face sequence classifiers; model sizes are not stated.
baselines: Single model, S = 1 (conventional fine-tuning)
Unmitigated SISA with S = 3, 5, 7 (majority vote)
The three post-processing variants compared against each other: Aggregate-then-Post-process, Post-process-then-Aggregate, Ensemble Post-process
headline_results: Values below are approximate readings from scatter plots; the paper gives no numeric tables. Results are averaged over 5 seeds, with no error bars shown.
Accuracy falls as S grows. BERT: about 0.79 (S=1), 0.78 (S=3), 0.775 (S=5), 0.76 (S=7). DistilGPT2: about 0.755, 0.748, 0.717, 0.712.

EO is non-monotone in S and sometimes worse than a single model. BERT/Religion: about 0.195 at S=1 vs 0.20 at S=3 and 0.205 at S=5, but 0.175 at S=7. DistilGPT2/Race: about 0.12 at S=1 vs 0.15 at S=3 and 0.14 at S=5. DistilGPT2/Religion: about 0.20 at S=1 vs 0.23 at S=3.

Post-processing, BERT/Religion, S=3 (accuracy / EO): SISA about 0.78 / 0.20; Post-process-then-Aggregate about 0.75 / 0.02; Ensemble about 0.757 / 0.045; Aggregate-then-Post-process about 0.734 / 0.055.

Post-processing, DistilGPT2/Religion, S=3 (accuracy / EO): SISA about 0.747 / 0.23; Post-process-then-Aggregate about 0.728 / 0.03; Ensemble about 0.715 / 0.09; Aggregate-then-Post-process about 0.717 / 0.12.
Overall, Post-process-then-Aggregate usually gives the best accuracy-EO trade-off, Aggregate-then-Post-process the worst, and Ensemble Post-process the highest accuracy at moderate EO.

One balanced ('fair') shard with the others skewed (BERT/Religion): unmitigated SISA EO is about 0.29 (S=3) and 0.36 (S=5), far above random splitting. Ensemble post-processing gets about 0.763 accuracy / 0.035 EO (S=3) and about 0.745 / 0.09 (S=5), the highest accuracy among the post-processors. Post-process-then-Aggregate gets about 0.725 / 0.03 (S=3); Aggregate-then-Post-process about 0.70 / 0.027 (S=3).

Inconsistency in the GPT2 appendix: Fig. 3(a) shows SISA accuracies of about 0.42-0.50, but Fig. 4(b) shows the same EO points at about 0.735-0.74 accuracy. Fig. 3(b) Race EO values (about 0.10-0.115) also do not match Fig. 4(c) (about 0.13-0.21).

limitations: No unlearning requests are actually run. Fairness is measured only for SISA-trained ensembles, never tracked after deletions, and unlearning time is not measured.

The paper gives no causal explanation of why SISA hurts fairness. It only shows empirically that EO varies non-monotonically with S. Plausible mechanisms are fewer minority-group samples per shard and majority-vote amplification of group-specific errors; these are not analysed.

The models are small by today's standard (BERT, DistilGPT2, GPT2) despite the 'LLM' framing. There is one dataset, one binary task, two binary sensitive attributes, and only the majority-vote aggregator.
Slicing is dropped, so each unlearning request retrains a whole constituent model.
Post-processing needs the sensitive attribute at inference time and produces randomized predictions.
The post-processor is fitted on data (the split is unclear). After a deletion it must be refit, and whether its fitting data must itself be unlearned is not discussed.

The ensemble LP has 2^(S+1) variables, exponential in S, and estimating the joint distribution gets sparse as S grows. Optimality holds only on the fitting distribution, which may explain why the 'optimal' method does not dominate empirically.

Results are reported only as scatter plots without error bars or tables. Some figure inconsistencies remain (the GPT2 Fig. 3 vs Fig. 4 mismatch; the text cites Fig. 1(c) for DistilGPT2/Race, which is actually the legend).
future_work: Not explicitly stated (workshop paper). Implied directions: study the fairness of other unlearning methods for LLMs; apply the ensemble post-processing result outside SISA (the authors say it is 'of independent interest'); handle shards made unfair by unlearning-likelihood-aware data placement.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: This paper is a cautionary companion to SISA: the speed-up from sharding is not free, because more shards lower accuracy and can worsen group fairness (EO). Post-processing is a near-zero-cost repair that leaves the trained constituents untouched, which makes it a good fit for unlearning pipelines. Post-process-then-Aggregate is the most modular choice: after a shard is retrained, only that shard's 4-variable LP needs refitting. Ensemble post-processing needs a global LP whose size grows exponentially in S. The LP formulation over ensemble outputs, with linear TPR/FPR constraints, is a reusable tool. The 'one fair shard' experiment warns that efficiency-driven shard placement (e.g. grouping data that is likely to be deleted) can produce much less fair ensembles.
open_questions: Track fairness (EO) over a stream of real deletion requests in SISA, and design incremental or warm-started post-processor updates so fairness is restored without refitting from scratch.

Make the fairness post-processor itself exactly unlearnable: if its LP coefficients are estimated from data that later gets deleted, how should they be updated, and is the result still exact unlearning?
Reduce the ensemble LP from 2^(S+1) to 2(S+1) variables by conditioning only on the vote count (a symmetric derived predictor). How much optimality is lost, and does it scale to large S?
Fairness-aware sharding: stratify shards by (sensitive attribute, label) to bound per-shard EO while keeping deletion cost low, and analyse the conflict with unlearning-likelihood-aware placement.
Restore slicing for LLMs by storing per-slice LoRA/adapter deltas instead of full checkpoints, then re-evaluate the fairness-efficiency trade-off.
Prove bounds relating shard size, group proportions and the EO of a majority-vote ensemble, to explain the non-monotone EO-vs-S behaviour.

papers.title: FedShard: Federated Unlearning with Efficiency Fairness and Performance Fairness
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Zhejiang University
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
papers.venue: AAAI-26 (Fortieth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
papers.one_liner: Exact federated unlearning via a hierarchical tree of client shards that merge stage by stage, making unlearning both cheap and fair across clients.
papers.summary: When a client leaves a federated learning (FL) system, its right to be forgotten requires removing its data's influence from the global model (federated unlearning, FU). Prior FU work ignores fairness between clients. The authors define two kinds of fairness. Performance fairness: unlearning should lower accuracy only as much as the leaving client's data is unique, so remaining clients with similar data are not hurt. Efficiency fairness: the cost of unlearning a client should match its contribution and not depend on things like when it joined. Calibration-based approximate methods (FedEraser, RapidRetrain, FedRecovery) are fast but over- or under-forget, which hurts performance fairness. Exact methods are either slow (full retraining) or give very uneven costs (FATS). FedShard groups clients into shards that train in isolation and then merge stage by stage, forming a tree that ends in one global shard. Every shard's model is cached, so unlearning a client only retrains the shards on its path from leaf to root. Two adaptive algorithms keep this hierarchical training stable and fair: one merges shards with diverse update directions (A1), and one sets training rounds per shard from how varied its clients' contributions are (A2). The paper adds two fairness metrics (Mp, Me), proves exactness and an at-least-P/2 speedup, and shows FedShard avoids cascaded leaving and poisoning attacks.
papers.problem: Federated unlearning methods are judged on efficiency and effectiveness, but not on whether they are fair to clients. Approximate calibration methods cause extra accuracy loss on remaining clients, or forget too little for leaving clients (performance unfairness). Exact methods like FATS make unlearning costs depend on things like join time, so early-joined clients pay much more (efficiency unfairness). Unfair unlearning can trigger cascaded leaving of clients with similar data, and can be exploited for data poisoning attacks.
papers.core_idea: The design is 'isolated yet integrated'. Clients train in small isolated shards that are progressively merged (merging rate R) over P stages into one global shard, and every shard's model is cached. Unlearning a client retrains only the one shard per stage on its leaf-to-root path, which gives exact unlearning at a cost that depends only on the client's own path. Diversity-aware merging (A1) and variance-aware round allocation (A2) resolve the conflicts between convergence, efficiency and fairness that naive sharding creates.
papers.setting: federated (horizontal, cross-device style, client-level unlearning; supervised image classification)
contributions: FedShard, a sharded, hierarchical federated learning and unlearning framework, which the authors call the first FU method to target both performance fairness and efficiency fairness.
Two adaptive algorithms: A1, a cluster-based shard merging algorithm that promotes directional diversity, and A2, a variance-aware training-round allocation algorithm.

Formal requirements for performance fairness (P.F.) and efficiency fairness (E.F.) in FU, plus two new metrics, Mp and Me. The paper proves that minimizing them satisfies known fairness properties (envy-freeness, Pareto optimality, fairness axiom, reduction).

Theory showing exactness (equivalent to retraining) and a single-client speedup of at least P/2 over retraining from scratch. A multi-request speedup between r2- and m over one-by-one unlearning, with O(K) time for one client and O(K lg m) for m clients.

An evaluation showing that approximate FU methods cause cascaded leaving and are open to unfair-FU data poisoning attacks, and that FATS has very uneven unlearning costs. FedShard avoids all of these and unlearns 1.3-6.2x faster than retraining and up to 4.9x faster than FATS.
method_steps: Setup: K clients C = {c1..cK} and a user-chosen merging rate R (how many shards merge into one super-shard per stage). The number of stages is P (the main text writes P = ceil(K/R), but Algorithm 2 and Table 3 of the extended version use P = ceil(log_R K) with R^(P-1) < K <= R^P, so the main-text form looks like a typo). Clients are the tree's leaves, shards are its nodes and stages are its levels.

Compute each client's contribution factor alpha_c = arccos(<Delta_theta, Delta_theta_c> / (||Delta_theta||_2 ||Delta_theta_c||_2)). This is the angle between the client's local update and the global update; a smaller angle means a larger contribution. The shard-level alpha_s^p is the mean over the shard's clients.

Stage p, phase 1 (shard generation, A1): cluster the stage-(p-1) shards into 3 clusters by update-direction angle relative to the global average, using KMeans (App. D.2). Then form ceil(N_{p-1}/R) super-shards, each taking a similar number of shards from every cluster (children chosen to minimize Me), so each new shard mixes average, large-positive and large-negative directions.

Stage p, phase 2 (shard initialization and round allocation, A2): initialize each new shard's model theta_s^{p,0} from its children. Pick rounds T_s^p in a range [T0*, T1*] taken from a preliminary run (min and max rounds to converge in early stages, e.g. [4,7]), using Eq. 2: (T_s^p - T0*)/(T1* - T0*) = [(sigma^2(alpha_s^p) - sigma^2_min)/(sigma^2_max - sigma^2_min)]^(-1). Homogeneous shards (low contribution variance) get more rounds and heterogeneous ones get fewer.

Stage p, phase 3 (parallel federated training): each shard runs federated training (FedAvg-style aggregation with weights w_s^p) over its own clients only, for T_s^p rounds, in parallel with the other shards.

Stage p, phase 4 (state caching): the server stores each shard's membership, T_s^p, initial model theta_s^{p,0}, trained model theta_s^p, alpha_s^p and w_s^p in FLCache. Repeat until stage P has one shard with all clients. Its model theta_1^P is the global model. Space is O(K), the same order as FedAvg.

Unlearning (Algorithm 1): when client c_l asks to leave, find the affected shards (the one shard per stage that contains c_l, i.e. its leaf-to-root path). For p = 1..P, retrain each affected shard from its initial state with the remaining clients for T_s^p rounds. Unaffected shards reuse their cached models. Update FLCache with the retrained shards. Return theta_u* = theta_1^P.

Multiple simultaneous requests: retrain the union of all affected paths in one pass. Shared ancestors are retrained once, and after stage p' every shard contains a leaving client. This gives an extra speedup between r2- and m over unlearning the clients one by one.

key_definitions.name: Performance fairness (P.F.)
key_definitions.plain: Unlearning should cause a fair accuracy drop across clients. A leaving client with unique data should be forgotten fully, which may cause a large drop on its data. Remaining clients whose data resembles the leaver's should not suffer an excessive drop, since their data is still in the system. This protects both the leaver's RTBF and the remaining clients' right to good model performance.
key_definitions.formal: Measured by Mp (lower = fairer).

key_definitions.name: Efficiency fairness (E.F.)
key_definitions.plain: Every client should face a fair unlearning cost when it leaves. The cost should depend only on its own contribution or impact, not on factors like join time or shard placement. Unequal leaving costs discourage clients from participating.
key_definitions.formal: Measured by Me (lower = fairer).

key_definitions.name: Contribution factor alpha_c
key_definitions.plain: The angle between a client's local update and the global update, used as the client's impact on the global model. A smaller angle means a larger contribution. Loss similarity, Shapley value or information entropy could replace it (App. C).
key_definitions.formal: alpha_c = arccos( <Delta_theta, Delta_theta_c> / (||Delta_theta||_2 * ||Delta_theta_c||_2) ); alpha_s^p = mean of alpha_c over clients in shard S_s^p

key_definitions.name: Data distance Dis
key_definitions.plain: How different two clients' data are, judged by their contribution angles.
key_definitions.formal: Dis(c1, c2) = |alpha_c1 - alpha_c2|

key_definitions.name: Performance fairness metric Mp
key_definitions.plain: For each client, it compares the accuracy drop on its data caused by unlearning with how unique its data is (distance to the nearest remaining client). f_plus is lowest when the two normalized values match: unique leavers should get a big drop, and clients with lookalike remaining data should get a small one.
key_definitions.formal: Mp = (1/|C|) * sum_{c in C} f_plus( Delta_Y(D_c), min_{c_r in C_R} Dis(c, c_r) ); f_plus(x,y) = (x~ + y~) * (1/x~ + 1/y~), convex, minimized at x~ = y~; x~ = eps + (x - x_min)/(x_max - x_min) in (0,1]

key_definitions.name: Efficiency fairness metric Me
key_definitions.plain: The contribution-weighted variance of unlearning costs (computing time) across clients. If two clients contribute about the same but cost very different amounts to unlearn, Me is large.
key_definitions.formal: Me = (1/|C|) * sum_{c in C} (Z_avg - Z_c)^2 / |alpha_c|, where Z_c = unlearning cost (time) of client c and Z_avg = mean cost

key_definitions.name: Merging rate R and stages P
key_definitions.plain: R is how many shards merge into one super-shard at the next stage. P is the number of stages, or tree levels.
key_definitions.formal: Main text: P = ceil(K/R). Extended version, Alg. 2 / Table 3: P = ceil(log_R K), with R^(P-1) < K <= R^P.

key_definitions.name: Variance-aware round allocation (Eq. 2)
key_definitions.plain: Sets a shard's training rounds inversely to how varied its clients' contributions are. This avoids overfitting divergent shards and avoids under-training.
key_definitions.formal: (T_s^p - T0*)/(T1* - T0*) = [ (sigma^2(alpha_s^p) - sigma^2(alpha)_min) / (sigma^2(alpha)_max - sigma^2(alpha)_min) ]^(-1)

key_definitions.name: Cascaded leaving
key_definitions.plain: Unfair unlearning causes a large accuracy drop for remaining clients with data similar to the leaver's, which pushes them to leave too. This chain reaction threatens the FL system's sustainability. In the App. G.5 simulation, a remaining client leaves when Delta_Y > Y* - Z.
key_definitions.formal: Remaining-client payoff: stay W_r^k = -Delta_Y - Z + lambda_r, leave W_r^l = -Y* + lambda_r (extended version App. G.5)

key_definitions.name: Unfair-FU data poisoning attack (uf-DPA)
key_definitions.plain: Malicious clients join, train on data that resembles a target group's, and then request unlearning. A performance-unfair FU method over-unlearns, which degrades the targeted remaining clients.
key_definitions.formal: DPA precision = (# successfully poisoned clients) / (total # clients)

theory.name: Proposition 1 (exactness) + induction
theory.statement_plain: A training run whose dataset excludes D_l and whose initial model is not affected by D_l can be reused as-is when unlearning D_l, and this equals retraining from scratch on D0 \ D_l. By induction over stages, retraining only the shard that contains the leaver at each stage (with all other shards cached) is as effective as retraining from scratch.
theory.assumptions: The cached states of unaffected shards were never influenced by the leaver's data. The paper calls this assumption standard in the exact-unlearning literature (SISA, FATS, Exact-Fun). Whether the shard structure and round choices, which were computed while the leaver was present, also need recomputing is not discussed.
theory.significance: Makes FedShard exact unlearning, so it is performance-fair by construction (no over- or under-forgetting).

theory.name: Proposition 2 (single-client speedup, constant rounds T0)
theory.statement_plain: FedShard unlearning is r1 times faster than vanilla retraining (FedAvg from scratch).
theory.assumptions: Every shard trains for the same T0 rounds. R is a positive integer.
theory.significance: r1 = ((R-1)/R) * (K/(K-1)) * P >= P/2 (usually about P): the speedup grows with the number of stages.

theory.name: Proposition 3 (general case, variable rounds)
theory.statement_plain: With per-shard rounds between Tmin and Tmax, the speedup r1_hat satisfies r1*T0/Tmax <= r1_hat <= r1*T0/Tmin.
theory.assumptions: Rounds are set by A2 within [Tmin, Tmax].
theory.significance: Keeping the round range narrow (the goal of A2) keeps unlearning both efficient and fair. This is the theoretical case for A2.

theory.name: Proposition 4 (multiple simultaneous requests)
theory.statement_plain: Unlearning m clients together is between r2- and r2+ times faster than unlearning them one by one, with r2+ = m and r2- = (R/(R-1)) * ((K-1)/K) * m/(P - p') >= 1. Here p' is the stage after which every shard contains a leaving client.
theory.assumptions: The m clients leave at the same time.
theory.significance: Batching unlearning requests is never worse and can be up to m times better.

theory.name: Corollary 1 (time complexity)
theory.statement_plain: FedShard unlearning takes O(K) time for one client and O(K lg m) time for m clients. Space is O(K), the same as FedAvg, per extended version App. E/D.1.
theory.assumptions: Follows from Props. 2-4.
theory.significance: Gives a sublinear-in-m cost for batched deletions.

theory.name: Fairness properties of Mp and Me (Sec. 5.3; App. F, Props. 5-16 in extended version)
theory.statement_plain: FU algorithms that minimize Mp satisfy envy-freeness (FP.1), Pareto optimality (FP.2) and the fairness axiom (FP.3). Those that minimize Me satisfy the fairness axiom (FP.3) and reduction (FP.4). The appendix also lists continuity, homogeneity, non-saturation, partition and starvation for Mp, and reduction-to-equality, continuity, non-homogeneity, saturation and partition for Me.
theory.assumptions: Absolute Mp and Me values are meaningful only when comparing FU methods under identical settings. The two metrics are designed to be orthogonal.
theory.significance: Grounds the new unlearning-fairness metrics in axiomatic fairness theory from economics and networking (Lan et al. 2010; Feldman and Kirman 1974; Li and Xue 2013).

theory.name: Convergence (not proven)
theory.statement_plain: The paper gives no formal convergence bound for sharded hierarchical training. Convergence is argued informally (diverse merging, bounded rounds) and shown empirically (ablation, Fig. 5).
theory.assumptions: n/a
theory.significance: There is also no formal fairness bound: P.F. follows from exactness, and E.F. is argued via the bounded round range (Prop. 3) and shown empirically.

papers.complexity: Learning: P stages of parallel per-shard FL. The server stores per-shard, per-stage models and metadata in FLCache, which is O(K) space (same order as FedAvg; extended version). Unlearning one client retrains one shard per stage along its leaf-to-root path. That is O(K) time and at least P/2 times (usually about P times) faster than FedAvg retraining with equal rounds; with variable rounds the speedup is scaled by T0/Tmax to T0/Tmin. m simultaneous requests take O(K lg m) time, between r2- and m times faster than sequential. Communication cost is not analyzed separately; retraining still needs the remaining clients in affected shards to take part.

datasets: MNIST
Fashion-MNIST
CIFAR-10
CIFAR-100
EMNIST, SVHN, Purchase, Adult (appendix of arXiv extended version only; not in the AAAI PDF)
models: 2-layer CNN as in FedAvg (McMahan et al. 2017)
baselines: FA: vanilla retraining from scratch via FedAvg (exact)
FT: FATS (Tao et al. 2024, exact)
FE: FedEraser (Liu et al. 2021, calibration/approximate)
RR: RapidRetrain (Liu et al. 2022, Hessian-based calibration/approximate)
FR: FedRecovery (Zhang et al. 2023b, DP-based approximate)
headline_results: Abstract/intro: FedShard unlearns 1.3-6.2x faster than retraining from scratch and up to 4.9x faster than state-of-the-art exact unlearning (FATS). The exact settings behind 6.2x and 4.9x are in appendix G.2/G.3 and are not shown in the main-text tables.

Table 1 (K=512, rho=0.1): FS unlearning time on MNIST/FMNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 = 2485.1/2508.3/3361.1/6859.2 s vs FA 9244.6/9984.4/13459.3/29660.2 s (about 3.7-4.3x faster) and FT 6832.1/6163.7/8403.9/16822.5 s (about 2.5-2.8x faster). FR is far faster (10-18 s) but approximate.
Performance fairness Mp (Table 1): FS 6.08/5.95/6.08/5.94, close to FA (5.68-6.35) and FT (6.46-7.13); approximate methods are worse: FE 9.4-11.7, RR 9.2-10.9, FR 14.0-22.1.
Ablation (CIFAR-10, K=32, R=2, rho=0.1, 30 epochs): FedAvg 62.92%; naive sharding without A1/A2 collapses after each merge; with A1 only 56.3%; with A1+A2 64.14%, beating FedAvg.
Table 2 (CIFAR-10): MIA F1 non-unlearned 91.37; FA 34.18, FS 35.04, FT 36.07 vs over-forgetting FE 30.14, RR 28.65, FR 25.07. DPA precision: FA/FT/FS 0%, FE 20.83%, RR 22.91%, FR 28.50%.
Fig. 7: RR and FE have high Mp and cause cascaded leaving, more so as the data becomes more IID (higher rho). FS, FA and FT cause no cascaded leaving.
Fig. 6 (CIFAR-10, 256 clients): FT's per-client unlearning costs vary widely, while FS's are low and tightly concentrated.
Extended version: about 27% faster than retraining at K=32 and 3.7x at K=512. Speedup grows with the number of clients.

limitations: Client-level unlearning only (a whole client leaves). Sample-level deletion inside a client is not handled.
No formal convergence guarantee for hierarchical sharded training. Stability relies on the empirical A1/A2 heuristics, and naive sharding collapses.
[T0*, T1*] comes from a preliminary run (extra tuning cost). A1 uses a fixed 3-cluster KMeans.

Possible exactness subtlety (noticed, not discussed): the shard structure (A1 clustering on alpha), the round counts (A2 variance) and the normalization in Eq. 2 were computed while the leaving client was present. If they are not recomputed, the unlearned model may not match running FedShard from scratch without that client.

Notation inconsistencies: P = ceil(K/R) in the main text vs ceil(log_R K) in the extended version's algorithm. Table 1's caption says K=512 while Sec. 6.2 says 256 clients. The 6.2x and 4.9x headline numbers are not visible in the main-text tables.
FedShard is 'one of the fastest' only among exact methods. FedRecovery unlearns in about 10-18 s vs FedShard's 2,500-6,900 s.

Mp and Me are relative, setting-dependent scores. Me divides by |alpha_c|, so clients with a very small angle (the largest contributors) weight cost deviations very heavily, and alpha near 0 blows up. Both metrics depend on the chosen contribution factor.
Experiments use small models (2-layer CNN) and up to 512 clients; scaling beyond 1,000 clients is left to future work.
Every unlearning request must retrain at least the final global stage, and remaining clients in affected shards must come back online to retrain.
future_work: Scaling to more than 1,000 clients (stated in extended version).
Other contribution factors (loss similarity, Shapley value, information entropy), discussed in App. C.
Suggested by this extraction: dynamic client arrival, and sample-level unlearning within the hierarchy.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: FedShard shows how to carry SISA-style exact unlearning (sharding plus cached checkpoints) into federated learning. Instead of an ensemble of isolated shard models, it uses a tree of progressively merged shards, so retraining is limited to one leaf-to-root path of P nodes. Its speedup analysis (r1 >= P/2, bounds under variable rounds, batch speedup between r2- and m, O(K lg m) for m deletions) is a reusable template for analyzing hierarchical or divide-and-conquer unlearning. Mp and Me add a new evaluation axis: who pays for unlearning and who gets hurt by it. Me in particular could be applied to SISA, where unlearning cost depends on shard and slice position. Pitfalls to note: naive merging of shard models can collapse accuracy, and structure choices made from data that is later forgotten may break strict exactness.
open_questions: Make FedShard strictly exact under deletion of structure-defining clients. Either make A1/A2 decisions independent of the leaver's updates or recompute them cheaply, and prove equivalence to running FedShard from scratch without that client.
Prove a convergence bound for hierarchical shard-merging FL that depends on R, P, rounds T_s^p and directional diversity (e.g. under bounded heterogeneity).
Design an Me-style efficiency-fairness metric and a cost-equalizing shard/slice assignment for centralized SISA, where unlearning cost depends on slice position.
Combine FedShard's client-level tree with SISA-style slicing inside each client for sample-level federated unlearning, and analyze the combined speedup.
Extend the hierarchy to dynamic joining or continual settings (clients arrive over time), avoiding the join-time cost unfairness seen in FATS.
Apply Mp/Me-type fairness auditing to federated clustering unlearning (e.g. MUFC) or to group-fairness-aware unlearning (FairSISA).

papers.title: An Unlearning Framework for Continual Learning
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad
Deakin University
papers.one_liner: UnCLe uses a task-embedding-conditioned hypernetwork so tasks can be learned and later unlearned data-free by regressing their generated weights onto Gaussian noise.
papers.summary: Continual learning (CL) trains one model on a stream of tasks and throws away old task data; machine unlearning removes knowledge a model should no longer have. This paper studies a model that receives an arbitrary interleaved sequence of 'learn task t' and 'unlearn task t' requests, where no data of a task is available when it must be unlearned. The authors first adapt six standard unlearning methods (BadTeacher, SCRUB, SalUn, SSD, GKT, JiT) to CL using the DER++ replay buffer and observe two failure modes: unlearning one task damages accuracy on retained tasks (spill), and an unlearned task regains accuracy when later, similar tasks are learned (relapse). UnCLe avoids storing per-task networks: a shared hypernetwork generates a whole task-specific ResNet from a small learned task embedding. Learning a task trains the hypernetwork and a new embedding with a regularizer that keeps the weights generated for old embeddings unchanged. Unlearning trains only the hypernetwork so that the forget-task embedding outputs Gaussian noise (MSE averaged over 10 noise samples), while the same regularizer protects retained tasks; no data is needed. On Permuted-MNIST, 5-Tasks, CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet, UnCLe reaches chance-level forget accuracy (about 10%), near-zero spill, low relapse, competitive retain accuracy and MIA of about 50%, and unlearning old tasks frees capacity for new ones.
papers.problem: Existing unlearning algorithms are designed for offline-trained models and mostly need the forget set and/or the retain set, while continual learning discards past-task data. When learn and unlearn requests are interleaved, offline unlearning methods adapted to CL through replay cause unlearning to spill into retained tasks and let unlearned tasks relapse after later learning. Exact solutions based on per-task networks (CLPU) avoid this but cause unbounded parameter growth.
papers.core_idea: Generate task-specific networks with a shared hypernetwork conditioned on per-task embeddings instead of storing them. Each task is then addressed by its embedding, so unlearning a task means retraining the hypernetwork to map that embedding to zero-centred Gaussian noise (a random-like, uninformative network), while a distillation-style output regularizer keeps the weights generated for all other embeddings fixed. This makes unlearning data-free and task-specific, and in experiments the forgotten task does not relapse when new tasks are learned later.
papers.setting: Task-incremental continual learning and unlearning (supervised image classification, centralized): an interleaved sequence of learn/unlearn task requests, past data discarded, task identity known at inference (separate generated network/head per task).
papers.unlearning_type: approximate (data-free, task-level; empirical evaluation only, no certified guarantee)
contributions: Formalizes continual learning and unlearning as a sequence of requests R_i = (I_i, T_i, D_i) with I in {learn, unlearn}, where an unlearn request carries no data (D_i = {}).

Empirical analysis showing that offline unlearning methods (BadTeacher, SCRUB, SalUn, SSD, GKT, JiT) adapted to CL via DER++ replay suffer two failure modes: spill (performance degradation on retained tasks) and relapse (unlearned tasks regaining accuracy after later learning).

UnCLe: a hypernetwork + task-embedding framework where learning uses an output-distillation regularizer and unlearning aligns the forget-task's generated parameters with Gaussian noise, with no data needed and only one small embedding added per task.
Two new metrics for continual unlearning: Spill (unlearning specificity) and Relapse (unlearning permanence), used alongside Retain-task Accuracy and Forget-task Accuracy.
Shows that unlearning obsolete tasks reduces model saturation and improves accuracy on later tasks (e.g., TinyImageNet retained-task accuracy 55.24 vs 50.47 for a learn-only hypernetwork).

Theorem 1 relating the averaged noise-MSE objective to an L2-norm penalty, plus ablations of noising strategies (fixed noise, L2-norm reduction, discarding the embedding) and a burn-in annealing schedule that reduces unlearning time.
method_steps: Set up a fully connected hypernetwork H(.; phi) (hidden layers 128, 256, 512) with Hyperfan initialization so that the generated main-network (ResNet-18/50) weights follow Kaiming-He statistics. The main network is generated in 200 chunks: each 32-dim chunk embedding is concatenated with a 32-dim task embedding, and separate output heads produce conv weights, batch-norm parameters and residual-connection parameters. Chunk embeddings are learned on the first task and then frozen.
On a learn request (L, t, D_t): randomly initialize a new task embedding e_t and freeze a copy of the current hypernetwork parameters phi* = phi.
For each mini-batch of D_t: generate theta_t = H(e_t; phi), compute predictions F(X; theta_t), and compute the task loss L_task (cross-entropy).

Add the regularizer L_reg = (1/(t-1)) * sum_{t'<t} ||H(e_t'; phi*) - H(e_t'; phi)||_2^2 over the stored previous task embeddings (needs no data), weighted by beta; optimize {phi, e_t} on L_task + beta * L_reg with Adam (lr 1e-3). Then store e_t and discard D_t.

On an unlearn request (U, f, no data): for E_u burn-in iterations (100 at first, reduced by 10% after each unlearning operation, minimum 20), sample n = 10 noise vectors z_i ~ N(0, I_d), compute L_fgt = (1/n) * sum_i ||H(e_f; phi) - z_i||_2^2, and update only phi on L_ul = gamma * L_fgt + L_reg, where L_reg keeps the retained tasks' generated parameters fixed (relative to the pre-unlearning hypernetwork).

At inference for a (retained) task t, generate theta_t = H(e_t; phi) and classify with that task-specific network (task-incremental: task identity is given). After unlearning, H(e_f; phi) produces near-zero/noise parameters, so forget-task predictions are near uniform (chance).

key_definitions.name: Request sequence
key_definitions.plain: The model receives an ordered list of requests; each says learn or unlearn a given task, and only learn requests come with data.
key_definitions.formal: R = {R_i}_{i=1}^{|R|}, R_i = (I_i, T_i, D_i); I_i = L => D_i = D_t = {(x_j^t, y_j^t)}; I_i = U => D_i = {} (data-free unlearning)

key_definitions.name: Hypernetwork task-parameter generation
key_definitions.plain: A shared network maps a small task embedding to the full weight vector of that task's classifier.
key_definitions.formal: theta_t = H(e_t; phi); prediction y_hat = F(x; theta_t)

key_definitions.name: Learning objective (Eq. 2)
key_definitions.plain: Fit the new task while keeping the weights generated for all earlier task embeddings unchanged.
key_definitions.formal: argmin_{phi, e_t} L_task(D_t, H(e_t; phi)) + beta * L_reg, L_reg = (1/(t-1)) sum_{t'=1}^{t-1} ||H(e_t'; phi*) - H(e_t'; phi)||_2^2

key_definitions.name: Unlearning objective (Eq. 3)
key_definitions.plain: Push the parameters generated for the forget task toward random Gaussian noise (averaged over n samples so no single noise vector is memorized), while the regularizer protects the other tasks.
key_definitions.formal: argmin_phi gamma * (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n ||H(e_f; phi) - z_i||_2^2 + L_reg, z_i ~ N(0, I_d), n = 10

key_definitions.name: Burn-in (E_u)
key_definitions.plain: Number of optimization iterations spent on one unlearning request; it controls how strongly the task is unlearned.
key_definitions.formal: E_u = 100, annealed by 10% per unlearning operation with floor 20

key_definitions.name: Retain-task Accuracy (RA) / Forget-task Accuracy (FA)
key_definitions.plain: Average accuracy at the end of the sequence over tasks that are still retained / that were unlearned; FA should be near chance (10% for 10-way tasks).
key_definitions.formal: unclear from text beyond 'average accuracy of the retained and the forgotten tasks at the end of the experimental sequence'

key_definitions.name: Spill (Eq. 4)
key_definitions.plain: Total change in accuracy on all non-target tasks caused by one unlearning operation; measures specificity.
key_definitions.formal: S_u = sum_{t != t_f} |a_t^{u-1} - a_t^{u}|, where a_t^{u} is task t's accuracy after operation u

key_definitions.name: Relapse (Eq. 5)
key_definitions.plain: How much a forgotten task's accuracy changes between right after it was unlearned and the end of the sequence; measures permanence.
key_definitions.formal: P_t = |a_t^{u} - a_t^{e}|, u = operation where t was unlearned, e = end of sequence

key_definitions.name: Task relapse
key_definitions.plain: An unlearned task regains accuracy as later (similar) tasks are learned, through backward knowledge transfer, even after its replay data is removed.

key_definitions.name: Unlearning desiderata
key_definitions.plain: Completeness (no remaining trace of the task), specificity (other tasks unaffected) and permanence (cannot come back). Per-task parameter isolation satisfies all three exactly.

key_definitions.name: Uniformity (UNI)
key_definitions.plain: Reported in the ablation table (Table 8) to measure how close forget-task outputs are to a uniform distribution (UnCLe = 100.0, fixed noise = -infinity). Its exact formula is not given in the text.
key_definitions.formal: unclear from text

key_definitions.name: Model saturation
key_definitions.plain: After many tasks a continually trained model loses plasticity and learns new tasks worse; unlearning old tasks restores capacity.

theory.name: Theorem 1 (Appendix E)
theory.statement_plain: For parameters theta in R^d and i.i.d. z_i ~ N(0, I_d), the average (1/n) sum_i ||theta - z_i||^2 converges (almost surely, by the strong law of large numbers) to ||theta||^2 + d as n -> infinity. So averaged noise alignment acts like an L2 penalty that drives the generated parameters toward zero, which makes the forget-task logits zero and its predictions uniform (maximum entropy).
theory.assumptions: theta fixed (not random) and noise samples i.i.d. standard Gaussian; the proof uses E[z_ij] = 0, E[z_ij^2] = 1 and the SLLN.
theory.significance: Explains why noise alignment produces near-uniform forget-task outputs. It also frames n as an interpolation: n = 1 (fixed noise) can be memorized and hurts retained tasks, while n = infinity (pure L2) drives the hypernetwork's own parameters to zero and destabilizes it (Fig. 8). n = 10 is the empirical compromise. Our note (not from the paper): for a single step, (1/n) sum ||theta - z_i||^2 = ||theta - z_bar||^2 + const with z_bar ~ N(0, I/n), so each step regresses onto a fresh random target of variance 1/n.

theory.name: Informal argument: parameter isolation gives exact unlearning (Methodology)
theory.statement_plain: If every task has its own separate model, deleting that model is exact unlearning: it is complete (no other network holds the task), specific (other networks are untouched) and permanent (nothing can be recovered from the rest).
theory.assumptions: Disjoint parameters per task and no shared components.
theory.significance: Gives the ideal UnCLe approximates: it keeps the task-addressable modularity through embeddings and avoids parameter growth by sharing a hypernetwork. The price is that unlearning is only approximate.

papers.complexity: No formal complexity analysis. Storage: one hypernetwork plus a 32-dim embedding per task (200 frozen 32-dim chunk embeddings), described as negligible growth, versus one full network per task for CLPU. Learning: each step generates a full ResNet in 200 chunks and evaluates L_reg over all previous task embeddings with both phi and frozen phi*, so the cost grows linearly with the number of past tasks. Unlearning: E_u burn-in iterations (100, annealed 10% per op, min 20) of hypernetwork-only optimization. No data and no main-network forward passes are needed, so the cost does not depend on dataset size. Measured average unlearning time on one V100 (Table 10): 33.28 s (5-Tasks), 13.16 s (Permuted-MNIST), 41.70 s (CIFAR-100), 29.63 s (TinyImageNet). SalUn takes 491.9/358.3/51.47/65.20 s and SCRUB 171.1/118.9/30.02/32.52 s, but SSD (5.73 s CIFAR-100, 5.81 s TinyImageNet) and BadTeacher (10.95/8.68 s) are faster on the larger datasets. Annealing cut TinyImageNet unlearning time from 45.12 to 29.63 s and CIFAR-100 from 43.98 to 41.70 s at the same FA of 10.00 (Table 7).

datasets: Permuted-MNIST (10 tasks x 10 classes; 15-request sequences)
5-Tasks / Five-datasets: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, KMNIST, notMNIST, SVHN (5 tasks x 10 classes; 7-request sequences)
CIFAR-100 (10 tasks x 10 classes; 15-request sequences)
TinyImageNet (200 classes; the analysis section and Table 4 sequences use 20 tasks x 10 classes, while the Datasets paragraph says 10 tasks; 30-request sequences)
models: Hypernetwork: fully connected MLP with hidden layers 128/256/512, task and chunk embedding dim 32, 200 chunks, separate heads for weights/BN/residual parameters, Hyperfan init
Main network: ResNet-18 (Permuted-MNIST main results; all datasets in appendix)
Main network: ResNet-50 (5-Tasks, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet main results)
baselines: Offline unlearning methods adapted to CL with DER++ replay: BadTeacher, SCRUB, SalUn, SSD (all need forget + retain data), JiT (forget data only), GKT (data-free)
UniCLUN (BadTeacher + replay for CL; treated as equivalent to the BadTeacher adaptation and not reported separately)
CLPU (separate network per task, exact unlearning by deletion)
Hypernetwork-based ablations: JiT-Hnet, GKT-Hnet, Hnet (unlearning only through natural catastrophic forgetting)
Oracle-style baselines with full retain-task data: FT* (fine-tune on retain set), RT* (retrain from scratch), RT-Hnet* (retrain a hypernetwork sequentially)
Noising-strategy ablations: Fixed-noise alignment (n=1), L2-norm reduction (n=inf), Discard e_f (replace embedding with random)
Only-Learning hypernetwork (saturation comparison)
metrics: Per-task accuracy trajectories over request sequences
headline_results: Table 1 (Seq. 1, 3 seeds) RA/FA: Permuted-MNIST UnCLe 96.87/10.00 vs BadTeacher 92.17/10.20, SalUn 92.39/59.24, CLPU 91.73/-; CIFAR-100 UnCLe 62.65/10.00 vs SalUn 66.56/44.89, JiT 65.94/43.93, BadTeacher 61.75/14.57; 5-Tasks UnCLe 94.12/10.04 vs CLPU 85.00, SalUn 74.75/25.02, BadTeacher 54.38/8.55; TinyImageNet UnCLe 55.24/10.00 vs SalUn 58.44/36.02, JiT 57.86/32.70, BadTeacher 52.79/15.73.
Table 2 Spill (lower is better): UnCLe 0.044 (PMNIST), 0.640 (CIFAR-100), 0.023 (5-Tasks), 0.722 (TinyImageNet) vs baselines roughly 5-83 (e.g., GKT 51.86/32.96/83.08/16.36).

Table 2 Relapse: UnCLe 8.703 (PMNIST), 0.507 (CIFAR-100, lowest), 0.539 (5-Tasks, 2nd after SCRUB 0.00), 2.233 (TinyImageNet; SCRUB 0.739 lower). SCRUB has low relapse but collapses RA (e.g., 9.97 on PMNIST). BadTeacher relapse is 30.51 (PMNIST) and 23.57 (CIFAR-100).

MIA: UnCLe 50.00 +/- 0.00-0.02 on PMNIST, CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet (50.01 on 5-Tasks). Most baselines are also about 45-53% because task-incremental forget heads are randomized, so MIA does not discriminate much in this setting.
Saturation (Table 3): retained-task accuracy for UnCLe vs Only-Learning hypernetwork is 55.24 vs 50.47 (TinyImageNet), 62.65 vs 60.51 (CIFAR-100), 96.87 vs 96.84 (PMNIST), 94.12 vs 94.12 (5-Tasks).

Noising ablation (Table 8): Fixed noise lowers RA (CIFAR-100 21.79, 5-Tasks 83.04); Norm reduction keeps RA but forgets poorly (FA 94.99 PMNIST, 34.42 CIFAR-100); Discard e_f leaves FA high (61.79 PMNIST); UnCLe FA 10.00 with UNI 100.0.

Appendix: the Hnet baseline that relies on natural forgetting keeps forget-task accuracy high (FA 96.91 PMNIST, 54.31 TinyImageNet), so hypernetworks barely forget on their own. FT* with full retain data still has FA 67.70 (PMNIST) and 55.44 (CIFAR-100).
ResNet-18 appendix: UnCLe RA/FA 66.97/10.00 (CIFAR-100), 59.22/10.00 (TinyImageNet), 93.77/9.60 ('PenTask', apparently 5-Tasks).

limitations: Stated: works only at task granularity; cannot learn or unlearn individual classes within a task (no class-incremental learning/unlearning).
Assumes task-incremental CL with known task identity at inference and a separate generated network per task, which makes forgetting easier to realize and MIA uninformative (all methods about 50%).

No formal unlearning guarantee: forgetting is judged by FA near chance, spill, relapse and MIA. Information about the forgotten task may persist in the shared hypernetwork weights phi (e.g., relearn-speed attacks are not tested).

Relapse is not uniformly the lowest (SCRUB is lower on PMNIST, 5-Tasks and TinyImageNet; UnCLe relapse is 8.70 on PMNIST). RA is below SalUn/JiT on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet and below the FT* oracle.

Unlearning time is not the lowest on larger datasets (SSD, BadTeacher and JiT are faster on CIFAR-100/TinyImageNet), and the learning-time regularizer cost grows with the number of stored task embeddings.
Short request sequences (7-30), vision classification only, 3 seeds, and per-dataset tuning of beta and gamma using FA/RA (the selection criterion uses the evaluation metrics).

Internal inconsistencies in the text: TinyImageNet described as both 10 and 20 tasks; unlearning described both as reverting to standard-normal/Kaiming initialization and as driving parameters to zero; gamma called a 'regularization' strength but multiplies the forget term; UNI metric is undefined; some table references are broken ('??'). It is unclear whether the forgotten task's embedding is deleted or kept in L_reg after unlearning.
future_work: Extend to class-incremental learning and unlearning, i.e., learning and unlearning individual classes within tasks (stated).
Develop robust verification mechanisms and unlearning algorithms that guard against relapse of supposedly forgotten information (stated in Broader Impact).
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: UnCLe shows a cheap, data-free way to unlearn: if knowledge is addressable by a small key (a task embedding feeding a hypernetwork), unlearning becomes a short optimization over the generator (100 or fewer iterations, no data passes, cost independent of dataset size) rather than retraining. It also gives an efficient-unlearning project two evaluation tools, Spill and Relapse, which expose failure modes that RA/FA miss and are relevant whenever unlearning is followed by more training. The noising-strategy ablation and Theorem 1 are a useful worked example of how the choice of 'unlearning target' (fixed noise vs averaged noise vs zero) trades off forgetting quality against damage to retained knowledge. As a pitfall, it shows that offline methods (SalUn, JiT, BadTeacher) look fine at one time step but relapse later.
