It also sits between exact isolation (SISA/CLPU-style, expensive in storage) and shared-parameter approximate unlearning, which is the main design axis for efficient unlearning.
open_questions: Class- or sample-level unlearning inside a hypernetwork framework, and class-incremental (no task-ID) settings where generated heads are shared.
Can noise-alignment unlearning be given a formal guarantee, e.g., bounding the distance between the post-unlearning hypernetwork and one never trained on task f, or a certified/DP-style bound?
How robust is UnCLe to relearning attacks (fine-tuning on a few forget-task samples) compared with a retrained-from-scratch hypernetwork, i.e., does knowledge persist in shared phi?
Reduce the O(#tasks) cost of the output regularizer (e.g., sampling a subset of stored embeddings per step) and analyse when it fails to protect retained tasks.
Combine hypernetwork-based data-free unlearning with federated continual learning (clients generating task heads), where per-client task removal must be cheap in communication.
Explain theoretically why averaged noise (n=10) beats both fixed noise and pure L2 shrinkage, and whether an adaptive n or target distribution gives better retain/forget trade-offs.

papers.title: BID-LoRA: A Parameter-Efficient Framework for Continual Learning and Unlearning
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Mandi, Mandi, India
papers.one_liner: Three separate LoRA adapters (retain, new, forget) on ViT attention layers plus 'escape unlearning' let a pretrained model repeatedly learn and forget classes while training about 5% of its parameters.
papers.summary: Systems like face-recognition access control must repeatedly enroll new identities (continual learning) and delete departed or privacy-protected ones (machine unlearning). The authors formalize this as Continual Learning-Unlearning (CLU). At each cycle t a model M(t-1) receives a forget set, a small replay buffer of retained data, and a new-class set, and must produce M(t) that forgets, retains and learns at once. They show that simply chaining existing CL and MU methods causes 'knowledge leakage': the retained knowledge slowly erodes over repeated cycles. Their fix, BID-LoRA, freezes a pretrained vision transformer and adds three LoRA adapters to the attention layers, one per objective (retain, new, forget). Each loss updates only its own adapter and its own classifier-head rows. For forgetting they propose 'escape unlearning': they compute an embedding direction as far as possible from every retained class centroid (a minimax problem on the unit sphere), scale it by lambda=10, and pull all forget-class embeddings onto that single point with an MSE loss. On a 6-cycle sliding-window benchmark (CIFAR-100 with DeiT; CASIA-Face100 with Face Transformer), BID-LoRA gets forget accuracy of about 0-0.9%, overall accuracy within roughly 2-6 points of a retrained oracle, and MIA close to 0.5. It trains about 5% of the parameters, while all five CLU baselines train 100%.
papers.problem: Continual learning methods are mature but machine unlearning methods are not, and there are few frameworks that learn new classes and remove old ones at the same time. Naively combining a CL method with an MU method causes knowledge leakage, a slow cross-cycle degradation of foundational/retained knowledge. Existing CLU methods (LSF, CLPU-DER++, UniCLUN, UG-CLU, UnCLe) update nearly all parameters, so they are too costly for large pretrained models, and they have been tested on only a few add/delete steps.
papers.core_idea: One adapter cannot serve three competing objectives (retain, acquire, forget) without gradient interference, and that interference accumulates as drift, which is knowledge leakage. BID-LoRA gives each objective its own low-rank adapter and lets each loss update only its own adapter and head rows. For forgetting, it does not use aggressive signals like gradient ascent. It 'passively' collapses forget-class embeddings onto a scaled escape point that lies maximally far from all retained class centroids, so forgetting barely disturbs retained representations.
papers.setting: Continual learning + class-level unlearning (CLU) on pre-trained vision transformers; centralized supervised image classification and face recognition; small replay buffer of retained data available
contributions: Formal definition of the Continual Learning-Unlearning (CLU) problem, with a sequential adaptation operator M(t)=F(M(t-1), Df(t), Dr(t), Dnew(t)) and success criteria for forgetting, retention and learning.
Empirical demonstration that naive CL+MU combinations (ER-ACE+GS-LoRA, DER++ + FU, EWC+SalUn, ER-AML+GS-LoRA) suffer progressive knowledge leakage across CLU cycles (Fig. 7).

BID-LoRA: three-pathway LoRA (retain/new/forget adapters on attention layers) with gradient-isolated updates and masked classifier-head gradients, training about 5% of parameters (5.08% DeiT, 5.00% Face Transformer).
Escape unlearning: a minimax-derived escape direction maximally distant from retained class centroids, scaled (lambda_esc=10), used as an MSE target for forget-class embeddings.
A sliding-window CLU benchmark protocol (6 tasks, each retaining 20, forgetting 10, learning 10 classes) on CIFAR-100 and CASIA-Face100, in which all pretrained knowledge is eventually replaced.
Application to face recognition / identity management with GDPR/CCPA-driven deletion plus new-user enrollment.
method_steps: Inputs for cycle t: previous model M(t-1) (pretrained DeiT / Face Transformer), forget data Df(t) (10 classes), replay buffer Dr(t) that is a 10% subset of the full retain data (20 classes), and new data Dnew(t) (10 classes).

Freeze backbone weights W. On the transformer attention layers, attach three LoRA adapters: retain (B_ret A_ret, rank 8), new (B_new A_new, rank 8) and forget (B_f A_f, rank 4). Classifier-head rows are grouped by retain/forget/new classes. Store a frozen copy of the model as teacher Mt.
Compute the class centroid c_k = mean of emb(x) over class k for each retain class in Dr (forget centroids are also computed but the escape problem uses only retain centroids).

Solve the minimax d* = argmin_{||d||=1} max_i d^T c_ri by iterative optimization from a random unit vector. This gives the unit direction least aligned with every retain centroid. Set the escape point t_escape = lambda_esc * d* (lambda_esc = 10, which pushes it outside the embedding sphere).

For each epoch and each mini-batch triple (Xret, Xf, Xnew), run the RETAIN update first. Freeze the forget and new adapters. Compute L_ret = lambda_ce * CE(z_r, y_r) + lambda_emb * MSE(e_r, e_teacher). Update only (B_ret, A_ret) and the retain-class head rows.

FORGET update: freeze the retain and new adapters. Compute L_f = MSE(emb(Xf), t_escape), a many-to-one collapse of all forget samples onto the escape point. Update only (B_f, A_f) and the forget-class head rows.

NEW update: freeze the retain and forget adapters. Compute L_new = CE(z_n, y_n). Update only (B_new, A_new) and the new-class head rows. Gradients of non-target head rows are masked to zero. If a cycle has only learning or only unlearning, the unused loss is masked.

After training, merge the adapters into the base weights. Algorithm 1 writes W <- W + S(B_ret A_ret + B_new A_new - B_f A_f), while Eq. (1) in Sec. IV-B writes +B_f A_f (sign inconsistency in the paper). The merged model M(t) runs inference with no extra cost.
Repeat for the next request: M(t+1) = F(M(t), ...). In the benchmark the class window slides by 10 each cycle, from classes 0-29 (pretrain) to 60-89 (task 6).

key_definitions.name: Continual Learning-Unlearning (CLU)
key_definitions.plain: A setting where a pretrained model repeatedly receives requests to forget some classes, keep others and learn new ones. Each request is handled by one adaptation step that modifies the previous model. Also called continual adaptation.
key_definitions.formal: D = Dr_full U Df, Dr_full ∩ Df = ∅, Dnew ∩ D = ∅; M(t) = F(M(t-1), Df(t), Dr(t), Dnew(t)), t = 1..T. After step t: (3a) f_M(t): X_Df(i) -/-> Y_Df(i) for all i <= t; (3b) f_M(t): X_Dr(t) -> Y_Dr(t); (3c) f_M(t): X_Dnew(i) -> Y_Dnew(i)

key_definitions.name: Three goals of CLU
key_definitions.plain: (i) precise deletion of unwanted knowledge, (ii) efficient integration of new knowledge while preserving prior information, (iii) minimizing knowledge leakage across cycles.
key_definitions.formal: Abstract / Sec. I

key_definitions.name: Successful CLU criteria
key_definitions.plain: Forgotten classes (including all earlier forgotten ones) should be at or below chance accuracy. Retained and new classes should match an oracle trained directly on the current target classes.
key_definitions.formal: Forgetting: Acc(M(t), Df(i)) <= 1/C for all i <= t; Retention: Acc(M(t), Dr(t)) ≈ Acc(Oracle, Dr(t)); Learning: Acc(M(t), Dnew(t)) ≈ Acc(Oracle, Dnew(t)); C = number of classes

key_definitions.name: Knowledge leakage
key_definitions.plain: Foundational and retained knowledge slowly degrades over repeated learning-unlearning cycles. Unlike catastrophic forgetting, it is gradual and cumulative across adaptation cycles. The paper attributes it to interference among competing objectives sharing one set of parameters.
key_definitions.formal: Measured empirically as the drop in overall accuracy Acco from Task 1 to Task 6, plus KL divergence to the oracle; Fig. 7 shows retain accuracy degrading per cycle for CL+MU combos

key_definitions.name: LoRA update
key_definitions.plain: A frozen weight matrix is augmented with a trainable low-rank product.
key_definitions.formal: h = W x + S (B A x), B in R^{d x r}, A in R^{r x k}, r << min(d,k)

key_definitions.name: Pathway-separated forward pass
key_definitions.plain: Three low-rank adapters share a layer, but each one is trained only by its own objective.
key_definitions.formal: h = W x + S (B_ret A_ret + B_new A_new + B_f A_f) x  (Eq. 1; Algorithm 1 merges with -B_f A_f)

key_definitions.name: Class centroid
key_definitions.plain: The mean embedding of all samples of a class.
key_definitions.formal: c_k = (1/|D_k|) sum_{x in D_k} emb(x)

key_definitions.name: Escape direction and escape point
key_definitions.plain: The unit direction whose largest dot product with any retain-class centroid is as small as possible. Scaling it by lambda_esc places a target point far from the retain embeddings in both direction and distance.
key_definitions.formal: d* = argmin_{||d||=1} max_i d^T c_ri ; t_escape = lambda_esc * d* (lambda_esc = 10)

key_definitions.name: Escape (forget) loss
key_definitions.plain: Pulls every forget-class sample embedding onto the same escape point, which destroys class-discriminative information.
key_definitions.formal: L_f = MSE(emb(X_f), t_escape)

key_definitions.name: Retention loss
key_definitions.plain: Cross-entropy on replayed retain samples plus an embedding anchor that keeps student embeddings close to a frozen teacher copy.
key_definitions.formal: L_ret = lambda_ce * CE(z_r, y_r) + lambda_emb * MSE(e_r, e_t)

key_definitions.name: New-knowledge loss
key_definitions.plain: Standard cross-entropy on new-class samples.
key_definitions.formal: L_new = CE(z_n, y_n)

key_definitions.name: Replay buffer assumption
key_definitions.plain: A small subset of retained data is stored and replayed. The paper uses 10% of the retain data.
key_definitions.formal: Dr ⊂ Dr_full, |Dr| >= 0.1 |Dr_full|

key_definitions.name: Oracle
key_definitions.plain: A model trained directly on the current target class range (e.g., classes 10-39 for task 1) without LoRA, incremental learning or unlearning. Used as the upper bound and as the reference for KL.
key_definitions.formal: Sec. V-A 'Theoretical Best'

key_definitions.name: Tunable ratio
key_definitions.plain: The fraction of model parameters updated during a CLU step. Lower is better.
key_definitions.formal: #trainable / #total parameters

key_definitions.name: Metrics Accf/Accr/Accn/Acco
key_definitions.plain: Accuracy on forgotten classes, retained classes and newly learned classes, and overall accuracy on retained plus new classes (definitions follow UG-CLU).
key_definitions.formal: Ideal: Accf -> 0; Accr, Accn, Acco -> oracle; MIA -> 0.5; KL -> 0

theory.name: No formal theorems
theory.statement_plain: The paper has no theorems, lemmas or proofs. All claims are supported empirically.
theory.assumptions: n/a
theory.significance: There is no unlearning guarantee (exact or certified). Forgetting is verified only by accuracy, label-only MIA and KL to the oracle.

theory.name: Minimax escape direction (Eq. 3)
theory.statement_plain: d* minimizes the maximum alignment (dot product) with any retain centroid over unit vectors. The paper finds it by iterative optimization from a random start and asserts that it converges to the direction maximally distant from all retain centroids.
theory.assumptions: Embeddings meaningfully clustered by class; centroids computed from the 10% buffer. No convergence or optimality proof is given (the problem is nonconvex because of the unit-norm constraint).
theory.significance: Gives a principled, data-driven 'dustbin' target for forget embeddings. Fig. 6 (t-SNE, PCA-sphere) shows forget centroids moving toward d*.

theory.name: Pathway-interference hypothesis (Sec. IV-B)
theory.statement_plain: A single adapter conflates retention, acquisition and forgetting. Their gradient interference causes cumulative drift, i.e., knowledge leakage. Separate adapters with gradient isolation prevent this.
theory.assumptions: Stated as a hypothesis; supported by Table IV (BID-LoRA vs standard LoRA) and Table VI (adapter ablation).
theory.significance: This is the main design rationale for using three adapters instead of one.

theory.name: Necessity of the retain buffer (Sec. VI-A, informal argument)
theory.statement_plain: For non-convex deep models, no viable method removes the dependence on retain data Dr without hurting retention. Df can in principle be replaced by noise proxies or source-free methods, but Dr cannot.
theory.assumptions: Literature-survey argument. Source-free unlearning is limited to convex losses and linear heads. Exceptions exist only in generative settings (FLAT, ESD).
theory.significance: Justifies the 10% replay buffer, and names buffer-free CLU as the main future-work target.

papers.complexity: Trainable parameters: 5.08% (DeiT, CIFAR-100) and 5.00% (Face Transformer), versus 100% for all CLU baselines. Rank ablation on DeiT-Tiny: r=1 1.09%, r=2 2.30%, r=4 3.24%, r=8 5.08%, r=16 8.56%, r=32 14.80%, r=64 25.03%. Standard single LoRA on QKV+head uses 2.54%. Using a 10% retain buffer gives a reported 10x speedup over the full retain set (Table V: 1.0 -> 1x, 0.5 -> 2x, 0.3 -> 3.3x, 0.1 -> 10x). Inference has no extra cost because the adapters are merged into W. Training-time memory includes a frozen teacher copy plus three adapters. Each mini-batch does three sequential forward/backward passes (retain, forget, new). Escape-direction optimization cost is not reported. The paper reports no wall-clock comparison with baselines and no retrain-from-scratch timing.

datasets: CIFAR-100 (classes 0-89 used via the sliding window)
CASIA-Face100 (100 identities sampled from CASIA-WebFace, constructed by GS-LoRA [11])
models: DeiT (data-efficient image transformer; DeiT-Tiny explicitly in the rank ablation, main-table variant unclear)
Face Transformer (Zhong & Deng) for face recognition
baselines: LSF (Learning with Selective Forgetting, Shibata et al. 2021)
CLPU-DER++ (Liu et al. 2022)
UniCLUN (Chatterjee et al. 2024)
UG-CLU (Huang et al. 2025)
UnCLe (Adhikari et al. 2025)
Oracle (retrained on target class window)
Standard LoRA (single adapter on QKV + head) in ablation
CL+MU combos for leakage analysis: ER-ACE+GS-LoRA, DER++ + FU (Tarun et al. fast unlearning), EWC+SalUn, ER-AML+GS-LoRA
metrics: Membership inference attack success rate (label-only MIA, Choquette-Choo et al.; ideal 0.5)
KL divergence between model and oracle logits
headline_results: Protocol: pretrain on classes 0-29. Each of 6 tasks retains 20, forgets 10 and learns 10 classes, and the window slides by 10 per task (task 1 = classes 10-39 ... task 6 = classes 60-89).
Tunable ratio is 5.08% (CIFAR) and 5.00% (face) for BID-LoRA versus 100% for every baseline.

Knowledge leakage (Acco drop from Task 1 to Task 6) is 2.52 points on CIFAR-100 (76.03 -> 73.51) and 1.98 on face (93.20 -> 91.22). The paper claims baselines such as LSF/UniCLUN drop 3-8%. In the table LSF drops 73.55 -> 68.46 on CIFAR, but UniCLUN goes 73.37 -> 73.33, which does not support the claim for UniCLUN.
BID-LoRA is not best in every task: on CIFAR-100, UnCLe has higher Acco in task 1 (76.83), CLPU-DER++ in task 4 (76.94) and UG-CLU in tasks 3 and 5 (75.81).
Rank ablation (DeiT-Tiny, 10 epochs), Acco: r1 41.58, r2 45.31, r4 57.77, r8 74.15, r16 78.86, r32 78.03, r64 78.74. Rank 8 was chosen, although r16 scores higher.
BID-LoRA vs standard LoRA (20 epochs): Acco 80.05 vs 77.88, Accr 77.14 vs 74.29, Accn 85.87 vs 85.07, Accf 0.13 vs 0.00, at 5.08% vs 2.54% params (not parameter-matched).
Retain-buffer ablation, Acco: ratio 1.0 -> 72.58, 0.5 -> 70.35, 0.3 -> 70.37, 0.1 -> 69.98 (10x faster). Accf = 0 at ratios <= 0.5.

Adapter ablation (pathways disabled at test). All on: Accf 0, Accr 84.09, Accn 56.82, Acco 75.00. Forget adapter off: Accf jumps back to 70.45. Retain off: Accr 0.23, Acco 21.67. New off: Accn 0. Pretrained model: Accf 73.64.

limitations: Needs a replay buffer of at least 10% of retain data. This conflicts with the paper's own GDPR/CCPA motivation, since it means storing face images (stated, and the main future-work item).
Forgetting is approximate and has no formal guarantee. It is verified only by accuracy, label-only MIA and KL to the oracle.

Table VI shows that switching off the forget adapter restores forget accuracy to 70.45%, so before merging, forgetting is a removable additive low-rank patch on top of intact base knowledge. Whether merged weights truly erase information (versus mask it) is not tested with relearning or adapter-subtraction attacks.

Accf of about 0% is far below the chance level 1/C that the paper itself sets as its criterion, which could itself make forgotten classes detectable (Streisand-type effect). Only a label-only MIA is used.
Only class-level unlearning. No instance/sample-level deletion and no task-agnostic mixed request patterns beyond the fixed 20/10/10 sliding window over 6 cycles.
Small scale: about 30 active classes per task, DeiT(-Tiny) and Face Transformer only. No experiments on large models despite the efficiency motivation.

Hyperparameters (lambda_ce, lambda_emb, LoRA scaling S, epochs and optimizer for the main tables, exactly which attention projections get adapters) are not fully specified. No seeds or variance are reported.

Internal inconsistencies: merge sign (+B_f A_f in Eq. 1 vs -B_f A_f in Algorithm 1). Task-5 baseline Acco values in Table I duplicate Task-3. The text claims Accr stays within 70.83-76.00 for tasks 2-6, but task 6 is 68.67. UG-CLU is called 'weight saliency-based' in Sec. V-B but gradient/Hessian/KL-based in Sec. II-D. The Discussion promises an 'algorithmic perspective' subsection that does not appear.

The standard-LoRA comparison is not parameter-matched (2.54% vs 5.08%). Baselines all train 100% of parameters, but their adaptation to pretrained DeiT (notably UnCLe, which the paper says cannot be directly applied to pretrained models) is not explained.
The criterion that all previously forgotten classes stay forgotten (for all i <= t) is stated, but the tables appear to report Accf only for the current forget set (unclear from text).
A single escape point is shared by all forget classes across cycles. Possible collisions with future new-class embeddings, or saturation after many cycles, are not analyzed.
future_work: Eliminate the retention buffer entirely (reduce from 10% to 0%).
Extend to other biometric modalities such as iris and fingerprint recognition, where privacy-driven unlearning is critical.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: BID-LoRA is a concrete template for cheap, repeated class-level unlearning on large pretrained models. It freezes the backbone, isolates the forgetting objective in a tiny rank-4 adapter, and merges it at the end, so each deletion request touches about 5% of parameters and needs only a 10% retain buffer (reported 10x faster than using full retain data). Escape unlearning is a simple, cheap alternative to gradient-ascent or random-label unlearning. It needs only class centroids, one small minimax solve and an MSE loss, and it avoids the retain-accuracy collapse that strong unlearning signals cause. For a project on efficient unlearning, the knowledge-leakage concept and the 6-cycle sliding-window protocol are useful evaluation tools: efficiency should be measured over many sequential requests, not just one. The main pitfalls are that the guarantees are only empirical, the forget adapter is literally separable from intact base knowledge before merging, and there is no wall-clock comparison against retraining. These leave room for combining adapter isolation with exact (SISA-style) or certified mechanisms.
open_questions: Buffer-free or privacy-preserving CLU: replace the 10% retain buffer with stored class prototypes/centroids, generative replay, or teacher-only distillation. Then quantify the retention loss and the privacy gain.

Robustness of forgetting: since disabling the forget adapter restores Accf to about 70%, test relearning attacks, adapter-subtraction and stronger MIAs (e.g., LiRA/U-LiRA) on merged models, and compare against a retrain-from-scratch oracle.

Theory for escape unlearning: characterize the minimax d* (it relates to a smallest-enclosing-cone / max-margin problem). Bound the interference between the escape point and retain or future-new classes, and study behaviour as forgotten classes accumulate over many cycles.

Exact-unlearning variant: shard adapters per class or per request (a SISA-style idea) so that forgetting means deleting an adapter. Compare its cost and guarantees with BID-LoRA's approximate escape loss.
Instance-level and federated CLU: extend the three-pathway design to sample-level deletion and to clients in federated continual learning, where adapters could be communicated instead of full models.

Fair efficiency evaluation: run parameter-matched comparisons (single LoRA at 5% vs three adapters), wall-clock and FLOP accounting per request, and longer horizons (T >> 6) to check whether knowledge leakage keeps accumulating.

papers.title: Knowledge Efficient Federated Continual Learning for Industrial Edge Systems
affiliations: Shien-Ming Wu School of Intelligent Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China
School of Mechanical and Automotive Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China
Pazhou Lab, Guangzhou, China
China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, Beijing, China
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Network Science and Engineering, vol. 12, no. 3, pp. 2107-2120, May/June 2025 (DOI 10.1109/TNSE.2025.3544614)
papers.one_liner: Federated continual learning that splits models into a meta-learned shared encoder plus task-specific heads stored in a server-side key-value pool retrieved by task embedding.
papers.summary: Industrial edge devices (e.g., vibration sensors on bearings) see data that differs across factories/clients (inter-client heterogeneity) and also drifts over time within each client as operating conditions change (intra-client heterogeneity). FedAvg assumes static client data, and naive training on new conditions causes catastrophic forgetting. MeCo is a federated continual learning method that splits every client model into a task-invariant part u (the early layers, shared and averaged across clients) and a task-specific part v (last residual block plus classifier). The shared part is trained with a MAML-inspired alternating scheme: on each task the client first adapts v on a support split, then updates u on a query split with v fixed, and the server averages u. Every finished task-specific part v is stored on the server in a knowledge pool keyed by a task embedding (mean feature vector of a few samples). When a client starts a new task it sends its embedding, the server returns the top-K most similar stored v's (cosine distance), and the client blends them in with learned attention weights to jump-start learning. On a bearing fault benchmark built from CWRU and SCUT-FD, MeCo reaches 92.26% mean average accuracy (about 2 points above FedWeIT), lower forgetting, and 1.74x lower server-to-client traffic than FedWeIT. There is no unlearning component and no formal theory.
papers.problem: Existing FL methods handle inter-client (spatial) data heterogeneity but assume each client's data is static, which fails in industrial edge systems where sensor data streams drift over time (intra-client, temporal heterogeneity). Retraining from scratch on every drift is too expensive, sequential training causes catastrophic forgetting, replay-based FCL needs memory that edge devices lack and raises privacy/communication concerns, and full-model knowledge transfer (e.g., FedWeIT rehearsing all task parameters) costs communication that grows with the number of tasks.
papers.core_idea: Decompose the model into a shared task-invariant encoder u and small task-specific heads v. Learn u with a meta-learning (support/query, alternating) procedure so it captures features common to all tasks and is robust to forgetting, aggregate it by FedAvg, and keep every task-specific head v on the server in a key-value knowledge pool keyed by a task embedding. New tasks query the pool and fuse only the top-K most similar heads, so knowledge is transferred selectively (reducing interference) and communication scales with K rather than with the total number of tasks.
papers.setting: Federated continual learning (synchronous; one server, N edge clients, each with a private sequential task stream; domain-incremental CL claimed; no replay buffer on clients); application: industrial bearing fault diagnosis from vibration time series converted to CWT images
contributions: MeCo, an FCL method for industrial edge systems combining Meta task-invariant knowledge consolidation and Consistent task-specific knowledge transfer, targeting both inter-client and intra-client data heterogeneity.

A server-side key-value knowledge pool of task-specific parameters, with task-embedding-based top-K selection (cosine distance) and attention-weighted fusion; positioned as orthogonal to rehearsal and suited to resource-constrained edges (no client-side sample storage).
Communication/computation complexity comparison (Table II): MeCo O(NP + NKV) communication vs FedWeIT O(NP + NTV).

Experiments on Overlapped-FD (CWRU + SCUT-FD bearing data, 150 classes, 30 tasks) and CIFAR-100 scalability tests, with ablations on components, backbones (MobileNet, ResNet18/50, ViT-B/16), distance metrics, pool size and K.
method_steps: Setup: model q = u o v. Task-invariant u maps input (CWT time-frequency image of a 1024-step vibration window) to a b-dim feature space; task-specific v (for ResNet: last residual block + classifier) maps features to labels. Server holds global u^(0); each client holds v_i^(0); knowledge pool P is empty; attention weights alpha_i^(0) are initialised (Alg. 1, line 1).
Round t: server broadcasts u^(t-1) to all clients; each client sets u_i^(t) = u^(t) (Alg. 1, lines 3-5).
Client randomly splits its current task data T_i^(t) into a support set T_{i,s} and a query set T_{i,q} (line 6).
Client computes the task embedding k_i^(t) = (1/|T_{i,s}|) * sum_j u_i^(t)(x_j) over support samples (Eq. 7; e.g., 32 samples suffice on CWRU) and uploads this b-dim vector to the server (line 7).

Server computes cosine distance Pi(k_i^(t), k_m) to every key in the pool and selects the K entries with smallest total distance (Eq. 8), then sends their task-specific parameters B_i^(t) = {v_s} to the client (lines 8-9; S2C cost O(NKV)).

Client builds a jump-started head v_i^(t) = alpha_i^(t) (elementwise*) B_i^(t) + v_i^(t-1), i.e., its own previous head plus attention-weighted retrieved heads (Eq. 9, line 10). How alpha is trained is not specified in detail.

ClientUpdate (Alg. 2): inner update - freeze u and take tau_v SGD steps (step gamma_v) on v using the support set; outer update - freeze the updated v^+ and take tau_u SGD steps (step gamma_u) on u using the query set; return (u^+, v^+). In experiments: 5 local epochs per round, Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-5, batch 64, early stop after 3 epochs without improvement.
Client uploads u_i and v_i to the server (line 12; C2S cost O(NP)).

Server aggregates the shared part by plain averaging u^(t) = (1/N) sum_i u_i (FedAvg on u only, line 13) and stores each (k_i, v_i^(t)) as a new key-value entry in the knowledge pool (line 14); stored entries are deliberately no longer linked to their client or round.
Repeat for subsequent rounds/tasks (60 communication rounds, 6 tasks per client in main experiments); u is refined during meta-training and fixed in meta-testing.

key_definitions.name: Inter-client data heterogeneity
key_definitions.plain: Different clients (machines/factories) have different data distributions at the same time (spatial non-IID); this is what classic FL work targets.
key_definitions.formal: D_i differs from D_j for clients i != j

key_definitions.name: Intra-client data heterogeneity (data drift)
key_definitions.plain: The data distribution of a single client changes over time as new tasks/operating conditions arrive; old task data is no longer available.
key_definitions.formal: client i sees a stream T_i^(1), ..., T_i^(t); T_i^(t) is only available at round t

key_definitions.name: Domain-incremental CL (domain-CL)
key_definitions.plain: Each task keeps the same label set but the input distribution changes; claimed to be the common industrial case and the paper's focus (though the benchmark has 5 distinct classes per task, so the exact label protocol is unclear).

key_definitions.name: Regularized CL objective
key_definitions.plain: Per-task loss plus a penalty for moving away from the previous task's parameters, summed over the task sequence.
key_definitions.formal: f_i(q_i^(t); q_i^(t-1), T_i^(t)) = F_i(q_i^(t); T_i^(t)) + lambda R(q_i^(t), q_i^(t-1)); min sum_t f_i (Eqs. 3-4)

key_definitions.name: FCL objective
key_definitions.plain: Average over clients and over each client's task sequence, where each client may use knowledge from all clients' previous parameters (spatio-temporal knowledge).
key_definitions.formal: min (1/N) sum_{i=1..N} sum_{t=1..N_i} f_i(q_i^(t); q_{1:n}^(t-1), T_i^(t)) (Eq. 5); with decomposition q = u o v (Eq. 6)

key_definitions.name: Parameter decomposition
key_definitions.plain: Split the network into task-invariant parameters u (shared feature extractor) and task-specific parameters v (small head per task).
key_definitions.formal: u: R^d -> R^b, v: R^b -> Y, q_i^(t) = u_i^(t) o v_i^(t)

key_definitions.name: Knowledge pool
key_definitions.plain: Server-side store of all historical task-specific parameter sets from all clients, each keyed by a task embedding; entries are detached from client identity.
key_definitions.formal: B = {(k_1, v_1), ..., (k_M, v_M)}, k_m in R^b; key set K = {k_m}

key_definitions.name: Task embedding
key_definitions.plain: A fixed-length summary of a task: the average feature vector produced by the shared encoder on a small support subset.
key_definitions.formal: k_i^(t) = (1/|T_{i,s}|) sum_j u_i^(t)(x_j) (Eq. 7; written with (u(x_j), y_j) pairs in the paper)

key_definitions.name: Consistent parameter selection (top-K)
key_definitions.plain: Server picks the K pool entries whose keys are closest (cosine distance) to the new task's embedding.
key_definitions.formal: K_i^(t) = argmin over {s_1..s_K} subset of [1,M] of sum_{k=1..K} Pi(k_i^(t), k_{s_k}) (Eq. 8)

key_definitions.name: Attention-weighted fusion
key_definitions.plain: The new head equals the client's previous head plus an elementwise-attention-weighted combination of the retrieved heads.
key_definitions.formal: v_i^(t) = alpha_i^(t) (elementwise*) B_i^(t) + v_i^(t-1) (Eq. 9)

key_definitions.name: Jump-starting
key_definitions.plain: Borrowed from RL: learning a good prior/initialisation for the current task by combining knowledge from previous tasks with a little new data.

key_definitions.name: Mean (macro-averaged) Average Accuracy, MAA
key_definitions.plain: For each client, average test accuracy over all tasks seen so far; then average over clients.

key_definitions.name: Forgetting
key_definitions.plain: How much a task's accuracy has dropped from right after it was learned to now, averaged over all earlier tasks.

key_definitions.name: F1_macro
key_definitions.plain: Mean of per-client F1 scores.
key_definitions.formal: F1_macro = (1/N) sum_i F1_i

key_definitions.name: S2C / C2S communication
key_definitions.plain: Total bytes sent server-to-client and client-to-server during training (reported in GB).

theory.name: No theorems/lemmas
theory.statement_plain: The paper contains no formal theorems, convergence proofs, or forgetting bounds; its analysis is a problem formulation (Eqs. 1-6) and an asymptotic cost comparison.
theory.assumptions: n/a
theory.significance: Any guarantee (convergence of the alternating u/v updates, forgetting bounds, privacy of embeddings) is an open gap.

theory.name: Communication/computation complexity (Sec. IV-D, Table II)
theory.statement_plain: Per round, MeCo communicates O(NP + NKV) (FedAvg-style u exchange plus top-K task-specific heads) and costs O(E n_c P + K V^2) computation per client; FedWeIT needs O(NP + NTV) communication and O(E n_c P + P + P^2) computation; FedAvg+EWC O(NP) / O(E n_c P + P^2); FedAvg+MAS O(NP) / O(E n_c P + P); FedAvg+iCaRL O(NP) / O(E n_c P + n_c^2 P); FedAvg O(NP) / O(E n_c P).
theory.assumptions: N clients, P model params, E local epochs, n_c samples per client, T tasks, V size of one task-specific head, K retrieved heads; derivation is informal (the K V^2 term for selection is not justified).
theory.significance: Explains the S2C saving vs FedWeIT: MeCo transfers K heads instead of heads from all T tasks, so cost does not grow with the task history.

theory.name: Task-distribution coverage assumption (Sec. IV-B)
theory.statement_plain: The data distribution of a new task is assumed to lie within the aggregate distribution of all historical tasks, so relevant knowledge can be found in the pool.
theory.assumptions: Stated as a 'mild assumption'; not formalised or tested.
theory.significance: Justifies similarity-based retrieval; it fails for genuinely novel tasks (cold start), where the retrieved heads may inject irrelevant knowledge.

papers.complexity: Learning: communication O(NP + NKV) per round (S2C: top-K heads O(NKV) plus global u; C2S: u and v), computation O(E n_c P + K V^2) per client per round. Empirically on Overlapped-FD/ResNet18: S2C 3.1 GB vs FedWeIT 5.4 GB (5.4/3.1 = 1.74x, the headline claim) and vs FedAvg 2.6 GB; C2S 2.6 GB for all FL methods. Server storage grows linearly with the number of (client, task) entries M times head size V; no client-side replay storage (vs iCaRL buffer of 12,000 samples). Training time per batch of 16 across 5 clients with ResNet18: MeCo 142 ms vs FedWeIT 150 ms vs FedAvg 125 ms; inference 87 / 100 / 75 ms. Unlearning cost: not discussed (the paper has no deletion mechanism).

datasets: Overlapped-FD (constructed): CWRU + SCUT-FD bearing fault data; CWRU split by 4 motor speeds (1730/1750/1772/1797 rpm) plus 6 pairwise speed combinations = 10 conditions x 10 classes x 2 tasks = 100 classes/20 tasks; SCUT-FD split by 500/800/1100/1400 rpm plus combinations = 10 conditions x 5 classes x 1 task = 50 classes/10 tasks; total 150 classes, 5 classes per task, tasks randomly assigned to clients; no task-boundary information used
CWRU bearing dataset (Case Western Reserve University; drive-end/fan-end deep groove ball bearings, fault types IF, OF, RoF plus normal, loads 0-3)
SCUT-FD (real industrial bearing fault dataset from SCUT, ref [36])
CIFAR-100 (scalability study only)
models: ResNet18 (main, trained from scratch, ~11.7M params; last residual block + classifier = task-specific)
ResNet50
MobileNet (MobileNetV2, ~4.2M params)
ViT-B/16 (~86M params)
Input: vibration time series converted to time-frequency images by continuous wavelet transform over 1024-step windows (0-12 kHz); no recurrent/temporal sequence model is used
baselines: STL (single-task learning, separate model per task)
EWC (local CL, regularization)
MAS (local CL, regularization)
iCaRL (local CL, rehearsal, buffer 12,000)
OML (local CL, meta-learning)
FedAvg
FedAvg + EWC
FedAvg + iCaRL
FedWeIT (main FCL competitor)
Not included: FedProx, FedKNOW, FedPer (FedPer only discussed in Remark 1); FedAvg+MAS appears only in the complexity table
metrics: MAA (called Mean Average Accuracy in abstract, Macro-averaged Accuracy in Sec. V)
headline_results: Overlapped-FD, ResNet18, 5 clients x 6 tasks, 60 rounds (Table IV): MeCo MAA 92.26 (+/-0.17), F1 91.25 (+/-0.34), forgetting 0.02, S2C 3.1 GB, C2S 2.6 GB
FedWeIT 90.13 / 87.45 / 0.03 / 5.4 GB / 2.6 GB -> MeCo +2.13 MAA and 1.74x cheaper S2C (5.4/3.1)
Local-only: STL 82.36, EWC 80.82, MAS 80.63, iCaRL 82.42, OML 82.57 MAA; all FL methods beat local CL
Ablation (Table V): w/o consistent knowledge transfer MAA 81.66, F1 79.2; w/o meta consolidation MAA 85.74, F1 84.4 (paper's printed deltas -10.50/-11.05/-6.42/-6.85 do not all match the arithmetic)
Backbones (Table VI) MAA MeCo vs FedWeIT vs FedAvg: MobileNet 88.92/86.71/84.55; ResNet50 94.03/91.99/88.72; ViT-B/16 95.41/92.61/89.52
Distance metric (Table VII): cosine 92.26 > KL 91.77 > Euclidean 91.13 MAA
Fig. 9 (read from plot, approximate): MAA rises from ~83% to ~92% as pool size grows 5 to 25; best K is about 3 (~92.3%), K=1 ~87.5%, slight drop for K=4-5 (irrelevant knowledge)
Scalability (Table VIII): CIFAR-100 N=5 to 10 (N_i=10): MeCo 70.01 to 69.95 MAA, forgetting 2.75 to 3.40%; FedAvg 66.31 to 60.14; FedAvg+iCaRL 67.98 to 63.19
Overlapped-FD N_i=6 to 12: MeCo 92.26 to 91.72 MAA, forgetting 2.20 to 2.93%; FedAvg 88.46 to 85.06 (forgetting 12.60 to 14.70%)

limitations: No theoretical guarantees (no convergence or forgetting bounds); the task-coverage assumption is informal and untested on novel tasks.
Evaluation is mostly one constructed fault-diagnosis benchmark with 5-10 simulated clients and 3 runs; CIFAR-100 only for scalability.
Task boundaries are effectively known/discrete; authors note task-transition detection would be needed in real deployments.
The server keeps every client's task-specific parameters and receives task embeddings; privacy of these artefacts is claimed but not analysed (no DP, no attack evaluation).
Knowledge pool grows without bound (one entry per client per task); pool storage and retrieval cost at scale are not studied (Fig. 9 only up to 30 entries).

Pool entries are deliberately decoupled from their client/round, and retrieved heads are additively merged into other clients' heads, so a client's knowledge spreads with no record - a problem for deletion requests.

Training of attention weights alpha and the exact meta-learning objective are under-specified; the 'meta' step is a first-order alternating support/query scheme rather than true MAML bi-level optimisation.

Inconsistencies: Sec. III-B says pre-trained models are used but Sec. V-A says no pre-trained weights; forgetting is reported as 0.10 (FedAvg) in Table IV but 12.60% for the apparently same setting in Table VIII; '1997 rpm' vs 1797 in Table III; 'C_4^2 = 10' (actually 4 + 6 conditions); domain-CL is claimed but tasks have distinct classes; ablation deltas do not match.
Weak baseline coverage: no FedProx, FedKNOW, or other parameter-decomposition FCL methods; FedPer only discussed.
future_work: Apply MeCo beyond industrial fault diagnosis to other domains and tasks.
Extend the framework to continual pre-training tasks.
Add task-transition detection for non-discrete, realistic task boundaries.
Balance the growing communication/computation overhead as the number of clients increases.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: MeCo has no unlearning, but its structure shows where an unlearning mechanism would have to go in federated continual learning. Forgetting a client or a task would need three things: (1) deleting that client's/task's (key, head) entries from the server knowledge pool, which is cheap only if provenance is kept, while MeCo deliberately drops the client/round link; (2) undoing the spread of those heads into other clients' heads through Eq. 9 (v_i^(t) = alpha * B + v_i^(t-1)) and on into later pool entries, which needs a retrieval/lineage log (the additive form even suggests an approximate 'subtract alpha*v_s' correction, but later gradient steps make it inexact); (3) removing the client's influence from the FedAvg-aggregated, meta-learned task-invariant encoder u, which is a standard federated-unlearning problem (retrain from a checkpoint, or shard clients SISA-style). The parameter decomposition itself is a useful efficiency idea: if retrieval were turned off or tracked, task knowledge sits in small isolated modules whose deletion is exact and costs O(V), much like SISA's isolation or adapter-based CL+unlearning (BID-LoRA). Task-embedding keys could also find the pool entries relevant to a forget request. Pitfalls to avoid: shared-encoder entanglement, cross-client mixing of heads, and an unbounded pool that keeps everything forever.
open_questions: Design a provenance-tracked knowledge pool (record client, task, and which entries each head retrieved via Eq. 9) and an exact client/task deletion procedure; measure its cost against retraining MeCo from scratch.
How should the shared, FedAvg-aggregated encoder u be unlearned? Compare freezing u after meta-training, checkpoint rollback, and SISA-style client sharding of u, in accuracy vs unlearning time.

Exploit the additive fusion v = alpha*B + v_prev for approximate unlearning (subtract the forgotten head's weighted contribution, then briefly fine-tune), and bound the leftover influence after later local updates.
Task-level continual unlearning in MeCo: does deleting a pool entry actually remove the capability (forget accuracy, membership-inference success), given leakage into u and into other clients' heads?
Privacy audit: can stored heads v or class-conditioned task embeddings k leak client data (membership/attribute inference), and can DP noise on k/v keep retrieval accuracy?
Provide convergence and forgetting guarantees for the alternating u/v (support/query) update under the task-coverage assumption, and handle novel tasks that violate it.

papers.title: Making AI Forget You: Data Deletion in Machine Learning
affiliations: Stanford University, Dept. of Electrical Engineering
Stanford University, Dept. of Computer Science
Stanford University, Dept. of Biomedical Data Science
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2019 (33rd Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
papers.one_liner: Defines exact data deletion as distributional equality with retraining, measures it by amortized runtime, and gives two provably deletion-efficient k-means algorithms.
papers.summary: Laws such as the GDPR's right to be forgotten let people withdraw their data, but a trained model still carries what it learned from it. Retraining from scratch on the remaining data always works, but it is expensive. This paper treats data deletion in machine learning as a computational problem. A deletion operation is exact if the updated model has exactly the same probability distribution as a model retrained without the point, which also covers randomized learners. Deletion is framed as an online problem: after training on n points, m deletion requests arrive one at a time. Efficiency is the amortized runtime per request, which can be no better than Omega(n/m). The paper proposes four design principles for deletion-friendly learners: linearity, laziness, modularity and quantization. It then builds two exact deletion algorithms for k-means. Q-k-means rounds the centroids to a randomly shifted grid at every Lloyd iteration. Removing a few points then almost never changes the rounded centroids, so most deletions need only a cheap check against stored metadata. DC-k-means splits the data at random into w leaf sub-problems and merges their centroids at a root, so a deletion recomputes only one leaf and the root. Both come with runtime and quality guarantees. On six datasets they average more than 100x faster than retraining, with similar clustering quality.
papers.problem: When a user withdraws consent, the deployed model should become independent of that user's data, as if it had never been trained on it. For most models the only known way to do this is full retraining, which is too costly when deletion requests keep arriving. Before this work there was no definition of deletion for stochastic learning algorithms and no notion of asymptotic deletion efficiency or its trade-offs.
papers.core_idea: Exact deletion means the updated model is equal in distribution to the retrained model. Its efficiency is the amortized time over a stream of deletions, measured against an Omega(n/m) lower bound. To make deletion cheap, design the learner so its output depends on the data in a controlled way. Q-k-means quantizes the centroids so that small changes to the data almost never change the model, which can be checked from stored metadata. DC-k-means splits the computation into modules so that a deletion only touches one small sub-problem plus the root.
papers.setting: Centralized unsupervised clustering (k-means). One model and one database, one data point per deletion request, and a stream of deletion requests that arrives online after training.
contributions: A formal definition of a data deletion operation for possibly randomized learning algorithms: R_A(D, A(D), i) must equal A(D_{-i}) in distribution. The appendix adds a robust (adversarial) variant and a delta-approximate relaxation, and discusses how they relate to differential privacy.

An online data deletion model in which m deletion requests are processed one at a time and cost is the amortized runtime. This gives an Omega(n/m) lower bound and the notion of alpha-deletion efficiency (amortized O(n^{1-alpha}) when m = Theta(n^alpha)).

Q-k-means, a quantized Lloyd's algorithm. It uses a random-phase epsilon-lattice, memoized metadata, a gamma-balance correction and a loss-based early stop. m deletions take expected time O(m^2 d^{5/2} / epsilon), which does not depend on n for fixed m and epsilon. Its expected loss is bounded relative to k-means++.
DC-k-means, a w-ary divide-and-conquer k-means with uniform random leaf assignment. With a depth-1 tree and w = Theta(n^rho), m deletions take expected time O(m * max{n^rho, n^{1-rho}} * d).
Conditions for alpha-deletion efficiency. Q-k-means with epsilon = Theta(n^{-beta}) needs alpha <= (1-beta)/2. DC-k-means needs alpha <= 1 - max{rho, 1-rho}, which is at most 1/2.
Experiments on 6 datasets: amortized runtime (train once plus 1,000 deletions) averages over 100x speedup against k-means++/Lloyd's retraining, with comparable loss ratio, silhouette and NMI.

Four engineering principles for deletion-efficient learning (linearity, laziness, modularity, quantization), and a discussion of how to apply them to segmented regression, random-feature kernel regression, decision trees and random forests, and DNNs trained with SGD.
Open-source Python code: github.com/tginart/deletion-efficient-kmeans.
method_steps: [Preprocessing] Min-max scale the data into the unit hypercube [0,1]^d; MNIST is already scaled. The theory assumes data in [0,1]^d or a bounded radius.
[Q-k-means train 1] Initialize k centroids with k-means++ and save them as metadata. Compute the initial partition pi and the loss L.
[Q-k-means train 2] For tau = 1..T (T = 10 in experiments), store the previous centroids c' and compute the analog centroids c as the means of the current partition.

[Q-k-means train 3] Balance correction: for any cluster with |pi_k| < gamma*n/k (gamma = 0.2), replace its centroid with a mass-weighted average of the current centroid (weight |pi_k|) and the previous centroid c'_k (weight gamma*n/k - |pi_k|). In effect the small cluster is padded with mass at the old centroid so it cannot move too much.

[Q-k-means train 4] Draw a fresh random phase theta ~ Unif[-1/2, 1/2]^d and quantize each centroid to the nearest vertex of the shifted epsilon-lattice: Q(x) = epsilon*(theta + argmin_{j in Z^d} ||x - epsilon*(theta + j)||).

[Q-k-means train 5] Reassign points to the nearest quantized centroid. Save (c, theta, c_hat, cluster sizes) to metadata, an extra O(kTd) memory. Compute the new loss L'. If L' < L, accept the step; otherwise stop early, because quantization means a step can increase the loss. Output the quantized centroids.

[Q-k-means delete] For a point p: if p is one of the k-means++ initial centroids, retrain from scratch. Otherwise, for each stored iteration, find p's cluster, compute that cluster's centroid without p (linearity: subtract p's contribution from the mean), apply the gamma-correction, and re-quantize with the same stored phase theta. If any quantized centroid changes, retrain from scratch. Otherwise update the stored analog centroids and counts and return the unchanged model. The check costs O(kTd) per deletion.

[DC-k-means train 1] Build a perfect w-ary tree of height h. Experiments use depth 1 with w ~ n^0.3 rounded to the nearest power of 2. Assign each point to a leaf independently and uniformly at random (a multinomial partition).

[DC-k-means train 2] At each leaf, run k-means++ seeding plus T Lloyd iterations to get k centroids. Pass these centroids up as data for the parent. The root dataset has k*w points. Run k-means at the root and output the root centroids. Save all nodes (leaf datasets and centroids) as metadata.

[DC-k-means delete] Find p's leaf and remove p. Re-solve that leaf's k-means, replace its old centroids in the parent's dataset, re-solve each node up to the root, and return the new root centroids. The number of leaves is held fixed by rounding to a power of 2; if a deletion changes the rounding, retrain from scratch.

[Online deletion benchmark] Train once on the full dataset, then process 1,000 deletions chosen uniformly at random without replacement, producing a valid model after each. Report the wall-clock time of training plus all deletions divided by 1,000. The baseline handles each deletion by retraining k-means++ plus Lloyd's.

key_definitions.name: Learning algorithm (Def. A.1)
key_definitions.plain: A possibly randomized algorithm that maps a dataset to a model plus arbitrary metadata, such as stored partial computations used later for deletions. It must touch every data point at least once and runs sequentially, so it takes Omega(n) time.
key_definitions.formal: A: D -> H x M, randomized; runtime Omega(n)

key_definitions.name: Data deletion operation (Def. 3.1 / A.2)
key_definitions.plain: A procedure that takes the dataset, the trained model (with metadata) and an index i, and returns a model with exactly the same distribution as retraining from scratch without point i. This is exact deletion. For deterministic algorithms it reduces to equality.
key_definitions.formal: R_A(D, A(D), i) =_d A(D_{-i}) for all D and all i chosen independently of A(D)

key_definitions.name: Robust data deletion operation (Def. A.3)
key_definitions.plain: The same distributional equality, but it must hold even when the deleted index is chosen by an adversary who can see the model and its internal state.
key_definitions.formal: R_A(D, A(D), i) =_d A(D_{-i}) for any i, possibly chosen adversarially with knowledge of A(D)

key_definitions.name: Online data deletion, average case (Def. A.4, Alg. 3)
key_definitions.plain: Train once. Then m = Theta(n^alpha) indices, chosen uniformly at random without replacement, are deleted one at a time, and a valid model must be output after each. Cost is the expected total runtime divided by m.
key_definitions.formal: mu <- A(D); for tau = 1..m: i ~ Unif; mu <- R(D, mu, i); D <- D_{-i}. Amortized cost = E[total time]/m

key_definitions.name: Fractional power regime
key_definitions.plain: The asymptotic regime in which the number of deletions grows as a fractional power of the dataset size.
key_definitions.formal: m = Theta(n^alpha), 0 < alpha < 1

key_definitions.name: alpha-deletion efficient (Def. A.5)
key_definitions.plain: An algorithm whose amortized time over the online deletion stream matches the Omega(n/m) lower bound when m = Theta(n^alpha). Retraining costs at least n per request; deletion-efficient algorithms spread the training cost over all m requests.
key_definitions.formal: amortized runtime O(n^{1-alpha}) when m = Theta(n^alpha)

key_definitions.name: delta-approximate deletion (Def. A.6)
key_definitions.plain: A relaxation of exact deletion: for any event S, the deletion output can be at most 1/delta times more likely to land in S than a retrained model. Outcomes that the deletion operation never produces are still allowed.
key_definitions.formal: Pr[A(D_{-i}) in S | D_{-i}] >= delta * Pr[R_A(D, A(D), i) in S | D_{-i}] for all measurable S in H x M

key_definitions.name: epsilon-differential privacy (recalled, App. A.2.1)
key_definitions.plain: Output probabilities change by at most a factor e^epsilon when one data point changes. The paper discusses DP as a possible route to approximate deletion (privatize the model and ignore deletion requests) and lists its problems.
key_definitions.formal: Pr[A(D1) in S] <= e^epsilon Pr[A(D2) in S] for neighbouring D1, D2

key_definitions.name: gamma-balanced partition (Def. B.1)
key_definitions.plain: Every cluster holds at least a gamma fraction of the average cluster size n/k. Small clusters make the quantized centroids unstable, so Q-k-means corrects them.
key_definitions.formal: |pi_k| >= gamma*n/k for all clusters k

key_definitions.name: Random-phase epsilon-lattice quantization (App. B.1.2)
key_definitions.plain: Round each coordinate to a grid of spacing epsilon whose offset is shifted by a uniformly random phase that is redrawn at every iteration. The random shift removes bias, much like dithering, and makes the chance that a point sits near a grid boundary computable.
key_definitions.formal: a(x) = argmin_{j in Z^d} ||x - epsilon(theta + j)||_2; Q(x) = epsilon(theta + a(x)); theta_tau ~ Unif[-1/2, 1/2]^d iid

key_definitions.name: Linearity (principle)
key_definitions.plain: If parameters are linear functions of the data (sums, means, least-squares solutions), one point's influence can be subtracted out exactly, for example with Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury or QR updates. Deleting from linear least squares takes O(d^2).

key_definitions.name: Laziness (principle)
key_definitions.plain: Delay computation until inference time, as in k-nearest neighbours or Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression. Deletion is then trivial: just drop the point. Computation moves from training to inference.

key_definitions.name: Modularity (principle)
key_definitions.plain: Restrict each part of the model state to depend only on one partition of the data, so a deletion only requires recomputing the affected modules. DC-k-means does this with its divide-and-conquer tree.

key_definitions.name: Quantization (principle)
key_definitions.plain: Use stability, the fact that small changes to the data cause small changes to the model, by discretizing the map from data to model. A few deletions then most likely leave the quantized model unchanged, and this can be checked cheaply.

theory.name: Remark 3.1 (amortized lower bound)
theory.statement_plain: In the online setting with n points and m deletion requests, any sequential learning algorithm needs Omega(n/m) amortized time per request. Training alone costs Omega(n), and even a constant-time deletion oracle cannot avoid that cost.
theory.assumptions: The learning algorithm processes every point at least once and runs sequentially. Best case is an O(1) deletion oracle.
theory.significance: Sets the benchmark for optimal deletion efficiency, which motivates the definition of alpha-deletion efficiency. Tight bounds for ridge regression, decision trees and stochastic optimization are left open.

theory.name: Theorem 4.1 (Q-k-means deletion time)
theory.statement_plain: For data in [0,1]^d and fixed T, k, epsilon and gamma, Q-k-means handles m deletions in expected total time O(m^2 d^{5/2} / epsilon). For fixed m and epsilon this does not depend on n, because the chance of stability rises as fast as the problem grows.
theory.assumptions: Expectation over the random quantization phases and the k-means++ initialization. Worst case over all normalized datasets. Deletions are uniformly random and independent of the model (average case). k, T and gamma are treated as constants.
theory.significance: Shows that quantization gives sublinear-in-n deletion in expectation. Most deletions cost only an O(kTd) check; retraining at O(nkTd) happens with probability O(mTkd^{3/2}/(epsilon*gamma*n)). It scales badly with dimension (d^{5/2}) and quadratically in m.

theory.name: Correctness of Q-k-means deletion (App. C.1)
theory.statement_plain: The deletion operation returns a model equal in distribution to retraining. (i) Given that the deleted point is not a k-means++ seed, the k-means++ seeds of D_{-i} have the same distribution as those of D. (ii) If, under the same stored phases, every quantized centroid is unchanged, the training trajectory and output are exactly those of running on D_{-i}. (iii) Otherwise it retrains. Because the phases are iid and independent of the data, the law of total probability gives R =_d A(D_{-i}).
theory.assumptions: Deleted indices are chosen independently of the model, so non-adversarial. Analog centroids and phases are stored in metadata.
theory.significance: A reusable proof pattern for exact unlearning: share randomness between the trained run and the hypothetical retrained run, check cheaply that the output would be identical, and otherwise fall back to retraining. Exactness is preserved without retraining most of the time.

theory.name: Lemma C.1 (boundary probability in a cube)
theory.statement_plain: Let X be uniform in a cube of side epsilon. The probability that X lies within epsilon'/2 of the cube's boundary, outside the inner cube of side epsilon - epsilon', is at most 2d*epsilon'/epsilon.
theory.assumptions: epsilon' < epsilon. Proof uses the per-dimension marginal probability 2*epsilon'/epsilon plus a union bound over d dimensions.
theory.significance: The basic geometric step behind quantized stability.

theory.name: Lemma C.2 (random-phase lattice stability)
theory.statement_plain: For an epsilon-lattice with uniform random phase and any point X, the probability that the epsilon'-ball around X does not map to a single lattice point is less than 2d*epsilon'/epsilon. Small perturbations rarely change the rounded value.
theory.assumptions: Phase theta ~ Unif[-1/2, 1/2]^d, independent of X. Translation invariance makes X uniform within its lattice cell.
theory.significance: Turns a deterministic sensitivity bound (how far a centroid moves) into a probability that the quantized output changes. This is randomized stability, not differential privacy.

theory.name: Lemma C.3 (quantized centroid stability)
theory.statement_plain: With probability greater than 1 - 2mTkd^{3/2}/(epsilon*gamma*n), over the quantization phases, Q-k-means outputs exactly the same centroids on D and on D minus Delta, for any deletion set Delta of size at most m that avoids the initial centroids. Proof: each centroid averages at least gamma*n/k points (guaranteed by the gamma-correction), and each point has norm at most sqrt(d). Deleting m points therefore moves an analog centroid by at most m*k*sqrt(d)/(gamma*n). Apply Lemma C.2 with epsilon' set to that value, then take a union bound over T iterations and k centroids.
theory.assumptions: Data in [0,1]^d. Same initialization and phase sequence for both runs. Delta does not intersect the initial centroids. The bookkeeping of k-factors in the union bound is loose in the text.
theory.significance: The core stability result. The probability of needing a retrain grows linearly in m, T, k and d^{3/2} and shrinks as epsilon*gamma*n grows. This is why larger datasets and coarser lattices make deletion cheaper.

theory.name: Theorem C.4 (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, k-means++)
theory.statement_plain: k-means++ seeding gives expected loss at most (8 ln k + 16) times the optimal k-means loss L*.
theory.assumptions: Standard k-means++ D^2 seeding.
theory.significance: Imported result used to bound Q-k-means' statistical quality.

theory.name: Corollary 4.1.1 (Q-k-means statistical performance)
theory.statement_plain: E[L_Q] <= (8 ln k + 16) L* + epsilon * sqrt(n d (8 ln k + 16) L*) + (1/4) n d epsilon^2. Quantization adds at most a per-coordinate rounding penalty on top of the k-means++ bound. If the data are iid from a nonatomic distribution, then L* = O(n) and the ratio of the upper bounds is 1 + O(d*epsilon^2 + epsilon*sqrt(d)). Choosing epsilon << 1/sqrt(d) matches the k-means++ guarantee.
theory.assumptions: The bound relies only on the k-means++ initialization. Proof adds a worst-case epsilon/2 rounding error in each coordinate, then applies Cauchy-Schwarz/Jensen.
theory.significance: Quantifies the trade-off: a smaller epsilon gives better loss but deletion time grows like 1/epsilon (Theorem 4.1).

theory.name: Proposition 4.2 (DC-k-means deletion time)
theory.statement_plain: With a depth-1 w-ary tree, w = Theta(n^rho) and 0 < rho < 1, DC-k-means handles m deletions in expected time O(m * max{n^rho, n^{1-rho}} * d). Each deletion re-solves one leaf, of expected size O(n^{1-rho}), and the root, which holds k*w = O(n^rho) points.
theory.assumptions: Expectation over the random leaf partition. Points are assigned independently and uniformly to leaves. k and T are constants. The number of leaves is fixed by rounding to a power of 2, and a retrain occurs if the rounding changes, which happens only a constant number of times in the fractional regime.
theory.significance: The modularity principle gives deletion cost of about sqrt(n) at rho = 1/2. The proof computes the size-biased expected leaf size from the second moment of a Binomial(n, n^{-rho}). Correctness holds because removing a point does not change how the remaining points are distributed over leaves.

theory.name: Corollary 4.2.1 (Q-k-means alpha-deletion efficiency)
theory.statement_plain: With epsilon = Theta(n^{-beta}), 0 < beta < 1, the amortized time is O(n^{1-alpha} + n^{alpha+beta}). Q-k-means is therefore alpha-deletion efficient in expectation when alpha <= (1 - beta)/2.
theory.assumptions: m = Theta(n^alpha). Other parameters are constant. Training is O(n).
theory.significance: Optimal deletion efficiency holds only for small deletion rates. A finer lattice (larger beta) improves loss but shrinks the range of alpha that is efficient.

theory.name: Corollary 4.2.2 (DC-k-means alpha-deletion efficiency)
theory.statement_plain: With w = Theta(n^rho) and a depth-1 tree, DC-k-means is alpha-deletion efficient in expectation when alpha <= 1 - max{rho, 1 - rho}. The main text writes a strict <. The best choice is rho = 1/2, which allows alpha up to 1/2.
theory.assumptions: Sequential training. m = Theta(n^alpha). Per-deletion cost O(n^{max(rho, 1-rho)}).
theory.significance: The tree width is the knob that trades deletion efficiency against statistical quality. Experiments use rho of about 0.3.

theory.name: Robustness observations (App. A.1)
theory.statement_plain: Q-k-means deletion stays correct against an adaptive adversary, because of the enforced equality of outcome. But such an adversary can make it inefficient by always deleting initial centroids, which forces a retrain every time. DC-k-means stays efficient, because leaf sizes are fixed at random before any request. But exact distributional correctness can fail if the adversary keeps deleting from one leaf, since leaf counts stop being uniform and independent of the requests.
theory.assumptions: The adversary has read access to the model and metadata and issues deletion requests.
theory.significance: Shows that average-case deletion guarantees are not security guarantees. Designing deletion operations that are both robust and efficient is left open.

papers.complexity: Training: Q-k-means costs O(nkTd), like Lloyd's, plus O(kTd) metadata memory (stored centroids, phases and counts). DC-k-means with a depth-1 tree trains the leaves in O(nkTd) in total plus a root problem of size kw. Its metadata stores every node, including the leaf datasets (O(nd)). Deletion: Q-k-means needs an O(kTd) stability check per deletion and a full retrain at O(nkTd) with probability about O(mTkd^{3/2}/(epsilon*gamma*n)), for an expected O(m^2 d^{5/2}/epsilon) over m deletions. DC-k-means recomputes one leaf (expected size O(n^{1-rho})) plus the root (O(n^rho) points), for O(max{n^rho, n^{1-rho}} d) per deletion; at rho = 1/2 this is O(sqrt(n) d). The naive baseline retrains at O(nkTd) per deletion. Online regime m = Theta(n^alpha): the lower bound is Omega(n/m) = Omega(n^{1-alpha}) amortized. Q-k-means is optimal if alpha <= (1-beta)/2 with epsilon = n^{-beta}; DC-k-means if alpha <= 1 - max{rho, 1-rho}.

datasets: Celltype (n=12,009, d=10, k=4): mouse single-cell RNA-seq, PCA-reduced from 23,433 dims
Covtype (n=15,120, d=52, k=7): forest cover types
Postures (n=74,975, d=15, k=5): hand-posture motion capture
Botnet / N-BaIoT (n=1,018,298, d=115, k=11): IoT traffic, benign plus attack classes
Gaussian (n=100,000, d=25, k=5): synthetic spherical Gaussian mixture, variance 0.8
models: k-means centroid model (k = number of ground-truth classes); k-means++ seeding plus Lloyd iterations as subroutine
baselines: Canonical k-means: k-means++ seeding plus Lloyd's algorithm, with deletion by retraining from scratch. For the runtime benchmark it is fixed at 10 iterations; for the quality metrics it runs to convergence.
metrics: Loss ratio (k-means objective normalized to the baseline)
Normalized mutual information against ground-truth labels
Amortized runtime: wall-clock (training + 1,000 deletions)/1,000 on a single Xeon E5-2640v4 core
Number of retrains triggered during the deletion stream (Q-k-means, App. D.3.1)
headline_results: Q-k-means speedup over retraining: Celltype 163.3x, Covtype 13.5x, MNIST 2.2x, Postures 64.4x, Gaussian 525.6x, Botnet 584.4x (Table 4).
DC-k-means speedup: Celltype 15.6x, Covtype 13.0x, MNIST 25.4x, Postures 22.8x, Gaussian 34.5x, Botnet 70.9x.

The claimed 'average over 100x' is consistent with the arithmetic mean over both methods and 6 datasets, about 128x (my calculation). The per-method means are about 226x (Q) and about 30x (DC); the medians are about 114x (Q) and about 24x (DC).
Botnet amortized runtime: 607.8 s for the baseline vs 1.04 s for Q-k-means and 8.57 s for DC-k-means.
Loss ratio vs baseline: Q-k-means 1.014 to 1.158 (worst on Celltype 1.158 and MNIST 1.11); DC-k-means 1.003 to 1.439 (worst on Celltype 1.439 and Botnet 1.118).
Silhouette is comparable, e.g. Botnet 0.583 (k-means), 0.639 (Q), 0.627 (DC) and Celltype 0.384, 0.367, 0.422. Table 2's row labels list 'Gaussian' twice, and the third row is presumably MNIST.
NMI is comparable, e.g. MNIST 0.494, 0.459, 0.494 and Botnet 0.708, 0.73, 0.705. The largest drop is Q-k-means on Gaussian (0.245 vs 0.319).

Q-k-means gains least on high d/n data (MNIST, then Covtype), and on MNIST it keeps retraining at a roughly constant rate over the stream (Fig. 2). DC-k-means speedup grows with n for fixed d and varies less across datasets.

Parameter sweeps: Q-k-means loss degrades quickly as epsilon approaches 1, and its runtime rises steadily as epsilon approaches 0. DC-k-means loss depends only weakly on w, and on Covtype its runtime is lowest at about 32 to 64 leaves.
Clustering quality barely changes over the 1,000 deletions, which are less than 10% of every dataset.

limitations: Concrete algorithms and proofs cover only k-means. Supervised models and deep networks get only a qualitative discussion.

Q-k-means deletion time grows like d^{5/2} and quadratically in m, so it does poorly in high dimensions and in overparameterized settings (MNIST speedup is only 2.2x). Its runtime is also more variable.
alpha-deletion efficiency holds only for small deletion rates: alpha <= (1-beta)/2 for Q-k-means and alpha <= 1/2 for DC-k-means.

Guarantees are average-case, for uniformly random deletions independent of the model. An adversary can make Q-k-means retrain on every request by deleting initial centroids, and can break DC-k-means' exact distributional equality by targeting one leaf.
The model assumes a single model and a single database, and that each user's request deletes exactly one data point.
DC-k-means has no theoretical bound on statistical quality as a function of w. It also stores all leaf datasets as metadata, a memory cost the paper does not analyze.

Hyperparameters (epsilon, w, gamma) and min-max scaling can depend on data that is later deleted. The paper uses data-light heuristics and retrains when extreme points are deleted, but a full treatment is left open.
The DP route to approximate deletion has unresolved problems: DP does not hide n, group privacy needs a budget fixed at training time, and that budget can leak how many deletions have happened.

Noticed while reading: the Q-k-means deletion pseudo-code (Alg. 5) does not explicitly re-check the loss-based early-termination decision, which also depends on the deleted point. Whether this affects exactness is unclear from the text.

Noticed while reading: the constants in k in Lemma C.3 and Theorem 4.1 are loosely tracked (the union bound appears to give k^2 while k is stated). There are also cross-reference typos ('Proposition 3.2', 'Theorem 3.1').
future_work: Tight upper and lower bounds on deletion efficiency for ridge regression, decision trees and models trained by stochastic optimization.
Worst-case (adversarial) online deletion, and deletion operations that are both robust and efficient.
Memory-bounded deletion, i.e. a constraint on metadata size.
Approximate deletion and its relation to differential privacy.
Systems with many models and databases and complex user-to-data relationships, where one user owns many points.
Trade-offs between training, inference and deletion time for lazy and non-parametric methods.
DC-k-means extensions: weighting centroids by cluster mass as they move up the tree, and deeper trees.

Applying the principles to segmented regression (Q-k-means plus per-cluster least squares), random Fourier feature kernel regression, quantized or randomized decision trees and bagged random forests, and quantized SGD for DNNs, which would need larger batches and fewer steps.
Metric-preserving dimensionality reduction (Johnson-Lindenstrauss) to make quantization workable for high-dimensional or overparameterized models.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: This is the foundational theory paper for exact, efficient unlearning. It supplies the definition of exact deletion as equality in distribution with retraining, which SISA and MUFC adopt, and a cost model to measure against: the online stream with amortized runtime, the Omega(n/m) lower bound and alpha-deletion efficiency. Its two algorithms are reusable templates. One is quantize, memoize and verify: a cheap check with a rare full retrain. The other is modular random partitioning: recompute only the affected sub-problem. The second is an ancestor of SISA sharding and mirrors one-shot federated clustering, with clients as leaves and the server as root. Proof tools worth reusing include the random-phase lattice boundary probability, the cluster-mass bound on centroid sensitivity, and the shared-randomness, law-of-total-probability argument for exactness. Another is the size-biased binomial second moment for expected shard size. It also flags pitfalls a student must handle: d^{5/2} and m^2 dependence, adversarial deletions, and leakage through hyperparameters, scaling and early-stop decisions.
open_questions: Prove a statistical (loss or approximation) guarantee for DC-k-means as a function of tree width w and depth, and analyze deeper trees and mass-weighted centroid merging.

Design k-means deletion that is both robust and efficient under adversarial requests. For example, re-seed only the affected centroid when an initial seed is deleted instead of retraining fully, or use seeding that does not single out individual points.
Reduce Q-k-means' d^{5/2} and m^2 dependence: project with JL before quantizing, quantize per cluster, or recompute locally from the first unstable iteration instead of retraining from scratch.
Batch and user-level deletion: analyze stability and cost when one request removes b correlated points, and when requests arrive in batches rather than one at a time.

Port quantization-plus-verification to supervised learning, e.g. quantized SGD or quantized decision trees, and compare cost and accuracy against SISA-style sharding under the same exact-deletion definition.

Bring Q-/DC-k-means into federated clustering (clients as leaves) and compare with MUFC. Alternatively, build a certified-approximate (DP-style) variant and measure the deletion-cost versus clustering-quality trade-off against the exact versions.

papers.title: Machine Unlearning of Federated Clusters
affiliations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
papers.one_liner: First exact-unlearning scheme for federated K-means: client-side K-means++ seeding that rarely needs retraining, plus Reed-Solomon-based secure sparse aggregation (SCMA).
papers.summary: This paper is the first to study machine unlearning for federated clustering (FC), where K-means data is spread across many clients and users can ask for their points to be deleted. The authors build a one-shot FC system, MUFC, designed so that deletions are cheap and exact. Each client runs only K-means++ seeding (no Lloyd iterations), snaps its K local centroids to a uniform grid, and records how many points each centroid represents in a sparse histogram vector of length B^d. SCMA, a new protocol, sums these vectors securely by treating them as Reed-Solomon 'errors' and sending 2KL masked syndromes. Communication is logarithmic in the vector length, and the server learns only the total histogram. The server regenerates points from the histogram and runs full K-means++. To delete points, a client keeps its seeding unless a deleted point was one of its chosen centroids. If one was, it resamples from the first affected centroid onward, and the paper proves the result is distributed exactly like retraining. The theory gives an O(log^2 K) approximation plus a quantization error term, and an expected removal time of O(RK^2 d) for random deletions (independent of n), versus O(nKd) for retraining. Across seven datasets the paper reports a ~84x average speed-up over retraining, and lower loss than K-FED/DC-KM on imbalanced data.
papers.problem: Federated clustering methods (e.g., K-FED, DC-k-means) either leak per-client centroid statistics to the server or are expensive, and none supports efficient data removal. With the right to be forgotten, clients may ask to delete some points (cross-silo) or leave completely (cross-device). Naive retraining of local and global clustering on every request is costly, and existing federated unlearning methods are empirical, with no guarantees on the unlearned model or on unlearning efficiency.
papers.core_idea: K-means++ seeding picks actual data points as centroids by sequential D^2 sampling. If none of the deleted points was picked, the seeding stays valid: conditioned on not having picked them, each choice has exactly the D^2-sampling probability on the reduced dataset, a rejection-sampling-style argument. Retraining is therefore needed only with probability about RK/n, and only from the first removed centroid onward. Clients send only quantized centroid counts, aggregated through a Reed-Solomon-syndrome-based secure sparse aggregation (SCMA). The server rebuilds a surrogate dataset from these counts and reclusters it, which is cheap because it depends only on K*L points.
papers.setting: federated unsupervised clustering (federated K-means), one-shot (single client-to-server round), cross-silo and cross-device removal
contributions: Introduces the problem of machine unlearning for federated clustering, and an end-to-end secure FC framework (MUFC) that supports simple exact unlearning.

Proposes a one-shot FC algorithm: client K-means++ seeding, then quantization and weighted counts, then server K-means++. It has an order-optimal O(log^2 K) approximation (plus quantization error) for the federated K-means objective and performs especially well on highly imbalanced clusters.

Proposes SCMA (secure compressed multiset aggregation), which uses Reed-Solomon codes with bin indices as evaluation points plus additive secret masks. The server recovers the exact sum of sparse vectors with per-client communication logarithmic in vector dimension (prior sparse secure aggregation is linear), and learns only the aggregate.

Proves that unlearning via K-means++ seeding is exact (probabilistic model equivalence), with expected removal time min{O(RK^2 d), O(nKd)} for random and min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(nKd)} for adversarial removals, independent of n, versus O(nKd) for retraining.

Compiles seven benchmark datasets for federated-cluster unlearning, including two new biomedical ones (TCGA cancer methylation, TMI gut microbiome), and reports ~84x average speed-up over complete retraining.
method_steps: Setup: scale all client data into the unit hypercube. Pick quantization step gamma (default 1/sqrt(n)), giving B = 1/gamma bins per dimension and B^d bins total. Pick a prime p >= max{n, B^d}. Offline, generate secure-aggregation masks z_i^(l), i in [2KL], with sum over clients of z_i^(l) = 0 mod p.

Client l (in parallel): run ONLY the K-means++ initialization (first centroid uniform, then D^2 sampling) on X^(l). This gives K centroids C^(l), which are real data points, plus local cluster sizes |C_k^(l)|. Store the centroids in their sampling order. Cost O(n^(l) K d).

Client l: uniformly quantize each local centroid to its grid bin index j. Build the sparse count vector q^(l) of length B^d with q_j^(l) = |C_k^(l)| for the bin holding c_k^(l), and 0 elsewhere (at most K nonzeros).

SCMA encode (client): send the 2KL masked syndromes S_i^(l) = (sum over nonzero j of q_j^(l) * j^(i-1) + z_i^(l)) mod p, for i = 1..2KL. The bin indices act as Reed-Solomon evaluation points and the nonzero entries as substitution errors.

SCMA decode (server): sum S_i^(l) over clients, which cancels the masks and leaves S_i = sum_j q_j j^(i-1). Berlekamp-Massey finds the locator polynomial g(x) = prod_{q_j != 0}(1 - j x). Factoring g over F_p (Kedlaya-Umans) gives the nonzero bin indices. Solving the 2KL-equation Vandermonde system gives the counts q_j. The server learns only q = sum_l q^(l).

Server data generation: for each nonzero bin j, sample q_j points uniformly at random inside the bin (default in experiments), or place the bin center with weight q_j (weighted K-means++, reduces problem size from n to KL). The result is the server dataset X_s.
