Server: run full K-means++ (seeding + Lloyd's, up to T iterations) on X_s to get the global centroids C_s, at cost O(K^2 L T d). Clients keep C^(l). The server keeps X_s, q, and C_s.

Unlearning, single-client (cross-silo; R points X_R removed from client l): run Alg. 3. If no current centroid is in X_R, keep C^(l). Otherwise let i be the index just before the first removed centroid in sampling order, keep c_1..c_i, delete X_R, and resample centroids i+1..K by D^2 sampling on X' = X \ X_R. Recompute q^(l) only if client l reseeded. Other clients do nothing.
Unlearning, multi-client (cross-device; R clients leave entirely): set q^(l) = 0 for the departing clients. No client computation is needed.

Server update: re-run SCMA to get q'. If q' = q, keep C_s. Otherwise regenerate X_s' from q' and rerun full K-means++ at the server to get C_s', at cost O(K^2 L T d), or O((L-R) K^2 T d) for multi-client removal.

key_definitions.name: Centralized K-means objective
key_definitions.plain: Sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest chosen centroid.
key_definitions.formal: phi_c(X; C) = ||X - C||_F^2, where row i of C is argmin_{c_j in C} ||x_i - c_j||; optimum phi*_c(X)

key_definitions.name: Induced global clustering / federated K-means objective
key_definitions.plain: Each client point is assigned to the global server centroid that its LOCAL centroid is assigned to, not to the globally nearest centroid. The federated loss sums squared distances under this induced assignment.
key_definitions.formal: P_k = {x_i^(l) : x_i^(l) in C_j^(l), c_j^(l) in C_k^s}; phi_f(X; C_s) = sum_l ||X^(l) - C_s^(l)||_F^2

key_definitions.name: Exact unlearning (probabilistic model equivalence)
key_definitions.plain: The unlearned model has exactly the same output distribution as a model retrained from scratch without the removed point.
key_definitions.formal: for all C in M, x in X: P(U(A(X), X, x) = C) = P(A(X \ x) = C)

key_definitions.name: K-means++ initialization (D^2 sampling)
key_definitions.plain: Pick the first centroid uniformly at random. Pick each next centroid with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest centroid chosen so far.
key_definitions.formal: P(x) = d^2(x, C) / phi_c(X; C); E[phi] <= 8(ln K + 2) phi*

key_definitions.name: Random vs adversarial removal
key_definitions.plain: Random: every point is equally likely to be removed. Adversarial: a malicious user removes the points that matter most, e.g. boundary points or those contributing most to the objective. Experiments simulate this by removing the highest-cost point each round.

key_definitions.name: Cluster-size imbalance eps1 (Assumption 5.2)
key_definitions.plain: How much smaller the smallest optimal cluster is than a perfectly balanced cluster.
key_definitions.formal: eps1 = n / (K * s_min); eps1 = 1 means all clusters have size n/K

key_definitions.name: Outlier with parameter eps2 (Assumption 5.3)
key_definitions.plain: A point much farther from its nearest optimal centroid than the RMS radius of that cluster.
key_definitions.formal: ||x_i - c*_j|| > sqrt(eps2 * phi*_c(C*_j) / |C*_j|), where c*_j is the nearest optimal centroid, eps2 >= 1

key_definitions.name: Uniform quantization
key_definitions.plain: Round each coordinate to the nearest multiple of gamma. The grid cells are the 'bins'.
key_definitions.formal: y_hat = gamma * argmin_{j in Z} |y - gamma j|; B = 1/gamma bins per dim, B^d bins total

key_definitions.name: SCMA privacy criterion
key_definitions.plain: The server learns only the aggregated per-bin counts over all clients, not which client contributed points to which bin.
key_definitions.formal: server learns q = sum_l q^(l) only; masks z_i^(l) uniform on F_p with sum_l z_i^(l) = 0

key_definitions.name: Loss ratio
key_definitions.plain: Federated clustering loss divided by the (approximate) optimal centralized K-means loss. Lower is better; 1 is optimal.
key_definitions.formal: phi_f(X; C_s) / phi*_c(X), with phi*_c approximated by the best of several centralized K-means++ runs

theory.name: Theorem 4.1 (clustering quality of Alg. 1)
theory.statement_plain: With uniform quantization step gamma, the expected federated K-means loss of MUFC is at most O(log^2 K) times the optimal centralized loss plus a quantization error O(n d gamma^2 log K).
theory.assumptions: Data scaled to the unit hypercube; quantization uses the bin center as the reconstruction point (per-point distortion <= sqrt(d) gamma / 2); holds for any distribution of data across clients.
theory.significance: The O(log^2 K) factor is argued to be order-optimal for one-shot FC (two rounds of K-means++, each costing O(log K)). Choosing gamma = Theta(1/sqrt(n)) makes the quantization term independent of n. SCMA adds no distortion because it returns the exact sum.

theory.name: Lemma D.1 and remarks (no quantization, Alg. 5)
theory.statement_plain: Without quantization, E[phi_f] < O(log^2 K) * phi*_c(X). Restricted to non-outlier points, the bound is O(eps2 log K). If each client knows its true number of clusters K^(l) and runs K^(l)-means++, the bound is O(log K * log K'). In the extreme case where each client holds one whole cluster (L = K, K' = 1), E[phi_f] = 2 phi*_c, independent of K.
theory.assumptions: Uses the K-means++ guarantee at clients and server, and the triangle inequality ||a-b||^2 <= 2(||a-c||^2 + ||c-b||^2). Mirrors the distributed K-median result of Guha et al. (2003): an O(b) client and O(c) server approximation compose to O(bc).
theory.significance: Shows that data heterogeneity across clients can help FC quality.

theory.name: Lemma 5.1 (exactness of Alg. 3 unlearning)
theory.statement_plain: For any dataset X and removal set X_R, the centroids returned by Alg. 3 have exactly the same distribution as re-running K-means++ seeding on X' = X \ X_R, and E[phi_c(X'; C')] <= 8(ln K + 2) phi*_c(X').
theory.assumptions: Model = K-means++ initialization only (no Lloyd's iterations); seeding order is stored.
theory.significance: The proof is by induction over seeding rounds. Given c_i not in X_R, P(pick c_i from X | c_i not in X_R) = [d^2(c_i,C')/phi_c(X;C')] / [1 - sum_{x in X_R} d^2(x,C')/phi_c(X;C')] = d^2(c_i,C')/phi_c(X';C'), which is exactly the D^2 probability on X'. This conditional, rejection-sampling-style identity is the core tool. The paper states Alg. 4 (federated) is exact by the same argument; the server reruns from scratch whenever q changes.

theory.name: Lemma F.1 (retraining probability)
theory.statement_plain: If the probability that the dataset contains at least one outlier is O(1/n), a removal set of size R hits the K-means++ centroid set with probability < O(RK/n) for random removals and < O(RK^2 eps1 eps2 / n) for adversarial removals.
theory.assumptions: Assumptions 5.2 (imbalance eps1) and 5.3 (outlier definition eps2). Outliers are pessimistically assumed to always be chosen as centroids. The per-round bound is P(choose x_i as (k+1)-th centroid | C_k) <= 10 K eps1 eps2 / n, and a union bound over K rounds and R points is used.
theory.significance: Even a worst-case non-outlier point is unlikely to be a centroid, because the D^2 mass of any non-outlier is at most O(K eps1 eps2 / n) of the total.

theory.name: Theorem 5.4 (expected removal time)
theory.statement_plain: Alg. 3 removes R points in one request in expected time min{O(RK^2 d), O(nKd)} for random removals and min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(nKd)} for adversarial removals. Complete retraining costs O(nKd).
theory.assumptions: Same as Lemma F.1 (outlier probability <= O(1/n), Assumptions 5.2-5.3).
theory.significance: The expected unlearning cost does not depend on n. The proof gives E[time] <= O(nKd + RK) * O(RK/n) + O(RK) = O(RK^2 d). In the federated setting the client cost replaces n with n^(l), other clients do nothing, and the server costs at most O(K^2 L T d), or O((L-R) K^2 T d) for multi-client removal.

theory.name: SCMA communication and computation complexity (Sec. 4.3, App. C)
theory.statement_plain: Each client sends 2KL ceil(log p) <= max{2KL log n, 2KL d log B} + 1 bits, which is order-optimal given the lower bound max{O(KL log n), O(KL d log B)}. Client computation is O(K^2 L log(KL)) field operations. Server computation is max{O(K^2 L^2), O((KL)^1.5 log p + KL log^2 p)} (average case, because polynomial factorization is randomized).
theory.assumptions: Mask generation is done offline and its cost is not counted, following standard practice.
theory.significance: Communication is logarithmic in the vector length B^d, whereas prior sparse secure aggregation (Beguier et al. 2020; Ergun et al. 2021) is linear in the model dimension. Unlike sparsification approaches (Han et al. 2020), SCMA is exact.

theory.name: Unique decodability of SCMA (App. J)
theory.statement_plain: Two different aggregate vectors q and q' cannot produce the same 2KL syndromes S_i, so the server's decoding is unique.
theory.assumptions: At most KL nonzeros in q, so the difference has at most 2KL nonzeros; bin indices are distinct field elements.
theory.significance: The difference would satisfy B v = 0 with B a square Vandermonde matrix on distinct generators, which is invertible. This is a contradiction, so 2KL syndromes suffice.

theory.name: Deterministic low-complexity SCMA decoding (App. K)
theory.statement_plain: Replacing the prime p with a large non-prime p' >= max{K L B^(2dKL), n} + 1 avoids overflow. The server can then work over the reals, apply Berlekamp-Massey, and find the integer roots by bisection search on h(x) and h'(x). Worst-case complexity is O((MK)^3 d^2 log^c(MK) log B) for c < 2.
theory.assumptions: The symbol M in this bound is not defined in the text (probably L, the number of clients).
theory.significance: Removes reliance on randomized factorization over finite fields; deterministic poly(log p) factorization remains an open problem.

papers.complexity: Learning: client K-means++ seeding O(n^(l) K d). Client SCMA encoding O(K^2 L log(KL)) ops over F_p. Server SCMA decoding max{O(K^2 L^2), O((KL)^1.5 log p + KL log^2 p)} (average case). Server K-means++ + Lloyd's O(K^2 L T d). Communication per client 2KL ceil(log p) <= max{2KL log n, 2KL d log B} + 1 bits, logarithmic in the B^d-length vector and order-optimal; a naive secure sum of the full vector would cost B^d = gamma^-d entries, exponential in d. Unlearning: client expected cost min{O(RK^2 d), O(n^(l) K d)} (random) or min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(n^(l) K d)} (adversarial); other clients do nothing; server <= O(K^2 L T d) (single-client) or O((L-R) K^2 T d) (multi-client, no client computation). Retraining: O(nKd) per client plus the server. Compared with Q-k-means (Ginart et al. 2019), whose expected removal time is O(R^2 K^3 T^2 d^2.5 / eps), MUFC client unlearning needs only O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d) even for adversarial removals. Storage: clients keep their ordered seeding C^(l); the server keeps X_s, q, and C_s.

datasets: Gaussian (synthetic GMM; n=30000, d=10, K=10, equal clusters of 3000)
Celltype (Mouse Cell Atlas single-cell RNA, PCA to d=10; n=12009, K=4; cluster sizes 6506/2328/2201/974)
Postures (motion-capture hand postures; n=74975, d=15, K=5)
Covtype (forest cover type; n=15120, d=52, K=7)
FEMNIST (LEAF; 100 writers with >=350 points each; n=36725, d=784, K=62)
TCGA methylation (new; 4 cancer types; n=1904, d=57, K=4)
TMI gut microbiome (new; NIH Human Microbiome; n=1126, d=984, K=4; highly imbalanced 934/125/46/21)
models: K-means clustering (K-means++ seeding at clients; K-means++ + Lloyd's at server)
baselines: K-FED (Dennis et al., 2021), clustering quality only, since it does not support removal
DC-Kmeans / DC-KM (Ginart et al., 2019), adapted to FC with a computation tree of height 2 whose leaves are clients
Complete retraining (K-means++ locally and globally on each removal)
metrics: Accumulated removal time (s) over rounds of single-point removal
Single-round speed-up when no retraining is triggered
headline_results: Table 1 loss ratio (MUFC / K-FED / DC-KM): TMI 1.24/1.84/1.54; Celltype 1.14/1.72/1.46; Gaussian 1.25/1.25/1.02; TCGA 1.18/1.56/1.15; Postures 1.10/1.13/1.03; FEMNIST 1.20/1.21/1.18; Covtype 1.03/1.60/1.03. MUFC is best on the imbalanced TMI and Celltype; DC-KM is better on balanced Gaussian.
Single-round MUFC speed-up when the removed point is not a client centroid: TMI 151x, Celltype 1535x, Gaussian 2074x, TCGA 483x, Postures 613x, FEMNIST 53x, Covtype 267x.

Random removals, average speed-up over retraining (MUFC vs DC-KM, Fig. 3 legends): TMI 21x vs 5x; Celltype 44x vs 9x; Gaussian 30x vs 9x; TCGA 43x vs 2x; Postures 164x vs 7x; FEMNIST 6x vs 2x; Covtype 27x vs 4x. The text claims an ~84x average across the seven datasets; the arithmetic mean of these legend values is only ~48x, and it is unclear how 84x was computed.
Adversarial removals (MUFC vs DC-KM): TMI 9x vs 4x; Celltype 13x vs 8x; TCGA 51x vs 2x; Postures 224x vs 6x; Covtype 16x vs 4x (Figs. 3e, 4e-h).

Batch removals (App. M.5): TCGA 10 points/request 10x vs 2x and 30 points/request 4x vs 2x; Postures 10 points/request 18x vs 6x and 30 points/request 8x vs 5x. The speed-up shrinks as batch size grows.
The loss ratio stays nearly constant over 200-500 rounds of unlearning for both random and adversarial removals.
With full client K-means++ (Table 2), MUFC's loss ratio is best on all datasets: 1.05, 1.03, 1.02, 1.02, 1.02, 1.12, 1.02. Unlearning then costs about as much as DC-KM.
Non-iid data (K' < K) lowers the loss ratio (Fig. 3a). gamma has little effect on Gaussian data but strongly affects TMI, where the loss ratio explodes for large gamma (Fig. 3b,c).

limitations: Clients run only K-means++ seeding, not Lloyd's iterations, to keep unlearning cheap. Running full client K-means++ improves the loss but triggers retraining far more often (Table 2 vs Table 1).
Server-side unlearning is plain retraining: any change in q forces regeneration of X_s and a full K-means++ + Lloyd's rerun, O(K^2 L T d).

The removal-time guarantees need an outlier assumption (probability of any outlier <= O(1/n)) and depend on the imbalance eps1 and outlier parameter eps2. Outliers are almost always chosen as seeds and so force retraining.
Batch and adversarial removals reduce the gains (the union bound grows with R, and speed-ups shrink to 4-8x at 30 points per request).

The privacy notion is informal. The authors note there is no formal secrecy definition for FC, there is no differential privacy, and the server still learns the aggregated histogram of quantized centroid locations and counts. Leakage from comparing q and q' before and after unlearning is not analyzed (my observation).
Assumes a unique optimal clustering and no identical data points across clients. Data must be scaled into the unit hypercube, and the quantization error grows with d (O(n d gamma^2 log K)).

SCMA's efficient decoding is average-case, relying on randomized polynomial factorization over F_p. The deterministic variant needs an exponentially large modulus p'. Client dropouts and mask generation (done offline) are not treated.

Exactness of the federated Alg. 4 is asserted ('same as Lemma 5.1') rather than proved separately. Multi-client removal still requires a new SCMA round involving the remaining clients (my observation).
The headline 84x average speed-up cannot be reproduced from the per-dataset legends in Fig. 3 (mean ~48x) (my observation).
Only exact K-means (no other clustering objectives) is studied, and there is no conclusion or future-work section.
future_work: Not stated explicitly; the paper has no conclusion or future-work section.
Implied: a deterministic poly(log p) polynomial factorization over finite fields for SCMA decoding (stated as an open problem in App. K).
Implied: a formal secrecy or privacy definition for federated clustering (App. A notes none exists).
Implied: applying SCMA to other sparse secure FL aggregation problems ('as well as more general problems').
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: MUFC shows a reusable design pattern for efficient exact unlearning: build the model from actual data points chosen by sequential randomized sampling. A deletion then matters only if the deleted point was selected, and when it was, you resample only from that step onward. The conditional-probability (rejection-sampling-style) proof of Lemma 5.1 is a compact tool that could transfer to coresets, prototype or exemplar selection, and other sampling-based learners. Expected cost scales with the probability that a point is 'used' (about K/n), not with n. It contrasts with Ginart et al.'s Q-k-means, which relies on stability of quantized centroids under small perturbations, and with SISA-style sharding; together these give three distinct routes to exact unlearning. Pitfalls to note: any Lloyd-style iterative refinement breaks the cheap path, the server still retrains fully, outliers and batch deletions erode the gains, and the 84x claim does not match the figure legends. For federated settings, SCMA is a practical tool: it delivers an exact secure aggregate of sparse updates at communication cost logarithmic in dimension.
open_questions: Make the server side incremental: apply the Alg. 3 seeding trick to the server's K-means++ on X_s, or bound how often Lloyd's output changes, instead of rerunning from scratch whenever q changes.

Extend exact unlearning to clients that run Lloyd's iterations, e.g. by combining MUFC seeding with Ginart et al.'s quantized-centroid stability (Q-k-means), and analyze the combined removal-time bound.

Formalize privacy for FC unlearning: quantify what the server learns from the difference q - q' between pre- and post-deletion aggregates, and add differential-privacy noise to SCMA while keeping exactness or certified unlearning.

Give tighter bounds for batch and sequential deletions (amortized cost over many requests) and design outlier-robust seeding (e.g., k-means-- or trimming) that keeps both exactness and low retraining probability.

Unlearning for multi-shot federated clustering (MFC) or fair/personalized FC (FFC): can the 'retrain only if a selected representative is removed' principle extend to multi-round or fairness-constrained clustering?
Generalize SCMA plus seeding-based unlearning to other unsupervised objectives (k-median, GMMs, spectral clustering) and empirically evaluate client dropout and mask regeneration during unlearning.

papers.title: Fair Federated Data Clustering through Personalization: Bridging the Gap between Diverse Data Distributions
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Ropar, Punjab, India
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (v2, 12 Jul 2024; marked 'Preprint submitted to Journal', journal not named)
papers.one_liner: p-FClus: single-round federated k-means/k-medoids where clients fine-tune server-aggregated centers locally, lowering per-client cost and cost deviation across clients.
papers.summary: This paper studies federated clustering: many clients (phones, banks, hospitals) each hold unlabeled data and want to find k cluster centers together without sharing raw data. Earlier methods (k-FED, one round; MFC, several rounds) produce one set of global centers, which under skewed non-IID data can sit far from some clients' data, giving those clients much higher cost and little reason to stay. The authors treat this spread of per-client cost as the fairness problem. They measure it with σ, the standard deviation across clients of each client's mean per-point clustering cost. Their method, p-FClus (personalized-Federated Clustering), needs one communication round. Each client clusters its own data and uploads its k local centers. The server clusters the union of all uploaded centers into k global centers and sends them back. Each client then fine-tunes its own copy of the global centers with point-wise SGD on a regularized objective, ending up with personalized centers. Matching each point to its nearest local and global center avoids aligning center indices across clients. The method works for any finite ℓ-norm, including k-means (ℓ=2) and k-medoids (ℓ=1). On synthetic, UCI, FMNIST, FEMNIST and WISDM data it usually gets lower mean and maximum cost than k-FED and MFC, and often lower σ. The paper has no theoretical guarantees.
papers.problem: Federated k-centroid clustering methods output a single global center set. Under non-IID or skewed client data, some clients incur much higher clustering cost than others (high cost deviation), which discourages them from participating. Existing methods either depend on the data distribution (k-FED does well only at high heterogeneity), need multiple rounds (MFC), or are computationally heavy (GAN- or encryption-based), and only handle k-means. Supervised personalization (e.g., Ditto) does not carry over directly because cluster centers have no canonical ordering across clients.
papers.core_idea: Do one-shot aggregation (local (k,ℓ)-clustering, then server-side (k,ℓ)-clustering of the union of local centers) and let each client fine-tune the received global centers on its own data. The update is point-wise SGD on P(x) = ½||c^g − x||_ℓ + λ||c^g − c^(z)||², where c^g and c^(z) are the global and local centers nearest to x. Matching through each data point's nearest centers avoids the center-correspondence problem. Per-client personalized centers lower both each client's cost and the spread of cost across clients.
papers.setting: Horizontal federated unsupervised learning: hard (k,ℓ)-clustering (k-means ℓ=2, k-medoids ℓ=1, any finite ℓ) of unlabeled data spread over Z clients; one round of client-server communication; no labels; benign clients; static data
papers.unlearning_type: none (paper is not about unlearning; it lists unlearning in clustering as client join/leave future work, citing Pan et al. 2022 = MUFC)
contributions: Claims to be the first to bring personalization into federated data clustering: p-FClus gives per-client personalized centers with lower or comparable cost deviation (σ) across clients, i.e., a fairer clustering.

Gets lower mean per-point objective cost in a single round of server-client communication, independent of how data is divided among clients; claims to combine k-FED's single-shot efficiency with MFC's independence from data distribution.
Works for any finite ℓ-norm, including k-means (ℓ=2) and k-medoids (ℓ=1), whereas k-FED and MFC handle only k-means.
Point-wise gradient personalization with nearest local/global center mapping, which removes the need for center ordering or synchronization across clients.

Empirical study on synthetic (3 overlap levels), extrinsic (Adult, Bank, Diabetes, FMNIST) and intrinsic federated (FEMNIST, WISDM) datasets, with balanced/unequal splits, H in {2,5,7,10} and 50 to 1000 clients; code is public (github.com/P-FClus/p-FClus).
method_steps: Client initialization (Alg. 2, in parallel): each client z runs (k,ℓ)-clustering on its local data X^(z) (Lloyd's k-means for ℓ=2; Charikar et al. 1999 k-median/k-medoid for ℓ=1) and gets k local centers C^(z). It always computes k centers even if it holds only H<k distributions.
Upload: each client sends its k local centers C^(z) (k vectors of dimension h) to the server. This is the only uplink message; raw data never leaves the client.

Server (Alg. 3): form S = C^(1) ∪ ... ∪ C^(Z) (Z·k points, unweighted as described), run (k,ℓ)-clustering on S to get k global centers C^g, and broadcast C^g to all clients. This completes the single round.

Client personalization (Alg. 4): each client starts from C^g and, for t tuning steps or until convergence, loops over its local points x. For each x it finds the nearest local center c^(z) in C^(z) and the nearest current global/personalized center c^g in C^g.

It sets the learning rate η = 1/(number of local points currently assigned to c^g) and updates c^g ← c^g − η∇P(x), where P(x) = ½||c^g − x||_ℓ + λ||c^g − c^(z)||². For ℓ=2 the gradient is (c^g − x) + 2λ(c^g − c^(z)) (Eq. 6); for ℓ=1 it is written as 1/2 + 2λ(c^g − c^(z)) (Eq. 7).
It records the assignment φ^(z)[x] = c^g. λ (fine-tuning level) can be shared or set per client.
For k-medoids (ℓ=1), each final personalized center is replaced by the nearest data point in the client's local data, so centers remain data points.

Output: per-client personalized centers C^g(personalized) and assignments φ^(z). Evaluation computes µ, σ and max with each client's own personalized centers, whereas k-FED and MFC use their single global set.

key_definitions.name: Heterogeneity level H (Def. 1)
key_definitions.plain: The maximum number of true distributions (clusters) that any single client's data comes from; H ≤ k. Low H means each client sees only a few clusters, the hard non-IID case.
key_definitions.formal: H = max over z of #true distributions present in X^(z), H ≤ k

key_definitions.name: (k,ℓ)-clustering objective cost (Def. 2)
key_definitions.plain: A client's cost is the sum over its points of the ℓ-th power distance to the assigned center; the global cost sums these over clients.
key_definitions.formal: L_ℓ^(z)(C^g) = Σ_{x∈X^(z)} Σ_{c^g∈C^g} I[φ^(z)(x)=c^g] d(x,c^g)^ℓ ; L_ℓ(C^g) = Σ_z L_ℓ^(z)(C^g)

key_definitions.name: Mean cost per point µ (Eqs. 2-3)
key_definitions.plain: Per-client average cost per data point, then averaged uniformly over clients, so large clients do not dominate.

key_definitions.name: Fair federated clustering / cost deviation σ (Def. 3, Eq. 4)
key_definitions.plain: Center set C1 is fairer than C2 if the standard deviation across clients of their per-point costs is lower, i.e., costs are more uniform across clients. This is client-level performance fairness, not group or demographic fairness.
key_definitions.formal: σ(C^g) = sqrt( Σ_z (µ^(z)(C^g) − µ(C^g))² / Z ); C1 fairer than C2 iff σ(C1) < σ(C2)

key_definitions.name: Maximum cost per point (max)
key_definitions.plain: The worst per-point cost any single client suffers, used as a second fairness metric.
key_definitions.formal: max = max_z µ^(z)(C)

key_definitions.name: Personalization objective P(x) (Eq. 5)
key_definitions.plain: For each local point, a trade-off between the cost to its nearest global center and an L2 penalty that keeps that global center close to the point's nearest local center. λ is the fine-tuning level.
key_definitions.formal: P(x) = ½||c^g − x||_ℓ + λ||c^g − c^(z)||², with c^g = argmin_{c∈C^g} d(x,c), c^(z) = argmin_{c∈C^(z)} d(x,c)

key_definitions.name: Personalization SGD step (Eq. 8)
key_definitions.plain: Online-k-means-style step whose learning rate is the inverse of the number of points currently assigned to that center.
key_definitions.formal: c^g ← c^g − η ∇_{c^g} P(x), η = 1/|{x : argmin_{c∈C^g} d(x,c) = c^g}|

theory.name: No theorems
theory.statement_plain: The paper has no theorems, lemmas, propositions or proofs. It states no approximation ratio, convergence result, fairness bound or privacy guarantee for p-FClus.
theory.assumptions: n/a
theory.significance: All claims rest on experiments. Formal analysis is open: approximation quality of server clustering on the union of local centers, convergence of personalization SGD, a bound on σ, and deletion sensitivity.

theory.name: Eq. 6 (k-means gradient)
theory.statement_plain: For ℓ=2 the gradient of P(x) with respect to c^g is (c^g − x) + 2λ(c^g − c^(z)). The clustering term is treated as ½||c^g − x||², justified by 'minimizing euclidean distance is the same as minimizing squared euclidean'.
theory.assumptions: ℓ=2; c^g and c^(z) are the global and local centers nearest to x
theory.significance: Gives a MacQueen-like online update plus a pull toward the local center. The derivation silently replaces Eq. 5's non-squared norm with a squared one.

theory.name: Eq. 7 (k-medoids gradient)
theory.statement_plain: For ℓ=1 the gradient is written as 1/2 + 2λ(c^g − c^(z)). The subgradient of ½||c^g − x||_1 is ½·sign(c^g − x), so the constant 1/2 is probably a typo (missing sign term).
theory.assumptions: ℓ=1; afterwards the center is snapped to the nearest local data point
theory.significance: This is how ℓ=1 is supported; taken literally, Eq. 7 does not depend on x.

theory.name: Implicit approximation via subroutines
theory.statement_plain: Local and server steps call Lloyd (k-means heuristic) or Charikar et al. 1999 (a constant-factor k-median approximation). The paper does not derive any end-to-end guarantee from these.
theory.assumptions: n/a
theory.significance: A student could try to prove a bound for 'cluster the union of local centers', as in k-FED/Awasthi-Sheffet-style analyses, and then for personalization.

papers.complexity: No formal statement. From the algorithm: one communication round. Uplink is k·h numbers per client (Z·k·h in total); downlink is k·h per client. Client compute is local (k,ℓ)-clustering (Lloyd: O(I·n_z·k·h)) plus personalization O(t·n_z·k·h), with two nearest-center searches per point per step. Server compute is (k,ℓ)-clustering of only Z·k points. No wall-clock or communication measurements are reported. Unlearning costs are not discussed. By inspection, removing a client means dropping its k centers from S, re-clustering Z·k points and re-broadcasting, after which every client must re-personalize.

datasets: Synthetic 2-D Gaussian mixtures, 10 components: Syn-NO (no overlap, N(10i,1)), Syn-LO (little overlap, sd 2), Syn-O (overlapping, sd 3)
Adult (UCI census, 32,562 records; age, fnlwgt, education-num, capital-gain, hours-per-week)
Bank Marketing (UCI, Portugal, 41,108 records; 6 numeric attributes)
Diabetes 130-US hospitals (UCI; age, time in hospital)
Fashion-MNIST (60,000 training images)
FEMNIST (LEAF; intrinsic H=62, 500 clients)
WISDM (accelerometer activity recognition, 1,098,207 samples, H=6, 36 clients)
models: k-means (ℓ=2) and k-medoids (ℓ=1) center-based clustering; no neural models
baselines: CentClus: centralized Lloyd k-means / Charikar et al. k-medoids
k-FED (Dennis et al., ICML 2021): one-shot, Awasthi-Sheffet locally plus a farthest-point heuristic at the server
MFC (Makkar et al., ECAI 2023): multi-shot extension of k-FED
For k-medoids, only CentClus is compared because k-FED and MFC are k-means-only
metrics: Mean cost per data point µ (lower is better)
Cost deviation per data point σ (fairness, lower is better)
Maximum per-client cost per point, max (lower is better)
headline_results: Setup: balanced and unequal (deliberately skewed) splits; H in {2,5,7,10}; 50/100/500/1000 clients; mean ± std over 5 seeds {0,300,600,900,1200}; Intel Xeon 6246R with 280 GB RAM. The values of λ and t used are not reported.

WISDM, k-means (Table 1): µ p-FClus 5.64e11 vs MFC 3.35e12 vs k-FED 5.71e12; σ 1.96e11 vs 2.51e12 vs 1.32e13; max 1.19e12 vs 1.10e13 vs 7.21e13. That is about 6-10x lower µ and an order of magnitude or more lower σ and max. The text's claim of µ reduced 'by an order of 10^5' does not match the table.
FEMNIST, k-means (Table 1): µ k-FED 2.806 (best), p-FClus 3.103, MFC 3.158; σ MFC 0.3110 (best), k-FED 0.3518, p-FClus 0.3640 (worst); max p-FClus 4.170 (best) vs MFC 4.371 vs k-FED 4.478.

Balanced splits (Figs. 1-3, figures only, no numbers in text): p-FClus has lower µ and max than k-FED/MFC across H, especially at low H. σ is lower on Adult and Bank for most H. On Diabetes, k-FED/MFC have lower σ but higher variance. FMNIST σ is similar for all methods. On synthetic data, MFC ≈ p-FClus with no overlap but degrades with overlap, and k-FED is always much worse.
Unequal splits (Figs. 4-6): on Adult, k-FED/MFC σ is higher at small H but falls below p-FClus as H grows. The authors argue p-FClus has a tighter confidence interval and much lower µ.

k-medoids vs CentClus (Tables 2-3): Adult µ is 1.08-1.32 for p-FClus vs 1.64 for CentClus. Bank µ is 1.09-1.71 for p-FClus vs 0.61 for CentClus. p-FClus σ ranges 0.03-0.23, vs CentClus 0.03 (Adult) and 0.14 (Bank).

k-medoids intrinsic (Table 4): FEMNIST p-FClus µ 6.87, σ 0.96, max 9.69 vs CentClus 2.91, 0.65, 4.32. WISDM p-FClus µ 1.08e13, σ 2.64e13, max 1.30e14; CentClus was infeasible there (about 8 TB of memory needed).

limitations: No theoretical guarantees of any kind (approximation, convergence, fairness bound, privacy).

The comparison is not like-for-like. p-FClus is scored with each client's own personalized centers (effectively Z·k centers), while k-FED and MFC are scored with one global set of k centers, which favours p-FClus on µ.

Fairness means only the dispersion (σ) and maximum of per-client mean cost; this is not group or demographic fairness. p-FClus's σ is sometimes worse (unequal-split Adult at higher H; FEMNIST σ 0.364 is the worst of the three).

Eq. 5's regularizer λ||c^g − c^(z)||² pulls the personalized center toward the nearest local center. The text says it stops C^g 'collapsing to C^(z)', which contradicts the math. Unlike Ditto, which anchors to the global model, global knowledge is kept only through initialization at C^g and the finite number of steps t.
The math has slips: Eq. 6 assumes a squared norm, and Eq. 7 drops the sign(c^g − x) term.

The tables have inconsistencies. The CentClus Adult row shows max 0.60 below µ 1.64, which is impossible. The Table 2 caption says 100 and 1000 clients but its header says 500. The text says k-medoids µ is 'quite close' to centralized, yet on Bank it is about 2x worse and on FEMNIST about 2.4x worse.
The server sees raw local centers; there is no secure aggregation or differential privacy, and the privacy claim is only that raw data is not shared.
The union S is clustered without weighting by local cluster sizes, at least as described, so tiny clusters count as much as big ones.
λ and the number of tuning steps t are not reported; there is no sensitivity study for λ, and no runtime or communication measurements despite the efficiency claims.
The paper assumes benign, non-strategic clients, static data and a known k, and has no mechanism for clients joining or leaving.
future_work: Robust personalized federated clustering with malicious clients (Gupta et al. 2023a) and noisy data (Rehman et al. 2022).
Clients that strategically misreport features and so degrade the local centers (Stoica & Papadimitriou 2018).
Effects of unlearning in clustering as clients join and leave the federation (Pan et al. 2022 = MUFC).
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: p-FClus is not an unlearning method, but its one-shot design makes deletion easy to analyse. The global centers depend on client data only through the Z·k uploaded local centers. So deleting a client means dropping its k centers from S, re-clustering a tiny set and re-broadcasting, followed by local re-personalization: one extra round. Deleting a point affects only its own client's local centers, and everything else only if those centers move. Ginart-style quantized or stable local k-means could therefore make most deletions exact no-ops. Pan et al.'s MUFC, which this paper cites as future work, gives exact federated cluster unlearning through quantized, securely aggregated local summaries. p-FClus has no secure aggregation or guarantees, and a deleted client's influence persists in every other client's personalized centers until they re-personalize. The σ and max metrics give a ready-made way to measure whether unlearning hurts some clients more than others (unlearning fairness, as in FedShard).
open_questions: Design an exact unlearning protocol for p-FClus: client removal by deleting C^(z) from S and re-clustering, and point removal by quantized or stability-certified local centers (Ginart Q-k-means) so that most deletions trigger no communication. Bound the expected number of deletions that force a re-broadcast.

Does unlearning a client or point increase σ or max for the remaining clients? Define and bound 'unlearning fairness' for personalized federated clustering (cf. FedShard's efficiency and performance fairness).

Can re-personalization after a deletion be warm-started from the old personalized centers with a provable distance or cost bound, giving approximate or certified unlearning instead of full re-personalization?
Prove an approximation guarantee for 'cluster the union of local centers, then personalize', and a convergence guarantee for the Eq. 8 SGD with the inverse-count learning rate.
Add MUFC-style secure aggregation (SCMA) or DP to the uploaded local centers and measure the cost to personalization quality and to unlearning cost.
Weight S by local cluster sizes and test the effect on µ, σ and how much the global centers move when a client is deleted.

papers.title: MFC: A Multishot Approach to Federated Data Clustering
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Ropar, India
papers.venue: ECAI 2023 (26th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence; Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications vol. 372, IOS Press, doi:10.3233/FAIA230451)
papers.one_liner: Multi-round federated k-means: each client sends its highest-cost local center each round, needs no per-client cluster counts, and works across data regimes.
papers.summary: The paper studies federated data clustering: many clients hold private points and want k global k-means centers without sharing raw data. The one-shot method k-FED (Dennis et al., 2021) has each client cluster with its own cluster count k_z and upload centers once. It works only when each client holds few clusters (k_z <= sqrt(k)) and k_z must be known. MFC (Multishot Federated Clustering) instead has each client run Awasthi-Sheffet spectral k-means (SVD projection, approximate seeding, Lloyd steps) with the full k and send all k centers. The server runs Lloyd's algorithm on the pooled centers and broadcasts k global centers. In each later round, clients reassign their points, recompute local means and send only their highest-cost center. The server adds these to its pool and re-clusters. MFC_H sends a single random center at initialization, for lower communication and less disclosure. Under well-separability, local centers lie within c*sqrt(k)*||X-C||_2/sqrt(n_i^(z)) of the optimal global centers, and MFC_H inherits this once there are at least k^2 log k clients. On synthetic Gaussians, Adult and Bank, MFC/MFC_H approach centralized k-means in the homogeneous regime where k-FED fails, match k-FED in the heterogeneous regime, and spread per-device cost more evenly.
papers.problem: Existing federated k-means data-clustering methods are either expensive (cryptographic or generative-model approaches) or one-shot methods like k-FED. One-shot methods work only when data is heterogeneous across clients (k_z <= sqrt(k)) and assume each client knows its local cluster count k_z. When clients hold points from many or all clusters (the homogeneous, k_z = k, regime), k-FED's cost blows up, and per-device costs vary widely.
papers.core_idea: Do not try to infer k_z. Every client clusters with the full k, and the spurious extra centers that split one true cluster all stay close to that cluster's mean, so the server's clustering of the pooled centers absorbs them. Then spend a few extra communication rounds. In each round every client uploads only its worst-served (maximum-cost) local center, which steers the global centers toward under-represented regions and evens out per-client cost. MFC_H shares just one random center at the start and relies on enough clients (a coupon-collector argument, k^2 log k) so that every Gaussian component is still represented at the server.
papers.setting: federated unsupervised clustering (client-server federated k-means data clustering; IID-like homogeneous and non-IID heterogeneous client data)
papers.unlearning_type: none (paper is not about unlearning; federated k-means clustering with multi-round communication, no deletion mechanism)
contributions: MFC, a multishot federated k-means algorithm that needs no knowledge of the per-client cluster count k_z and works in both heterogeneous (k_z <= sqrt(k)) and homogeneous (k_z = k) regimes.
MFC_H, a heuristic variant in which each client shares a single random local center at initialization instead of all k, for communication efficiency and (informally) more privacy.

Theorem 1: under well-separability and a sufficient-local-cluster-size assumption, every local center from MFC's initial local step lies within c*sqrt(k)*||X-C||_2/sqrt(n^(z)) of the corresponding optimal global center, with c = 50/p' + alpha.
Lemma 6: with at least k^2 log k clients, MFC_H's first shot puts at least one representative from each Gaussian at the server (coupon-collector argument), so MFC's analysis carries over.
An informal client-fairness mechanism: uploading the maximum-cost center each round reduces the spread of per-device clustering cost (std and IQR), shown empirically against k-FED.
Experiments on a synthetic 10-Gaussian dataset, UCI Adult and UCI Bank with 50 clients, against centralized k-means, k-FED and a multishot extension k-FED_M that the authors construct.
method_steps: Setup: Z clients; client z holds X^(z) in R^d, drawn from k_z <= k of the k global clusters (k_z unknown). Everyone knows the target k (k = 10 in experiments).

Client init (Algorithm 1, Awasthi-Sheffet local k-means): (a) project local data X^(z) onto the span of its top-k right singular vectors (SVD) to get X_hat; (b) run any standard approximate k-means algorithm on X_hat to get k initial centers; (c) pruning step: for each center r, keep only points at least 3x closer to theta_r than to any other center (||X_hat_i - theta_r|| <= (1/3)||X_hat_i - theta_s|| for all s) and reset theta_r to their mean; (d) run Lloyd steps to convergence. Output k local centers theta^(z) and assignment phi^(z).
Client init upload: MFC sends all k local centers theta^(z) (k x d floats). MFC_H instead sends ONE randomly chosen local center (d floats).
Server init: pool S = union over z of the received centers (Z*k centers for MFC, Z for MFC_H); run Lloyd's k-means on S to get k global centers mu = {mu_1..mu_k}; broadcast mu to all clients.
Client update (each shot): reassign every local point x to its nearest global center, phi^(z)(x) = argmin_j ||x - mu_j||_2; recompute local centers theta^(z) as the means of the assigned points.

Client upload (each shot): compute each local cluster's cost sum_x I(phi(x)=theta_i)||x - phi(x)||^2 and send only theta_max^(z), the local center with the maximum cost (d floats per client per round).

Server update (each shot): S <- S union {theta_max^(1), ..., theta_max^(Z)} (the pool keeps growing); re-run Lloyd's k-means on S to get new global centers mu; broadcast mu. (The prose instead says Lloyd runs on 'the previous global centers and theta_max from all clients'; Algorithm 2 says the accumulated S.)
Repeat the client update, upload and server update for a few rounds until convergence (10 shots plotted in the experiments; no formal stopping rule).

Device churn: a newly joining or replacement device just downloads mu, computes its own assignments and starts sending its theta_max in later shots. Nothing is described for removing a departed client's past contributions from S.

key_definitions.name: Federated k-means clustering cost (Definition 1)
key_definitions.plain: Sum, over all clients and all their points, of the squared distance from each point to the global center it is assigned to.
key_definitions.formal: cost(X, mu) = sum_{z in [Z]} sum_{x in X^(z)} sum_{mu_j in mu} I(phi^(z)(x) = mu_j) ||x - mu_j||_2^2

key_definitions.name: Heterogeneous vs homogeneous regime
key_definitions.plain: In the heterogeneous regime every client holds points from only a few clusters, at most sqrt(k) of them. In the homogeneous regime every client holds points from all k clusters. k-FED's guarantees need the heterogeneous regime; MFC is meant to work in both.
key_definitions.formal: heterogeneous: k_z <= sqrt(k) for all z in [Z]; homogeneous: k_z = k for all z. In experiments, 'heterogeneity h' means each client gets points from exactly h of the k distributions.

key_definitions.name: Optimal-center matrix C
key_definitions.plain: An n x d matrix whose i-th row is the optimal (oracle) cluster mean of point i. ||X - C||_2 (spectral norm) measures how spread the data is around its true centers. C^(z) is the same matrix restricted to client z's points, using local cluster means.
key_definitions.formal: C_i = mu(T_{gamma(X_i)}), where T = {T_1..T_k} is the optimal clustering and gamma maps each point to its optimal cluster index

key_definitions.name: Well-separability (Definition 2, Assumption A2)
key_definitions.plain: Every pair of true cluster means is far apart compared with the spectral spread of the data, scaled by cluster sizes.
key_definitions.formal: ||mu(T_i) - mu(T_j)||_2 >= p * sqrt(k) * ||X - C||_2 * (1/sqrt(n_i) + 1/sqrt(n_j)), with p a large constant

key_definitions.name: Sufficient local cluster size (Assumption A1)
key_definitions.plain: Every non-empty piece of a global cluster that sits on one client has enough points for its sample mean to concentrate around the global cluster mean.
key_definitions.formal: n_i^(z) >= (8 sigma_i^2 / epsilon^2) * (ln(1/delta) + 1/4) for all i, with 0 < epsilon < 1 sufficiently small and 0 < delta < 1

key_definitions.name: Maximum-cost local center theta_max^(z)
key_definitions.plain: The local cluster center on client z whose assigned points have the largest total squared distance. It is the only center uploaded after initialization.
key_definitions.formal: theta_max^(z) = argmax_{theta_i} sum_{x in X^(z)} I(phi(x) = theta_i) ||x - phi(x)||_2^2

key_definitions.name: Local-to-global index map beta^(z)
key_definitions.plain: Maps each of the k local centers to the closest local cluster mean. Because clients run with the full k even when they hold only k_z < k clusters, several local centers may map to the same true cluster.
key_definitions.formal: beta^(z)(r) = argmin_{i in [k]} ||theta_r^(z) - mu(T_i^(z))||_2

key_definitions.name: gamma (fraction parameter in Lemma 4)
key_definitions.plain: A quantity that relates a cluster's local share on one client to its global size. The paper calls it an 'upper bound on the fraction of points on any client' but writes gamma <= n_i^(z)/n_i, which makes it a lower bound (wording inconsistency).
key_definitions.formal: gamma = (8 sigma_i^2 / (n_i epsilon^2)) * (ln(1/delta) + 1/4)

theory.name: Lemma 1 (Vector Bernstein, Kohler & Lucchi 2017)
theory.statement_plain: For independent zero-mean d-dimensional random vectors with bounded norm and bounded second moment, the average exceeds epsilon in norm only with exponentially small probability.
theory.assumptions: E[x_i] = 0, ||x_i||_2 <= mu, E[||x_i||^2] <= sigma^2, 0 < epsilon < sigma^2/mu
theory.significance: Concentration tool used to show that a client's partial cluster mean is close to the global cluster mean.

theory.name: Lemma 2 (local mean concentration)
theory.statement_plain: If client z holds at least (8 sigma_i^2/epsilon^2)(ln(1/delta)+1/4) points of global cluster i, then the mean of those local points is within epsilon of the global cluster mean, with probability at least 1 - delta.
theory.assumptions: Assumption A1; sigma_i^2 bounds E||T_ij^(z) - mu(T_i)||^2
theory.significance: Links each client's local optimal centers to the global optimal centers.

theory.name: Lemma 3 (Dennis et al. 2021, k-FED)
theory.statement_plain: A client's local spectral spread is at most 2 sqrt(k) times the global spread.
theory.assumptions: As in the k-FED analysis
theory.significance: Lets global separability parameters be converted into local ones. Imported from the one-shot k-FED paper.

theory.name: Lemma 4 (local well-separability)
theory.statement_plain: If every pair of global clusters is well separated with constant p, then the local sub-clusters on each client are also well separated with constant p' >= (p sqrt(gamma) - alpha), with probability at least 1 - delta.
theory.assumptions: A1, A2, and epsilon <= alpha sqrt(k)||X-C||_2/sqrt(n_max^(z))
theory.significance: Needed so that the Awasthi-Sheffet guarantee can be applied locally on each client.

theory.name: Lemma 5 (Awasthi & Sheffet 2012) plus the beta-mapping extension (Eq. 2)
theory.statement_plain: If the local sub-clusters are well separated, the centers returned by Algorithm 1 satisfy ||theta_i^(z) - mu(T_i^(z))||_2 <= (25/p') ||X^(z) - C^(z)||_2 / sqrt(n_i^(z)). When a client holds only k_z < k clusters, the extra centers split true clusters, so separability between those duplicates fails. The authors argue (informally, via the CLT, treating duplicate centers as two sample means of the same population) that each duplicate is still close to its mapped cluster mean, which gives Eq. 2 with index beta^(z)(r).
theory.assumptions: Local well-separability (Lemma 4); for the k_z < k case an informal CLT argument rather than a proof
theory.significance: This is the step that removes the need to know k_z: clients can always run with the full k.

theory.name: Theorem 1 (main theorem, MFC)
theory.statement_plain: Assuming well-separability, every local center from MFC's initial step is close to the optimal global center it maps to: ||theta_r^(z) - mu(T_{beta^(z)(r)})||_2 <= c sqrt(k) ||X - C||_2 / sqrt(n^(z)_{beta^(z)(r)}), with c = 50/p' + alpha. Proof: Eq. 2 plus Lemma 3 gives a 50 sqrt(k)/p' term, then the triangle inequality plus Lemma 2 adds epsilon <= alpha-term.
theory.assumptions: A1 (enough points per local sub-cluster), A2 (well-separated oracle centers, large p), data from a mixture of k Gaussians
theory.significance: Shows that what clients send at shot 0 is a faithful summary of the global optimum regardless of data distribution. It bounds only the initial local centers. The claim that later shots 'only perform a Lloyd's heuristic and thus lower the bound' is not proved, and there is no convergence or approximation-ratio result for the final global centers.

theory.name: Claim 7 (coupon collector problem)
theory.statement_plain: The expected number of uniform draws needed to collect all m coupon types is m*H_m, where H_m is the m-th harmonic number (about m ln m).
theory.assumptions: Uniform, independent draws
theory.significance: Probabilistic tool for the MFC_H client-count bound.

theory.name: Lemma 6 (MFC_H client-count bound)
theory.statement_plain: If there are at least k^2 log k devices, then after the first shot at least one point from each Gaussian component is represented at the server. Argument: about k_z log k_z <= k log k devices suffice to cover any one distribution, and summing over the k distributions gives k^2 log k. With this, all of MFC's lemmas apply to MFC_H.
theory.assumptions: Each client picks its shared center uniformly at random across its distributions; data is a mixture of k Gaussians. The argument is in expectation (coupon collector), not a high-probability bound, and it switches between 'data points' and 'centers'.
theory.significance: Justifies sharing only ONE center per client at initialization: O(k^2 log k) clients are enough for MFC_H to match MFC's guarantee.

papers.complexity: No formal complexity analysis is given. From the algorithm: MFC sends Z*k*d floats upstream at initialization. Each later shot sends only Z*d floats upstream (one theta_max per client) and k*d floats per client downstream. MFC_H cuts the initial upload to Z*d. The paper calls MFC_H 'much more communication efficient' for large k and many clients but reports no communication measurements. Client compute: one top-k SVD plus approximate k-means plus Lloyd on local data at init, then one assignment and mean step, O(n_z k d), per shot. The server runs Lloyd on the pool S, which grows by Z centers every shot (|S| = Z*k + t*Z for MFC after t shots). One-shot k-FED uses fewer rounds but needs k_z. Unlearning cost is not discussed. By inference from Algorithm 2, removing a client exactly would mean dropping its centers from S at every shot and re-running all shots, because its uploads changed every later global mu and therefore every other client's later theta_max. That is the cost of retraining from scratch, unlike one-shot schemes where only the server aggregation must be redone.

datasets: Synthetic: 10 bivariate Gaussians N_i(mu = 10i, sigma^2 = 2), i = 1..10, 1000 points each (10,000 total); satisfies well-separability
UCI Adult (1994 census): 32,562 records, 5 features (age, fnlwgt, education_num, capital_gain, hours_per_week)
UCI Bank Marketing (Portuguese bank): 41,108 records, 6 features (age, duration, campaign, cons.price.idx, euribor3m, nr.employed)
models: k-means with k = 10 (no neural models)
baselines: Ckmeans: centralized Lloyd's k-means on pooled data (reference lower bound)
k-FED (Dennis et al., ICML 2021): one-shot method; each client runs Lloyd with its known k_z, the server clusters the union of centers
k-FED_M: the authors' multishot extension of k-FED (k-FED for shot 1, MFC-like max-cost updates afterwards)
metrics: Device-level fairness: mean, standard deviation and inter-quartile range (IQR) of per-device clustering cost

Setup: 50 clients, k = 10, up to 10 shots; homogeneous regime k_z = k; heterogeneous regime with each client getting points from exactly k_z distributions (the k_z used in the Fig. 1 heterogeneous row is not stated); i5 8th-gen CPU, 8 GB RAM, Python 3.8
headline_results: Homogeneous, synthetic (Fig. 1, values read off the plot): one-shot k-FED cost about 125 vs Ckmeans about 79. MFC starts at about 79 and MFC_H at about 84. k-FED_M needs about 2 shots to fall to about 81-83. All multishot methods settle around 84-86, slightly above Ckmeans.

Homogeneous, Adult (plot): k-FED about 6.15 vs Ckmeans about 4.2. MFC goes from about 4.5 to about 4.25 and MFC_H from about 4.7 to about 4.25 over 10 shots. k-FED_M goes from 6.15 to about 4.4, still with a gap.
Homogeneous, Bank (plot): k-FED about 1.75 vs Ckmeans about 1.23. MFC about 1.31-1.38, MFC_H about 1.35-1.42, k-FED_M from 1.75 to about 1.41.

Heterogeneous regime: one-shot k-FED is already near Ckmeans (synthetic about 80; Adult about 4.35 vs 4.2; Bank about 1.245 vs 1.23). MFC's initial cost is close. MFC_H on synthetic starts at about 84.4 and falls to about 80.5.

Not discussed by the authors (visible in Fig. 1): on heterogeneous Adult and Bank, every multishot method (MFC, MFC_H, k-FED_M) rises after the first shot (Adult about 4.8 to 6.0-6.7; Bank about 1.30 to 1.40-1.45) and ends above one-shot k-FED. The paper describes this as converging to 'akin equivalent cost values'.

Fig. 2 (synthetic, cost after a single shot vs k_z = 1..10): k-FED is about 125 at k_z=1, lowest (about 80) at k_z=3, and climbs to about 290 at k_z=10. MFC (about 90-100), MFC_H (about 85) and Ckmeans (about 78) stay roughly flat.

Table 1 (synthetic per-device fairness, k-FED vs MFC): at k_z=1, mean/std/IQR = 149.672/175.013/108.448 for k-FED vs 8.698/2.461/1.965 for MFC; at k_z=10, 182.989/48.496/56.827 vs 85.635/12.553/19.413. MFC has the lower std at every k_z. k-FED has the lower mean per-device cost at k_z = 2, 3, 4 (14.861 vs 16.604; 15.948 vs 24.601; 29.013 vs 30.952) and the lower IQR at k_z=3 (4.036 vs 5.537). MFC_H fairness results were omitted for space ('similar to MFC').

limitations: The privacy claims are informal. MFC_H is 'more private' only because it shares one center instead of k. There is no differential privacy, secure aggregation or formal leakage analysis, and every shot still reveals a raw local center (theta_max), which for small clusters can be close to individual points.

The theory bounds only the initial local centers (shot 0). The final server-side global centers and the multishot iterations come with no convergence, monotonicity or approximation guarantee, and experiments show cost can increase across shots (heterogeneous Adult/Bank; slightly on synthetic/Bank homogeneous).
The case where a client holds k_z < k clusters (spurious duplicate centers) is handled by an informal CLT argument, not a proof.
Lemma 6 (k^2 log k) is an expected-value coupon-collector argument with a loose summation over distributions. It mixes up 'data points' and 'centers' and assumes uniform random selection.
The results rely on a mixture-of-Gaussians model, well-separability with a large constant p, and a large-sample assumption A1. The authors admit that real data (Adult, Bank) may violate these.

There are notation inconsistencies: gamma is called an upper bound but defined as a lower bound on the local fraction; Algorithm 2 writes theta_max^(1..k) where it should be (1..Z); and the prose and Algorithm 2 disagree about what the server re-clusters (previous mu plus theta_max vs the accumulated S).
The server's pool S grows without bound across shots, and the stopping rule ('until convergence') is not specified.

The evaluation is narrow: three low-dimensional datasets, k=10, 50 clients and a single cost metric. Communication and runtime are not measured, and there is no comparison with Chung et al., SecFC or DP federated clustering. The fairness study covers only synthetic data and MFC vs k-FED.
The global k must still be known.
There is no unlearning support. 'Removal of devices' covers only assignment, not erasing a departed client's influence on the global centers.
future_work: Detailed analysis of fairness notions such as group fairness and individual fairness in federated clustering.
Adapting the approach to problems such as client selection in federated learning.
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: MFC is a federated k-means baseline with no deletion mechanism, and it shows exactly where unlearning gets expensive. Its initial shot (local clustering, then server clustering of pooled centers) is a two-level divide-and-conquer tree, the same structure that makes Ginart et al.'s DC-k-means and MUFC's one-shot aggregation cheap to unlearn: delete a point, recompute one client's leaf, then re-cluster at the server. The multishot loop breaks this locality. Every theta_max upload depends on the global centers, which depend on every other client's earlier uploads, and the server pool S keeps them all. So exact client- or point-level unlearning in MFC means retraining all shots from scratch, unless one adds per-shot checkpoints of S and mu (SISA-style) or quantizes the messages (Q-k-means-style) so that most deletions leave the transmitted centers unchanged. The paper therefore gives a clean test case for a research question: how much clustering quality and per-client fairness does multishot interaction buy, and how much deletion efficiency does it cost compared with one-shot MUFC/k-FED? Its device-level fairness metrics (std and IQR of per-client cost) can also be reused to check whether unlearning a client hurts the remaining clients unevenly.
open_questions: Make MFC deletion-efficient. Checkpoint the server pool S and the global centers mu after every shot and quantize theta_max and mu (as in Ginart's Q-k-means). Then prove a bound on the expected number of shots that must be recomputed when one point or one client is deleted.

Approximate or certified client unlearning for multishot federated clustering. After removing a client's centers from S, how many warm-started shots are needed to get within epsilon (in centers or in cost) of a full retrain? Can Theorem 1-style separability arguments bound that gap?

Compare one-shot schemes (k-FED, MUFC) with multishot schemes (MFC) on clustering cost, per-client fairness, communication and unlearning time under the same deletion workload, and identify regimes (k_z vs sqrt(k)) where multishot is worth its higher unlearning cost.

Formal privacy for MFC_H. Add differential-privacy noise or secure aggregation (e.g. MUFC's SCMA) to the per-shot theta_max uploads and quantify the privacy-utility trade-off, since the current 'share one center' argument is informal.

Prove convergence or monotonicity for MFC's multishot iterations, or explain the cost increases seen on heterogeneous Adult and Bank. Then design a stopping rule and a bounded server pool S, which would also bound the state an unlearning procedure must edit.

Fairness under unlearning. When a client leaves and its influence is removed, does the per-client cost spread (std/IQR) of the remaining clients get worse? This connects to FedShard's efficiency and performance fairness and to FairSISA.

papers.title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
affiliations: Centre for Responsible AI, Wadhwani School of Data Science & AI, Indian Institute of Technology Madras
Department of Artificial Intelligence, Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology (SVNIT), Surat
Department of Electrical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Madras
papers.one_liner: Exact same-seed replay unlearning for federated socially fair k-means, using per-(client, group) summaries that stay valid when global group weights change.
papers.summary: Hospitals or banks may want to cluster their records together without pooling them (federated clustering). They may also want the centers to serve every demographic group comparably well, and they must be able to delete records on request. This paper uses socially fair k-means: minimize the larger of the two groups' average squared distance to the nearest center. Under this objective a deletion is global, because removing a group-g record changes the group size n_g and so the weight 1/n_g of every group-g record at every institution. The authors fix the issue by having each (client, group) slice build its own k-means++ (D^2-sampling) summary with no reference to global group sizes. Only the server divides counts by n_g. A deletion therefore leaves summaries at untouched institutions valid. Initial centers are then refined with a guarded Fair-Lloyd update computed from exact integer count, sum and squared-sum statistics. Unlearning replays the fully specified training map with the same seed: it reuses untouched summaries, recomputes touched ones, and patches statistics exactly, so the output equals retraining bit for bit. For two groups they prove an O(log^2 k) initialization guarantee that does not depend on client group proportions. Whole-client withdrawal is up to 35.8x faster than retraining at zero refinement rounds. Single-record deletions save only about 6%.
papers.problem: Federated clustering systems should both represent demographic groups fairly and honor exact data deletion (e.g., GDPR erasure). Under socially fair k-means each record of group g has weight 1/n_g, so deleting a record at one site changes the normalization of every site's records, can alter initial centers and later fair updates, and simple subtraction from cached cluster statistics does not reproduce retraining. The open question is which parts of a federated fair-clustering computation can be kept after a deletion while the released model stays exactly what retraining would produce, and when keeping them actually saves work.
papers.core_idea: Separate local summary construction from everything that depends on global group sizes. Each (client, group) ownership slice selects up to k representatives by D^2-sampling on its own keyed random stream and reports multiplicities, never using n_g, so only the server's weights h/n_g change after a deletion elsewhere. Combined with a fully specified ('declared') deterministic training map, exact integer sufficient statistics and per-entity seeded streams, same-seed replay can reuse untouched work and patch the rest so that it reproduces retraining's entire indexed center trajectory.
papers.setting: Horizontal federated (cross-silo) unsupervised k-means clustering with C institutions holding disjoint records, each record having a binary protected group (e.g., census SEX); socially fair (minimax group-average cost) objective; exact unlearning of record batches and whole clients; simulated locally on one machine.
contributions: Group-separated federated initialization SplitGroup-2k: per-(client, group) D^2-sampling summaries, reweighted by h/n_g only at the server, with an expected O(log^2 k) socially-fair approximation factor (plus a quantization term) independent of n, C, group imbalance and client group proportions under ideal sampling (Theorem 1).

A tight negative result for the natural locally balanced single-summary adaptation of MUFC (Merged-1k): expected loss Theta(kappa), linear in the local/global group-share mismatch kappa (Theorem 2), plus a matched-slot gap for Merged-2k that one fair refinement round removes (Proposition 7).

A guarded, finite, deterministic version of the Fair-Lloyd two-group center update driven by exact (N, S, SS) statistics, which equals the centralized update (Prop 6) and never increases the worst-group cost (Prop 3).

Exact batch replay (Algorithm 1) with exact integer patching and assignment certificates (all-competitor Lemma 4 and stronger O(1) runner-up certificate, Prop 8), proven to reproduce same-seed retraining's whole indexed center trajectory (Theorem 5); 810/810 replay comparisons matched retraining exactly.

Cost analysis showing where reuse pays off and where it fails: a work bound (Eq. 29), a conditional locally-stable replay bound (Prop 9), and a scoped obstruction where one legal deletion forces Omega(n) expected duplicated assignment work for the specified sampler/cache/fallback policy (Lemma 10, Prop 11).

Empirical mapping on Adult, Bank, Credit and 2018 ACS census data: whole-client deletion 35.8x faster than retraining at T=0 and 2.4x/1.7x at T=1/2, but only about 1.06x for record deletion, with certification increasing aggregate end-to-end cost.

Extensions: raw-data-free compact whole-client replay state (Prop 13, following Pan et al. 2023 Sec 5.3), multi-group (m>2) bounds and a Frank-Wolfe dual prototype (Appendices B.4, G, L), and Lean 4 proofs of several mathematical results.
method_steps: Fix preprocessing once: clip and encode every feature on a fixed-point grid x = m * 2^-b (b = 12 in experiments); give records persistent identities; derive a separate PCG64 random stream for each (seed, role, client, group) slice and for the server (keyed random streams). Use an exact rational categorical sampler with fixed tie, saturation and zero-potential completion rules (the 'declared training map').

Phase I, local (per ownership slice e = (c, g), i.e. the group-g records of client c): select k_e = min(k, |X_e|) representatives by D^2-sampling (k-means++ seeding, no Lloyd steps) using the slice's own stream. Assign every slice record to its nearest representative to get multiplicities h_{e,j}. Snap representatives to a grid of width gamma to get anchors q_{e,j}. Send (q_{e,j}, h_{e,j}), at most 2k anchors per client. No global group size is used.

Phase I, server: compute global group sizes n_A, n_B exactly. Weight each anchor by omega_{e,j} = h_{e,j}/n_g, the only step that uses global sizes. Select k initial centers by exact weighted D^2-sampling on the server stream. Optionally run T_a deterministic weighted anchor-Lloyd iterations that never increase the weighted anchor objective.

Phase II, each of T rounds: the server broadcasts the indexed centers. Each client assigns every record to its nearest center (exact squared-distance comparisons, smallest-index ties). For every group-cell (group g, cluster j) the client computes exact integer statistics N_{g,j} (count), S_{g,j} (vector sum) and SS_{g,j} (squared-norm sum), and these are exactly aggregated; secure aggregation is not implemented. Clients cache each point's label, nearest and second-nearest distances, and runner-up center ID.

Server GuardedFairUpdate_L: from the statistics form group means mu_{g,j} and masses alpha_j = N_{A,j}/n_A, beta_j = N_{B,j}/n_B. For two-group clusters the candidate is c_j(lambda) = (lambda alpha_j mu_{A,j} + (1-lambda) beta_j mu_{B,j}) / (lambda alpha_j + (1-lambda) beta_j); a single-group cluster uses its group mean; an empty cluster keeps its old center. Evaluate lambda = 0, 1 and L bisection midpoints, scoring each rounded candidate exactly. Pick the one with the lowest max(f_A, f_B), and accept it only if it does not exceed the current centers' cost.

Checkpoint for unlearning: (i) every slice's anchors and multiplicities; (ii) global group sizes and the server sampling state; (iii) indexed centers and exact aggregate statistics for every round; (iv) at clients, each point's cached label, d1, d2 and runner-up ID per round (about 64nT bytes in memory, 48nT serialized).

Unlearning a batch R (valid only if both groups stay nonempty): reuse the cached (q, h) of every slice with no deleted record. Rerun D^2-sampling, assignment and quantization on X_e minus R for touched slices, with their original streams. Recompute n_g and the weights h/n_g, then rerun the server's weighted D^2-sampling (and any anchor-Lloyd steps) from its original stream.

Replay each refinement round: broadcast the replay centers and the per-center shifts delta_m relative to the cached trajectory. Remove deleted records from their cached group-cells. Certify each surviving cached label with the all-competitor test delta_j + max_{m != j} delta_m < d2 - d1 or the runner-up test (Eq. 28), and exactly reassign every failure. Patch (N, S, SS) with signed exact integer corrections. If more than half of the attempted certificates fail, discard the round's patches, rebuild statistics from zero, and assign directly from then on. Apply the same GuardedFairUpdate_L.
Direct replay variant: keep the Phase-I reuse but reassign every retained record in every round with no certificates. This is the variant that wins most timing comparisons.

Whole-client withdrawal with T = 0 (compact path, Prop 13): store only per-client summaries, exact per-client group counts and server settings. Drop the departing clients' summaries, update n'_g, rebuild the anchor list with weights h/n'_g, and rerun the server sampler from its original stream. No raw records are needed. This mirrors MUFC's server-only retraining.
Output the indexed center trajectory and final centers. Replay marks its cache invalid, so any later record deletion must first rebuild the per-point cache (about (n-r)kT distance queries).

key_definitions.name: Socially fair k-means objective
key_definitions.plain: Compute each group's average squared distance to its nearest center and minimize the worse (larger) of these group averages; each group-g record effectively carries weight 1/n_g.
key_definitions.formal: Phi_g(C) = (1/n_g) * sum_{x: g(x)=g} min_j ||x - c_j||^2 ; Phi(C) = max_{g in {A,B}} Phi_g(C)

key_definitions.name: Balanced surrogate G
key_definitions.plain: Sum of the two group-average costs, used in proofs; within a factor 2 of Phi.
key_definitions.formal: G(C) = Phi_A(C) + Phi_B(C), Phi <= G <= 2 Phi

key_definitions.name: Ownership slice (pseudo-client)
key_definitions.plain: The records of one group held by one client; the unit that builds an independent local summary.
key_definitions.formal: e = (c, g), X_e = X_{c,g} = {x in X_c : g(x) = g}

key_definitions.name: Group-cell
key_definitions.plain: Records of group g currently assigned to center j; depends on the current assignment, unlike ownership slices which depend on who stores the record.
key_definitions.formal: P_{g,j}^(t) = {x : z_t(x) = j} intersect X_g

key_definitions.name: Anchor weight
key_definitions.plain: Server weight of a quantized representative: its multiplicity divided by its group's global size.
key_definitions.formal: omega_{e,j} = h_{e,j} / n_g

key_definitions.name: Local/global mismatch kappa
key_definitions.plain: Largest ratio, over mixed clients, between a client's shares of the two global groups; measures how much local group balancing distorts global weights (hospital example: 30% of A vs 3% of B gives 10).
key_definitions.formal: a_c = n_{c,A}/n_A, b_c = n_{c,B}/n_B, kappa = max{1, max_{c: a_c b_c > 0} max(a_c/b_c, b_c/a_c)}

key_definitions.name: Declared training map
key_definitions.plain: The fully specified randomized training procedure Train(X; s), including orderings, tie-breaking, empty clusters, degenerate sampling cases, numeric encoding and per-entity random streams, relative to which exactness is defined.
key_definitions.formal: Train(X; s), FTF-1 specification (Appendix M)

key_definitions.name: Exact (same-seed) unlearning
key_definitions.plain: After deleting batch R, the released model and its entire indexed center trajectory must equal what retraining on the retained data with the same seed would produce.
key_definitions.formal: pi(Unlearn(Train(X; s), R; s)) = pi(Train(X \ R; s)) for every seed s

key_definitions.name: Assignment certificate
key_definitions.plain: Sufficient condition that a point's cached nearest center is still uniquely nearest after centers move.
key_definitions.formal: delta_j + max_{m != j} delta_m < d2 - d1 (Lemma 4); runner-up: d1 + delta_j < min{|d2 - delta_r|, max(0, d2 - max_{m not in {j,r}} delta_m)}

key_definitions.name: Useful coverage
key_definitions.plain: Share of survivor point-rounds whose assignment work certification actually saved after fallback discards.
key_definitions.formal: S/N with N = (n - r) T

key_definitions.name: Valid deletion batch
key_definitions.plain: A request that leaves both demographic groups nonempty (otherwise h/n_g and Phi_g are undefined).
key_definitions.formal: n_A(X \ R) > 0 and n_B(X \ R) > 0

theory.name: Theorem 1 (Split-group warm start)
theory.statement_plain: At gamma = 0, SplitGroup-2k's initial centers satisfy E[Phi(C0)] <= 2 alpha_k (sqrt(alpha_k) + 2)^2 Phi*, with alpha_k = 5(ln k + 2) (Makarychev-Reddy-Shan k-means++ factor). That is an O(log^2 k) factor independent of n, C, group imbalance and client group proportions. For gamma > 0 an additive O(d gamma^2 log k) quantization term appears (Eqs 14-16). Non-increasing anchor-Lloyd steps preserve the bound.
theory.assumptions: Two groups, both nonempty; ideal independent random bits for every slice and the server; exact rational categorical sampling; deterministic degeneracy rules; grid error ||q - z||^2 <= d gamma^2/4 (binary64 rounding handled in App B.3).
theory.significance: Shows that group-separated summaries can be reused after deletions without losing proportion-independent initialization quality. The proof bounds local replacement error slice by slice (weights are constant within a slice) and composes it with server D^2-sampling using L2 Minkowski inequalities.

theory.name: Theorem 2 (Tight heterogeneity dependence for Merged-1k)
theory.statement_plain: The locally group-balanced single-summary adaptation of MUFC has expected G/G* = O(kappa log^2 k) at gamma = 0 (Eq 26: E G <= alpha_k((1+sqrt(alpha_k)) sqrt(kappa) + 1)^2 G*). Conversely, for every rational kappa >= 1 there is a two-client, two-group, 1-D, k = 1 instance (gamma = T_a = 0) where the expected ratio is at least kappa/2 for G and kappa/4 for Phi.
theory.assumptions: Same as Theorem 1; the lower bound is not claimed for T_a > 0, for Merged-2k, or for the refined model, and is specific to the declared merged sampler.
theory.significance: Explains why fairness weights must not be balanced locally: a nearly pure client's tiny minority gets half its local sampling probability, a loss linear in the mismatch.

theory.name: Proposition 3 (Monotonicity)
theory.statement_plain: One nearest-center assignment step followed by GuardedFairUpdate_L never increases the worst-group cost Phi.
theory.assumptions: Exact scoring of the represented (rounded) candidates; the guard compares against the current centers on the current partition.
theory.significance: Refinement is safe to iterate. Appendix A.4 shows that without the guard, finite bisection can increase the cost (d = k = 1, A = {-1, +1}, B = {3}: one bisection step gives cost 13/4 > 25/9).

theory.name: Proposition 6 (Algorithm-relative centralized equivalence)
theory.statement_plain: If federated aggregation returns exact (N, S, SS), the federated GuardedFairUpdate_L returns exactly the same indexed centers as a centralized implementation with the same partition, candidate order and deterministic arithmetic.
theory.assumptions: Exact additive statistics; equivalence is to the declared finite guarded solver, not to the exact convex optimum.
theory.significance: Federation costs no quality relative to the centralized fair update, which the replay-exactness induction relies on.

theory.name: Proposition 7 (Pre-refinement gap with matched anchor slots)
theory.statement_plain: On a three-location, two-client, 1-D, k = 1 instance where Merged-2k and SplitGroup-2k each send two anchor slots per client, the expected ratios are E G/G* = (kappa+5)/3 vs 2 and E Phi/Phi* = (kappa+8)/6 vs 3/2. One full-data guarded fair-refinement round maps any incumbent to the optimum.
theory.assumptions: Rational kappa >= 1; gamma = T_a = T = 0; ideal categorical bits.
theory.significance: Matching the communication budget does not close the initialization gap, but the gap is an initialization effect that refinement can remove.

theory.name: Lemma 4 (All-competitor certificate)
theory.statement_plain: A retained point's cached unique winner j stays uniquely nearest if delta_j + max_{m != j} delta_m < d2 - d1, where delta_m is the displacement of center m between the cached and replay trajectories. The maximum must range over all competitors, not only the old runner-up.
theory.assumptions: Cached exact (or outward-bounded) d1 < d2 and displacement norms; strict inequality; ambiguous cases go to exact assignment.
theory.significance: Lets replay skip reassignment for points far from decision boundaries, using the Elkan/Hamerly movement-bound idea between the original and replay trajectories.

theory.name: Proposition 8 (Tightness and runner-up certificate)
theory.statement_plain: Given only (j, d1, d2) and displacement radii, Lemma 4 is the strongest universally sound test (tight for k >= 3 with exact norms; for k = 2 the condition is d1 + delta_j < |d2 - delta_r|). With the cached runner-up identity r, the strictly stronger test d1 + delta_j < min{|d2 - delta_r|, max(0, d2 - D_{not j,r})} is still O(1) per point after precomputing the three largest shifts.
theory.assumptions: A cache that stores only the label, d1, d2 and runner-up ID.
theory.significance: The cache cannot do much better, and richer caches (e.g. Yinyang-style) would be needed for more coverage.

theory.name: Theorem 5 (Seeded exact batch model-output unlearning)
theory.statement_plain: For every fixed seed s, the projection of Unlearn(Train(X; s), R; s) onto the entire indexed center trajectory and final model equals that of Train(X \ R; s). For a fixed or seed-independent R they are also equal in distribution over s.
theory.assumptions: Exact additive sufficient statistics; deterministic center arithmetic, quantization, ties, empty-cluster and zero-potential rules; separate seeded streams per slice and server; sound certificate comparisons; valid batch (both groups nonempty). There is no guarantee for adaptively chosen requests or for equality of full caches/state.
theory.significance: Core exactness result. The proof matches the initializer (untouched slices have the same inputs and tapes), then inducts over rounds: signed exact corrections turn cached statistics into fresh retained statistics, and abandonment preserves the update.

theory.name: Replay work bound (Eq. 29)
theory.statement_plain: At unit arithmetic cost, scanning replay costs O(W0 + W_I + nT + CkdT + Ck log k T + (L+2)kdT + rdT + [sum_t F_t + (n-r)|T_dir|](kd + k log k)), where W0 is per-call setup (Omega(n) even at T = 0), W_I is touched-slice plus server re-initialization, F_t counts failed certificates, and T_dir indexes full direct rounds. For a uniformly random batch, the expected touched-slice mass is at most r * s_max (Eq 34).
theory.assumptions: Unit-cost arithmetic model; bit complexity of exact integers is excluded.
theory.significance: Shows that exactness alone does not save work: per-round survivor scans and setup remain, so savings come mainly from Phase-I reuse.
