theory.name: Proposition 9 (Locally stable replay)
theory.statement_plain: Assume center perturbations satisfy delta_0 <= a0 r/n and delta_{t+1} <= q delta_t + a r/n with q < 1, and margin density #{x: d2 - d1 <= h} <= mu n h. Then delta_t <= L_s r/n with L_s = a0 + a/(1-q), ideal certificate failures are at most 2 mu L_s r per round, and Phase-II work is O(nT + rdT + Ck log k T + [mu L_s r T + sum B_t + (n-r)|T_dir|](kd + k log k)).
theory.assumptions: A stable local basin (locally contractive guarded map, nondegenerate fair dual, well-separated means). These assumptions are not unconditional, and numerical-only failures B_t are not bounded.
theory.significance: Certificate failures scale with r rather than n only if replayed centers stay close to the cached ones. The paper explicitly declines to claim an unconditional speed theorem.

theory.name: Lemma 10 (Shared words need not give a stable categorical coupling)
theory.statement_plain: For the declared sampler (gcd reduction plus low-bit rejection sampling), two categorical calls with masses (m, m) and (m, m-1) that read the same random word select different categories with probability m/(2m-1) > 1/2, although their total-variation distance is only 1/[2(2m-1)].
theory.assumptions: FTF-1 sampler with ideal independent 64-bit words, both calls starting at the same word offset.
theory.significance: A tiny change in distribution does not mean a similar coupled sample under same-seed replay, so exact replay can be unstable.

theory.name: Proposition 11 (One legal deletion can force linear discarded work)
theory.statement_plain: Take a three-client, two-group 1-D dataset with n = 3m, k = 2 and gamma = T_a = 0, and one fixed legal single-record deletion. With probability at least (m-1)^2/(4m(2m-1)) > 1/16, every one of the 2m-1 retained group-A labels changes at round zero. Both certificate variants then abandon under the strict-majority rule, giving expected certificate failures and duplicated assignments of Omega(n).
theory.assumptions: Ideal random words; T >= 1; specific to the declared sampler, indexed cache and strict-majority fallback policy. It is not a universal lower bound and not a wall-clock claim.
theory.significance: A scoped obstruction showing that certification can cost more than it saves even for single deletions. This matches the empirical observation that certificates almost always abandon at round zero.

theory.name: Proposition 12 (Direct cache reconstruction upper bound)
theory.statement_plain: Rebuilding the per-point cache after a replay takes (n-r)kT center-point distance queries and O((n-r)kdT) arithmetic plus nearest/second selection.
theory.assumptions: Direct construction; this is an upper bound, not a lower bound.
theory.significance: Sequential record deletions with T > 0 are not free: the replay output invalidates the cache.

theory.name: Proposition 13 (Whole-client summary replay at initialization)
theory.statement_plain: For T = 0 and whole-client deletions that leave both groups nonempty, the following returns exactly fresh training's C(0): drop the departing clients' summaries, recompute the retained n'_g exactly, rebuild the canonical anchor list with weights h/n'_g, and rerun the server procedure from its original stream.
theory.assumptions: Local summaries depend only on their ordered slice, fixed parameters and a stream keyed by (s, c, g); trusted, unmodified compact state; persistent IDs, never renumbered.
theory.significance: A specialization of Theorem 5 that follows Pan et al. (2023, Sec 5.3, Alg 4); the authors say it is not a new general theorem. It enables a raw-data-free compact state (O(Ckd) coordinates plus O(C) counts) that survives sequential withdrawals by induction.

theory.name: Multi-group extension (Appendix B.4, Eqs 22-24)
theory.statement_plain: For m nonempty groups and gamma = 0, E Phi_m(C0) <= m alpha_k (sqrt(alpha_k) + 2)^2 Phi*_m. For gamma > 0 an additive O(m d gamma^2 log k) term appears.
theory.assumptions: Same as Theorem 1, with all m global groups nonempty.
theory.significance: Group separation still works for m > 2, but the linear dependence on m does not improve on the best known centralized multi-group results.

theory.name: Multi-group fixed-partition dual (Appendix G)
theory.statement_plain: For m > 2 groups and a fixed partition, the minimax center update is the convex epigraph program min theta s.t. f_g(C) <= theta. Its concave Lagrange dual over the simplex gives candidate centers b_j(lambda)/A_j(lambda). Any feasible tuple with max_g f_g(C) - D(lambda) <= eta is eta-optimal by weak duality.
theory.assumptions: Fixed partition; exactness of replay needs only a deterministic solver, not optimality.
theory.significance: Basis for the Frank-Wolfe multi-group prototype with certified duality gaps.

papers.complexity: Training communication: Phase I sends at most 2k anchors plus multiplicities per client (one shot). Phase II sends dense packets of 2k(d+2) numbers per client per round (not measured as bytes or network cost). Server initialization costs O(Ck^2(d + log k)(1 + T_a)) on at most 2Ck anchors. Each training round assigns all n points in O(n(kd + k log k)). Storage: the per-point cache is 64nT bytes in memory (48nT serialized), and the ACS checkpoints averaged 103 MB (max 504 MB; mean build 2.44 s). Replay cost (Eq 29) is O(W0 + W_I + nT + CkdT + Ck log k T + (L+2)kdT + rdT + [sum F_t + (n-r)|T_dir|](kd + k log k)). W0 = O(nd + nr + (n+r) log(n+r+2) + C) is setup, unavoidable even at T = 0. W_I = O(M_s(kd + k log k) + Q_s d + Ck + Ck^2(d + log k)(1+T_a)) covers touched slices and the server, and E[M_s] <= r s_max for random requests. Direct replay still scans every survivor each round, so for T > 0 it saves only the Phase-I share. Whole-client T = 0 compact replay needs no raw records: it keeps O(Ckd) summary coordinates plus O(C) counts (0.28-3.35 MB versus 12.5-55 MB full checkpoints) and per request reruns only the server sampler. Rebuilding the cache for sequential deletions costs (n-r)kT distance queries (Prop 12).

headline_results: Exactness: all 810 original replay comparisons (525 P2 + 285 P3) match fresh retraining exactly in every indexed center and raw integer statistic; all 135 record-budget, 90 whole-client positive-budget and compact-state comparisons also match.

Whole-client deletion (k = 10, one preselected client per dataset, 5 seeds): at T = 0, compact replay is 35.79x faster than fresh (Adult 26.96, Bank 115.53, Credit 25.03) and direct replay 17.79x. Canonical Direct is 2.357x at T = 1 (2.053/2.646/2.647) and 1.696x at T = 2 (1.544/1.828/1.856), winning all 15 cases at each budget. These are resident request-time ratios with inputs in memory, excluding cold load, network and persistence.
Quality price of T = 0: worst-group cost is 18.2-62.1% above two-round training (mean Phi T=0 to T=2: Adult 117.96 to 96.00, Bank 45.90 to 32.63, Credit 20.12 to 13.01).

Record deletion P2 (Adult/Bank/Credit, T = 15, r = 30/45/30): Direct total algorithm ratio 1.061 (E2E 1.049), beating retraining in 173/175 trials. Basic 1.006 (E2E 0.996); Runner-up 1.005 (E2E 0.995); useful certificate coverage 0.76%; certificates abandon at round zero in 174/175 trials.

Record deletion P3 (ACS, 95 trials): Direct 1.056 (E2E 1.043), wins 80/95; Basic 0.938 (E2E 0.930); Runner-up 0.940 (E2E 0.931); useful coverage 1.35%; abandonment at round zero in 92/95 trials. Only three r = 1 trials never fell back, reaching 14-17x algorithm ratios.

Record deletion with small budgets (k = 10): Direct algorithm ratios at T = 0/1/2 are 4.12/1.74/1.42 (Adult), 1.39/1.23/1.16 (Bank), 3.70/1.97/1.59 (Credit). Phi falls 19.8/31.2/29.0% from T = 0 to T = 2.
Heterogeneity P1 at kappa = 128: Merged-1k mean G/G* = 63.53 (SE 1.10) versus SplitGroup-2k 2.24, Merged-2k 1.90, centralized 1.77.
Fair vs ordinary Lloyd from identical initialization at T = 2: worst-group cost 3.2-5.1% lower, but population-average cost 0.5-4.7% higher, in all 30 cases.
Three sequential T = 0 withdrawals: fresh/compact 34.99x (matched outputs), 22.27x including buffered state round-trip.
Multi-group prototype (9 RAC1P groups): fresh/direct request ratios 138.70/1.60/1.30 at T = 0/1/2; compact T = 0 139.14; Phi 16.374/9.994/9.445.

limitations: Stated: exactness is conditional on one fixed represented dataset and preprocessing state; it does not erase a record's influence on the fitted scaler, encoding or vocabulary.

Stated: refined batch outputs invalidate the per-point cache, so further record replay needs cache reconstruction ((n-r)kT distance queries). Only the T = 0 whole-client compact state supports cheap sequential deletion.
Stated: the canonical learner and main experiments are binary-group; multi-group is only a separate prototype tested on one population and one request.

Stated: timings come from a local single-machine simulation (Apple M3 Max, warm OS caches, nondedicated desktop, five seeds). Network, secure aggregation, stragglers, dropouts, durable persistence and physical purge are unmeasured.
Stated: federation is not differential privacy or cryptographic erasure. Group anchors (which can coincide with records at gamma = 0) and small group-cell changes can leak information.
Stated: group-average squared cost does not establish individual, intersectional, representation or downstream fairness, and fair updates raise population-average cost.

Stated: there is no fresh-independent distributional guarantee for deletion requests chosen adaptively from the seed-dependent checkpoint, and no equality of full internal state. Requests that empty a group are excluded.
Stated: the deletion settings where reuse pays most (whole client, T = 0) are the ones with worse fairness quality (worst-group cost 18-62% higher than T = 2).

Noticed: per-record gains are tiny (about 6% algorithm time). Certificates almost never pay off (useful coverage under 1.4%, abandonment at round zero in 174/175 and 92/95 trials) and increase aggregate E2E cost.
Noticed: for T > 0, replay still scans all survivors each round (O(n) per round). No sublinear exact replay for refinement is offered, so savings come only from Phase-I reuse.

Noticed: the headline 35.8x uses a separate compact implementation with 3 timing repeats, while the T = 1/2 ratios use canonical Direct with 4 repeats. The whole-client evidence uses one preselected client per dataset (two in K.2), and Bank's 115x reflects having only 20 clients / 380 anchor slots.

Noticed: the whole-client T = 0 path is essentially MUFC's server-only retraining with demographic reweighting (the authors say so). The new theory is mostly about initialization quality and replay exactness, not asymptotic deletion-time bounds like Ginart et al. or MUFC.

Noticed: exactness depends on bit-exact engineering (fixed-point encoding, exact rational sampling, canonical ordering). An implementation detail (pickle-restored array descriptors) changed a feature-sum reduction speed by 5-6x, which shows how fragile timing comparisons are.

Noticed: Adult/Credit raw-data provenance is incomplete (processed inputs only). An initial reporting error swapped Phi and G (corrected in App J.1). The authors also report using generative AI extensively, including for proofs (partially Lean-checked).
future_work: Implied: make the multi-group (m > 2) map canonical, with exact or certified fair updates, beyond the bounded Frank-Wolfe prototype.
Implied: measure networked deployments with secure aggregation, stragglers, dropouts, durable state and physical purge.
Implied: support sequential deletions at positive refinement budgets (cache maintenance or reconstruction) and longer or adaptive request sequences.
Implied: richer caches (e.g. Yinyang/Elkan-style bounds) or more stable samplers that let certification cover more work.
Implied: distributional guarantees for adaptively chosen requests (Ullah-Arora model-and-state targets).
papers.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: This is the graph's most direct bridge between MUFC-style federated clustering unlearning, Ginart-style exact deletion, and fairness. Its key design lesson for efficient exact unlearning is to keep cached summaries independent of any global normalization (here 1/n_g), so a deletion only changes cheap server-side reweighting and never invalidates untouched work, much like SISA's untouched shards. It provides reusable proof tools: a slice-wise D^2-sampling plus Minkowski composition argument for proportion-independent guarantees, an induction showing that exact signed patches of additive statistics reproduce retraining, and certificate soundness and tightness results. It is also an honest negative result: exact replay alone saves little when later iterative rounds must rescan all data, and same-seed D^2 sampling is discontinuous, so a single deletion can force Omega(n) wasted work under the studied policy. For a student this sets a concrete benchmark to beat: per-record exact unlearning for federated (fair) k-means with T > 0 that is clearly faster than 1.06x retraining.
open_questions: Design a deletion-stable seeded sampler for D^2/k-means++ seeding, such as per-record persistent exponential/Gumbel keys or priority sampling, whose selections rarely change when one record is deleted. It must keep same-seed exactness and avoid the Lemma 10/Prop 11 instability so that certificates actually save work.

Achieve sublinear exact replay for T > 0 refinement rounds by combining group-cell statistics with DC-k-means-style hierarchical partitions or SISA-style slicing of refinement, and analyze the quality vs deletion-time trade-off with an amortized bound.

Give a deletion-time analysis of the expected per-record unlearning cost for SplitGroup-2k (in the style of MUFC's Theorem 5.4 or Ginart's amortized bounds), since the paper gives only work bounds and conditional stability results.

Integrate secure aggregation (e.g. MUFC's SCMA) and privacy for group-separated summaries. Group anchors reveal group membership and can equal raw records at gamma = 0, so measure the communication and leakage costs of exact replay.

Extend exact replay to multi-group and intersectional fairness with an exact or certified fair update and per-group guarantees, testing whether replay stays efficient as m grows (the bound degrades linearly in m).

Combine demographic social fairness with client-level fairness (as in p-FClus, MFC or FedShard's efficiency fairness) under unlearning: when one client withdraws, can both group costs and client costs and burdens stay balanced?
Compare exact replay with approximate or certified unlearning for fair federated clustering (e.g. (eps, delta)-indistinguishable deletions), including guarantees for adaptively chosen requests.

adhikari2025-uncle.ev: 'Subsequent learning operations lead to unlearned tasks relapsing'

nodes.description: Assigns per-shard training rounds within an empirically set range [T0*, T1*], inversely to the variance of client contributions in the shard.

nodes.label: Vector Bernstein inequality
nodes.description: A concentration inequality bounding the probability that the average of independent bounded zero-mean random vectors deviates from zero in norm.

nodes.label: Whole-client summary replay exactness (Prop 13)

FedShard is cited as addressing client efficiency/performance fairness in federated unlearning. This paper's fairness is a demographic worst-group clustering cost and explicitly claims nothing about fair client computation burdens.

related.note: SISA cites Ginart et al. (ref [36]) under 'decremental learning'. It credits them with a formal deletion definition and noting that deletion and privacy are orthogonal, but doubts that Q-k-means generalizes (G5) or scales (G6) beyond k-means.
Studies and post-processes ensembles produced by SISA, without slicing.
Adds an inference-time fairness layer on top of SISA's constituent predictions.
Cited in related work, where it is grouped with approximate unlearning, even though its k-means deletion algorithms are exact.
Adapts SISA's sharded, isolated retraining to FL. Shards are merged over stages instead of ensembled, and no central access to raw data is needed.
CLU baseline at 100% tunable; MIA up to 0.67; best Acco on CIFAR task 1 (76.83).

UnCLe (cited as [36]) is one of five CLU baselines at 100% tunable parameters. BID-LoRA criticizes it as task-level only and as needing a hypernetwork trained from scratch rather than fine-tuning a pretrained model like DeiT. UnCLe still achieves the best CIFAR task-1 Acco (76.83).

DC-Kmeans from Ginart et al. is adapted to the FC setting (computation tree height 2, leaves = clients) as the main unlearning baseline. MUFC gets 6-164x vs DC-KM's 2-9x speed-up under random removals. Experiment repetitions follow Ginart et al.

Appendix G contrasts Alg. 3 with Q-k-means: Q-k-means relies on quantized-mean stability and costs O(R^2 K^3 T^2 d^2.5 / eps), with no removal-time guarantee unless randomly initialized, versus O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d) for MUFC. MUFC also borrows quantization ideas (random shifts, footnote 2) and the UK Biobank motivation.
Cited as a sharding-based exact unlearning method. MUFC achieves exactness through sampling-based seeding instead of sharding.
Main multi-shot baseline on k-means; comparable on non-overlapping synthetic data, worse elsewhere.
Aims for MFC's independence from data distribution and its fairness byproduct without multiple rounds; comes from the same IIT Ropar group.
Both pool local centers at a server, but MUFC supports exact removal with secure aggregation while p-FClus has no deletion mechanism or secure aggregation.
MFC is one of the two federated baselines on k-means; p-FClus beats it on µ and max in most settings, but MFC has the best σ on FEMNIST (0.311 vs 0.364).
Cited (as Pan et al. 2022 arXiv) only in Conclusion as future work: 'analyzing the effects of unlearning in clustering' as clients join and leave. No technical use.

Both give exact deletion through partitioning and isolation. Ginart's DC-k-means divide-and-conquer tree is closely related to SISA sharding, and Ginart's deletion-efficiency notion complements SISA's expected retraining cost analysis.

Reverse direction: FairSISA builds on SISA, adding ensemble post-processing to fix the unfairness that SISA sharding can introduce. SISA itself warns that grouping likely-deleters into shards may harm fair predictions.
Reverse direction (inferred from the title): FedShard brings SISA-style sharding into federated unlearning and adds efficiency and performance fairness across clients.
Both pursue exact, efficient unlearning that avoids full retraining; MUFC does it for federated clustering, and SISA is a standard reference point (inferred).
UnCLe studies unlearning in continual learning. SISA's slice-wise incremental training with checkpoints is a natural exact-unlearning reference when data arrives in stages (inferred).

BID-LoRA targets parameter-efficient continual learning and unlearning. LoRA-style adapters could cut SISA's per-slice checkpoint storage and per-shard retraining cost (inferred, not stated in either paper).

Both study fairness side effects of shard-based unlearning. FedShard targets client-level efficiency and performance fairness in federated unlearning, while FairSISA targets group (equalized-odds) fairness of centralized SISA ensembles.
Another fairness-focused paper in the set, but in federated clustering with a different fairness notion; FairSISA's post-processing does not apply directly to it.
Parameter-efficient (LoRA) unlearning could remove the per-slice checkpoint storage cost that made FairSISA drop SISA's slicing for LLMs.

Both combine sharded exact unlearning with fairness. FairSISA targets group fairness (e.g. equalized odds) of SISA ensembles, while FedShard targets client-level performance and cost fairness of unlearning itself.
Both do exact, efficient client-level unlearning in federated settings (MUFC for federated clustering, FedShard for supervised FL). FedShard's Mp/Me fairness metrics could audit MUFC.

Ginart et al.'s divide-and-conquer DC-k-means uses a tree of sub-problems where a deletion only reruns the affected leaf-to-root path. FedShard's hierarchical shard tree applies the same idea to federated deep learning.
Both study client-level fairness in federated settings. FedShard contrasts itself with clustered FL, which lacks a unified global model for exact unlearning.
MeCo's federated continual learning on edge systems faces clients joining and leaving. FedShard's sharded caching and fairness metrics show how departures could be unlearned fairly there.

Both target joint continual learning and unlearning. UnCLe generates full task networks with a hypernetwork and unlearns by noise alignment, whereas BID-LoRA uses parameter-efficient LoRA modules. UnCLe's Spill/Relapse metrics and baselines are natural comparison points.

UnCLe argues that isolating parameters (as in SISA-style sharding or CLPU per-task models) gives exact unlearning but grows storage. It instead shares one hypernetwork and accepts approximate, data-free unlearning. SISA is not cited.

MeCo addresses knowledge-efficient federated continual learning without an unlearning operation. UnCLe's embedding-addressable, data-free task unlearning is a candidate mechanism for adding unlearning to such FCL systems.

FedShard pursues efficient federated unlearning via sharded retraining, which is exact-style and data-dependent. UnCLe performs centralized, data-free approximate task unlearning by editing a hypernetwork.

SISA gives exact unlearning through sharded retraining, whereas BID-LoRA is approximate, class-level and adapter-based, and also learns new classes. SISA-style isolation of per-request adapters is a natural route to exact CLU. Not cited.

Both target parameter- and knowledge-efficient continual adaptation for resource-constrained deployment. BID-LoRA's forget pathway suggests how an unlearning direction could be added to (federated) continual learning. Not cited.
Ginart et al. formalize exact data deletion and deletion efficiency. BID-LoRA's CLU criteria are purely accuracy/oracle-based, with no distributional deletion guarantee. Not cited.

MeCo isolates task knowledge in per-(client, task) heads stored as separate pool entries, which resembles SISA's isolation; with provenance and retrieval tracking, deleting a client/task could become a constituent-level removal. MeCo has no deletion mechanism and its Eq. 9 cross-client mixing breaks isolation.

Both index task-specific knowledge with task embeddings in continual learning; UnCLe adds task unlearning, which MeCo's knowledge pool lacks, so it suggests how pool entries could support task-level forgetting.

BID-LoRA keeps per-task knowledge in parameter-efficient adapters for joint continual learning and unlearning; MeCo's small task-specific heads play a similar modular role but have no unlearning path.

MeCo's FedAvg-aggregated, meta-learned shared encoder u entangles every client's contribution; honouring a client-deletion request would need a federated-unlearning scheme like FedShard's sharded, efficiency-aware approach.

Ginart et al.'s deletion-efficiency principles (modularity, few dependencies per deletion) give a design target for an unlearnable MeCo knowledge pool, where currently one head can propagate into many others.

SISA (2021) also targets exact unlearning cheaper than full retraining. Its sharding and isolation scale up this paper's modularity principle (DC-k-means' random leaves) to deep networks. To my knowledge SISA discusses Ginart et al. as prior work; this 2019 paper cannot cite SISA.

MUFC takes exact unlearning for k-means-style clustering into the federated setting. Its clients-plus-server aggregation of local centroids resembles depth-1 DC-k-means. Whether MUFC adopts this paper's definitions or baselines cannot be checked from this paper, which came earlier.

MFC's federated clustering, in which clients cluster locally and the server clusters the uploaded centroids, has the same structure as depth-1 DC-k-means with clients as leaves. DC-k-means' leaf-to-root deletion is therefore a direct template for adding unlearning to MFC.
Fair federated clustering through personalization has no deletion mechanism. Q-k-means quantization and DC-style modular recomputation are candidate tools for making it deletion-efficient.
FairSISA builds on SISA-style exact unlearning (a descendant of this paper's modularity principle) and adds fairness post-processing to the shard ensemble.
FedShard pursues efficient exact-style federated unlearning through sharding, extending the modularity principle. Its efficiency fairness goal relates to this paper's amortized-cost view of deletion.
UnCLe handles unlearning in continual learning. This paper supplies the exact-deletion definition and amortized-cost framework against which such approximate deep-learning methods can be judged.
BID-LoRA confines task or data influence to small adapter modules, a parameter-level form of the modularity principle proposed here.
MeCo (federated continual learning on edge systems) has no deletion component. This paper's principles of modularity and quantized, stable shared knowledge suggest how one could be added.
Both study efficient federated unlearning. MUFC targets federated K-means clustering with exact guarantees; FedShard targets supervised FL with sharding and fairness.
MFC is a multishot federated clustering approach, while MUFC is one-shot (like K-FED). MUFC's unlearning-friendly seeding and SCMA could be explored for multishot FC.
FFC adds fairness and personalization to federated clustering. Combining it with MUFC-style exact unlearning is an open direction.

Both cluster pooled local centers at a server. MUFC adds quantized, securely aggregated local summaries and exact client or point removal, whereas p-FClus adds per-client personalization and a σ fairness metric. Combining them (unlearnable personalized federated clustering) is a natural project.

Not cited. Q-k-means (quantized centers stable under deletion) or DC-k-means could replace p-FClus's local and server clustering, so most point deletions leave C^(z) and C^g unchanged and no re-broadcast is needed.

Not cited. Both care about client-level fairness in federated systems. FedShard's efficiency and performance fairness for unlearning could be measured with p-FClus's σ and max metrics after client deletion.
Not cited. FairSISA targets group fairness (e.g., equalized odds) under unlearning in supervised LLMs, whereas p-FClus's fairness is uniformity of clustering cost across clients.

Not cited. Clients act like natural SISA shards: a client's influence on C^g passes only through its k uploaded centers, so client-level retraining is cheap (re-cluster Z·k points). Personalized centers on other clients, however, still need re-tuning.

Both do federated k-means data clustering and both build on k-FED (Dennis et al.). MUFC is one-shot with secure compressed aggregation and supports client/data unlearning; MFC is multishot with no unlearning, so a removal would force all shots to be re-run.

Q-k-means (quantization) and DC-k-means (divide-and-conquer tree) give deletion-efficient k-means. MFC's initial shot has a DC-tree shape with clients as leaves, but its multishot loop couples all leaves; quantizing theta_max and mu is a natural way to make MFC deletion-efficient.

Both are federated data clustering from what appears to be the same IIT Ropar group (Shivam Gupta, Shweta Jain). MFC's device-level cost fairness and its stated future work on fairness lead directly into fair federated clustering via personalization.
SISA-style checkpointing (store S and mu after every shot) and client sharding could limit retraining after a deletion in MFC to the rounds after a client's first contribution.

FedShard targets federated unlearning with efficiency and performance fairness. MFC's per-device cost std/IQR is a clustering analogue of performance fairness and could be used to check whether unlearning in federated clustering is fair.
MUFC's two-level seeding/server clustering and its server-only retraining for client removal are the closest architectural precedents.
Q-k-means stability checks and DC-k-means path recomputation precede its stability checks and reuse.
Sharded retraining is cited only as a different deletion procedure.
FedShard targets client efficiency/performance fairness; here fairness is demographic group cost, not fair client burden.

MUFC (with shared co-author Saurav Prakash) is the closest precedent. Its two-level k-means++ seeding/server clustering, secure aggregation and server-only retraining after client removal (Sec 5.3, Alg 4) are reused; the T=0 whole-client result (Prop 13) is explicitly a specialization, not a new theorem. New here: group-separated summaries with global demographic normalization, exact replay of fair refinement rounds, and showing that MUFC's single-summary design adapted to the fair objective (Merged-1k) loses Theta(kappa). MUFC's reported 84x is called not directly comparable.

Both study exact deletion for k-means. Ginart's Q-k-means (quantized centroids, stability tests) and DC-k-means (recompute affected tree paths) are cited as centralized precedents of the certificate-based stability checks and touched-slice reuse; this paper moves to federated socially fair k-means and same-seed pointwise exactness.

SISA's sharded retraining is cited only as a different deletion procedure. Conceptually, reusing untouched (client, group) slice summaries and recomputing touched ones mirrors SISA's untouched shards, but nothing is ensembled and the output equals full retraining.

FedShard is cited as addressing client efficiency/performance fairness in federated unlearning. This paper's fairness is a demographic worst-group clustering cost and explicitly claims nothing about fair client computation burdens.

p-FClus is not cited (the cited 'Gupta et al., 2025' is a different ARCANE k-means++ exact cluster unlearning paper). p-FClus equalizes per-client clustering cost, whereas this paper equalizes demographic group-average cost across clients and adds exact unlearning.

MFC is not cited. Both are federated k-means with client summaries and multiple rounds. MFC targets client-level cost fairness and heterogeneity without deletion; this paper targets demographic social fairness plus exact replay unlearning.

Not cited, but both study fairness and exact unlearning together. FairSISA post-processes a SISA ensemble for supervised group fairness; this paper builds the fair objective into federated clustering and keeps exact replay. Both cite Oesterling et al.'s fair machine unlearning.

threads.title: Delete by isolation: shards, trees and adapters
threads.blurb: Keep each data point's influence inside one small part of the model, so a deletion only rebuilds that part.
body: SISA splits the training set into shards and trains one model per shard. Deleting a point retrains only the shard that held it, starting from the slice checkpoint saved just before that point was added. Ginart's DC-k-means does the same for clustering: data goes into random leaves that are merged up a tree, so a deletion recomputes one leaf-to-root path.

FedShard carries the idea into federated learning, with clients as shards in a merge tree. FairSISA shows the price: more shards mean weaker constituent models and sometimes less fair predictions. BID-LoRA and MeCo isolate at the parameter level instead, with a separate forget adapter or per-task heads.

MUFSC keeps a separate summary for every (client, group) slice. A deletion only rebuilds the slices it touches, the same way SISA leaves untouched shards alone, but the result equals full retraining rather than an ensemble.

threads.title: Four ways to prove a deletion is exact
threads.blurb: Isolation, stability, lazy resampling and same-seed replay all make the updated model match retraining, at very different costs.
body: Ginart et al. define exact deletion: after a point is removed, the model must have the same distribution as one retrained without it. SISA uses the same definition, and the other exact methods here are judged against it.

Isolation (SISA, FedShard, DC-k-means) is exact because the untouched parts never saw the point. Stability (Q-k-means) is exact because quantized centroids rarely change when one point leaves, so most deletions cost nothing. Lazy resampling (MUFC) is exact because a k-means++ seed depends on a removed point only if that point was picked, which happens with probability about K/n.

Replay (MUFSC) is exact because training is rerun with the same random seed, reusing every cached summary the deletion did not touch; exact integer statistics make the patched result identical to retraining. Its own analysis shows the catch: with seeded k-means++ sampling, one deletion can change later random choices and waste a linear amount of work.

For the theory side of the project this is the core toolbox: SISA's expected retraining cost formulas, Ginart's deletion efficiency and amortized runtime, MUFC's conditional-probability exactness proof (Lemma 5.1), and MUFSC's replay-exactness induction (Theorem 5).

threads.title: k-means, where the proofs are possible
threads.blurb: Three papers delete from k-means with guarantees. Two others do federated k-means with no deletion at all.
body: Clustering is simple enough to analyse end to end, which is why the most rigorous unlearning results in this set are about k-means. Ginart et al. give Q-k-means and DC-k-means with deletion-time bounds. MUFC extends exact deletion to federated k-means with secure aggregation. MUFSC, from the same line of work as MUFC, adds a fairness objective and exact same-seed replay.

MFC and p-FClus are federated clustering methods from the same IIT Ropar group, and neither supports deletion. Their first step (cluster locally, then cluster the uploaded centres) has the same two-level shape as DC-k-means and MUFC. Adding an unlearning mechanism to them is a concrete open problem; MFC's later rounds and p-FClus's personalised centres are what make it hard.

threads.title: Learning and forgetting in a stream
threads.blurb: When unlearning requests arrive between learning tasks, new failures appear: relapse, spill and knowledge leakage.
body: UnCLe and BID-LoRA both handle an interleaved stream of learn and unlearn requests. UnCLe generates each task's weights with a hypernetwork and forgets a task without any data by pulling its generated weights toward noise. BID-LoRA keeps three LoRA adapters (retain, new, forget) and pushes forgotten-class embeddings away from everything it keeps.

Both papers show that offline unlearning methods break in this setting. Forgotten tasks come back after later training (relapse), and kept tasks get damaged (spill, knowledge leakage). MeCo is federated continual learning with no unlearning at all; it shows where a forgetting step would have to go: the server's knowledge pool and the shared encoder.

threads.title: Who pays for unlearning? Fairness in four senses
threads.blurb: Fair predictions across groups, fair unlearning cost across clients, fair clustering cost across clients, and fair clustering cost across demographic groups.
body: FairSISA measures equalized odds: does a SISA ensemble treat sensitive groups differently? It can, and a cheap post-processing step repairs it. FedShard asks something else: when a client leaves, does every remaining client pay a similar unlearning cost and lose similar accuracy? It defines two metrics for that.

MFC and p-FClus measure how unevenly clustering cost falls across clients, but never unlearn. MUFSC is the only paper here that keeps a fairness objective exact under deletion: it minimises the worst demographic group's average cost and replays training exactly when records or whole clients leave. Its fairness is about demographic groups, not clients, so client-level fairness under unlearning is still open.

threads.title: Federated: the data never leaves the client
threads.blurb: Six papers are federated. FedShard, MUFC and MUFSC unlearn; the other three are open candidates.
body: In federated learning the server never sees raw data, so the unit of deletion is often a whole client. FedShard, MUFC and MUFSC give exact federated unlearning: FedShard for neural networks through a client merge tree, MUFC for k-means through resampled seeds and secure aggregation, and MUFSC for fair k-means through per-(client, group) summaries and same-seed replay.

MeCo, MFC and p-FClus are federated methods with no deletion step. Non-IID data, communication cost and privacy leakage run through all five papers, and any unlearning step added to the last three would have to respect them.

threads.title: How do you show forgetting worked?
threads.blurb: Exact methods prove it. Approximate methods measure it with forget and retain accuracy, membership inference and speed-up.
body: Exact methods (SISA, FedShard, Ginart, MUFC, MUFSC) prove the result matches retraining, then report the speed-up over retraining. Approximate methods (UnCLe, BID-LoRA) can only measure: accuracy on forgotten data should fall to chance, accuracy on kept data should hold, and a membership-inference attack should not tell forgotten points from unseen ones.

UnCLe reports membership-inference success near 50% for almost every method in its setting, so the attack barely separates them. In BID-LoRA, switching off the forget adapter before merging brings forget accuracy back to about 70%. Both are reasons to compare against a model retrained from scratch, not only against these metrics.

MUFSC is a good model for honest reporting. It checks 810 replays against fresh retraining value for value, separates algorithm time from end-to-end time, and reports that its per-record deletion is only about 1.06× faster than retraining.

overview.lede: Each dark pill is one of the papers. The coloured marks around it are the ideas it defines, uses or measures. Ideas that several papers share sit between them and hold the folders together.
overview.howto: Folder 1 is about sharding-based exact unlearning and what it does to fairness. Folder 2 combines continual learning with unlearning. Folder 3 is clustering: deleting points from k-means, and federated k-means with no deletion yet. Folder 4 is one new paper that joins folders 1 and 3: exact unlearning for federated, socially fair k-means. Dashed arrows are real citations between the papers. Pick a thread to light up a line of ideas that crosses folders.

directions.intro: What the eleven papers add up to for a project on efficient unlearning algorithms with both theory and implementation. This is an interpretation across the papers, not something any one of them says.

camps.title: Exact unlearning
camps.text: After a deletion, the model has the same distribution as one retrained without that data. These papers prove it, then show it costs less than retraining.

camps.title: Approximate unlearning
camps.text: Forgetting is measured, not proved: forget and retain accuracy, and membership-inference attacks. Both papers expose weak spots. In BID-LoRA, switching off the forget adapter before merging brings the forgotten classes back to about 70% accuracy.

directions.campsNote: A project with “theory” in its title fits the exact camp best.

mechanisms.name: Isolation
mechanisms.idea: Each data point influences only one part of the model, so only that part is retrained.

mechanisms.name: Stability
mechanisms.idea: The model rarely changes when one point leaves, so most deletions cost nothing.
mechanisms.tool: Bound on the chance that a deletion changes the output (Q-k-means)

mechanisms.name: Lazy resampling
mechanisms.idea: Redo work only if the deleted point was actually used.

mechanisms.name: Same-seed replay
mechanisms.idea: Rerun training with the same random seed, reusing every cached piece the deletion did not touch.
mechanisms.tool: Induction showing exact patches of additive statistics reproduce retraining (MUFSC Thm 5)

directions.mechNote: A new exact algorithm will almost always be one of these four, or a mix of them.

tradeoffs.v: SISA's speedup only holds while deletion requests stay below about 3× the number of shards. On ImageNet it loses about 19 points of top-5 accuracy.

Deleting a whole client can be cheap (MUFSC: 35.8× faster than retraining with no refinement rounds), while deleting single records barely helps (about 1.06×), because later refinement rounds rescan all the data.
More shards can make predictions less fair (FairSISA). In federated unlearning, some clients pay much more of the cost than others (FedShard).
A checkpoint for every slice is expensive. FairSISA dropped slicing for LLMs because of it.
In federated learning you usually delete a whole client. In continual learning, forgotten tasks come back (relapse) and kept tasks get damaged (spill).

gap.text: Folder 4 fills part of the gap the first three folders left. MUFSC (IIT Madras, with MUFC co-author Saurav Prakash) adds exact unlearning to federated fair clustering. It leaves clear next steps open: single-record deletion is only about 1.06× faster than retraining, client-level fairness under deletion is untouched, and MFC and p-FClus still have no deletion step. Whether this is the direction your professor intends is still worth confirming.

options.title: Fast per-record deletion for federated fair k-means
options.what: MUFSC makes deletion exact, but deleting a single record is only about 1.06× faster than retraining. Seeded k-means++ choices shift after a deletion, and every refinement round rescans all the data.
options.approach: Build a deletion-stable seeded sampler for k-means++ (the paper suggests per-record random keys), so most deletions leave the chosen centres unchanged. Combine it with DC-k-means-style partitions or Q-k-means quantization for the refinement rounds. MUFSC's public code is the baseline.
options.theoryText: Bound the expected per-record unlearning cost, in the style of MUFC's Theorem 5.4 or Ginart's amortized runtime, while keeping same-seed exactness.

options.title: Exact unlearning for multi-round federated clustering
options.what: One-shot MUFC is cheap to unlearn, but MFC's later rounds tie every client to every other through the global centres.
options.approach: Save the server state after every round and quantize the uploaded centres (as Q-k-means does), so most deletions change nothing. MUFSC's exact replay of refinement rounds is a ready template.
options.theoryText: Prove a bound on the expected number of rounds a deletion forces you to recompute.

options.title: Client-fair clustering under unlearning
options.what: MUFSC keeps demographic-group fairness exact under deletion, but no paper checks whether deleting one client hurts the remaining clients unevenly (the fairness p-FClus and MFC care about).
options.approach: Remove a client by dropping its centres and re-clustering. Remove a point using stable or quantized local centres. Track the cost spread across clients before and after.
options.theoryText: Bound how far personalised centres move after a deletion, and when re-personalisation can be skipped.

options.title: Make MUFC fully incremental
options.what: MUFC's server reruns k-means++ and Lloyd's from scratch after every deletion, and clients skip Lloyd's to keep unlearning cheap.
options.approach: Apply the reseeding trick on the server as well, or allow Lloyd's iterations on clients while keeping exactness.
options.theoryText: Extend the Lemma 5.1 exactness argument and the expected removal-time bound.

options.title: Cost-fair SISA
options.what: In SISA, what a deletion costs depends on which shard and slice the point landed in.
options.approach: Assign shards and slices so the cost is spread evenly, using FedShard's efficiency-fairness metric.
options.theoryText: Mostly empirical, with SISA's cost formulas as the analysis tool.

options.title: Federated continual unlearning
options.what: MeCo learns tasks across clients but cannot forget any of them.
options.approach: Add a forgetting step using UnCLe's hypernetwork or BID-LoRA's adapters, and record what each client contributed to the knowledge pool.
options.theoryText: Little theory to build on; heavy deep-learning work.

recommendation.text: Start with direction 1. MUFSC is the closest existing work, its code is public (github.com/arareddy/mufsc), and it names its own weak spot: single-record deletion is barely faster than retraining. Direction 2 is a good fallback. Both run on a laptop and reuse the same baselines (retraining, DC-k-means, Q-k-means, MUFC), metrics (deletion time, worst-group cost, k-means cost) and datasets (Adult, Bank Marketing, Credit, ACS).
steps: Read MUFSC closely, alongside MUFC and Ginart: the three exact clustering-unlearning papers.
Run MUFSC's code and reproduce its whole-client (35.8× at T = 0) and single-record (about 1.06×) results.
Implement the baselines: retraining, Q-k-means, DC-k-means and MUFC's client-side seeding.
Prototype a deletion-stable k-means++ sampler and measure how often its choices change after one deletion.
Prove an expected per-record cost bound and compare against MUFSC's direct replay on Adult, Bank, Credit and ACS.
